zh:
有好几次，婧婧都觉得自己再也见不到明天的太阳了。
食物越来越少，大伙只能吃观音土甚至蛆虫，看着小猫还好端端地窝在营里头，有很多人都不干了。
"俺们都活不了，凭啥还能让猫活着？"说完，为首的大汉便一只手提着婧婧，另一只手拿着尖刀对着它。
每到这时候，就会有另一些人挡在婧婧面前。
"你懂啥咧？连小猫都能活下去，俺们这些大活人，有啥活不下去的？"
大汉听到这里，只好羞愧地把婧婧放下，摸一摸它日渐瘦弱的身体。然后用只有婧婧才能听到的声音说。
"唉，又委屈你了。俺要不演这一出……营里头又有好多人喊着活不下去了，让俺给个痛快。"
"能活，小猫能活，俺们，也能活下去的。"
en:
Many times, Jingjing thought she would never see the sun again.
Food was running low. People were forced to eat clay and even guanyin clay. Seeing a little cat still safe and sound in the camp, many grew resentful.
We're all dying! Why should a cat live? a big fellow shouted. He grabbed Jingjing in one hand and pointed a sharp knife at her with the other.
Every time, others would step in to protect her.
What do you know? If even a little cat can survive, why can't we?
Hearing this, the big fellow would lower Jingjing in shame and stroke her thinning fur. Then, in a voice only she could hear, he would whisper.
I'm sorry to put you through this again. If I didn't put on this show... so many in the camp would give up and ask me to end their misery.
You'll live. If a cat can live, so can we.

zh:
只剩最后一支箭了。
和人打赌把盘缠全都输光的时候他没害怕过，失手射中马蜂窝、被追得跳河的时候他没动摇过。
可此刻，站在这漆黑无边的山崖之间，冯继升握弓的手，竟控制不住地微微发抖。
眼前那靶子底下连着一整套庞然棘轮，若是射中，或许真能把他和身后这素未谋面的姑娘送出绝境。
可若射不中……
冯继升的目光不由自主滑向脚下。四周转动的棘轮构件如同有生命一般，吞吐着崖间的寒气。崖底深不可见，只有隐隐传来的流水声。
他不知这是何处，这位姑娘是谁，因何与自己一同困于此地。他只知道自己不能抛下她不管，独寻出路。于是冯继升想方设法，牵制机关，研究转轴——结果就是把两人都赔进了更深的绝路。

箭离弦而出。
分厘之差。冯继升听见箭羽被弹开的声音，几息之后，崖下传来微不可闻的落水声。
“对不住……姑娘，”冯继升还保持着放箭的姿势，声音有些干涩，“此番是冯某拖累你了。”
“你为何要去寻那墨山道？”姑娘忽然开口，问得冯继升有些摸不着头脑。
“说出来不怕姑娘笑话。”他苦笑，“你看此处，机关交错，自成险隘，虽无兵器之利，却将你我困得寸步难行。冯某一心追求的便是这等机关之术。若能将它用于弓箭之道，也许有一日天下人皆能能百步穿杨，拒敌千里……”
他说着说着，声音越来越低。他想过会被墨山道拒之门外，想过人家瞧不上他这野路子的本事，却独独没想过，自己会和箭一起，埋葬在这暗无天日的山崖间。
“你觉得，墨山道会收一个文津馆的弟子？”
“大道三千，殊途同归。从何处走，又如何走，真有那么重要吗？”冯继升望着石缝里漏下的一缕微光，喃喃说道，“我于弓箭一道，并无天赋。初学时，一百支箭里，也未必有几支能上靶。可我会一直紧盯靶心，分毫不移。一次不中，就再试一次；一百次不中，便试一百零一次……”

“可惜，我的箭，好像用完了。”
话音刚落，他眼前那道微光忽然消失，黑暗中，更深的黑影掠过，一只巨鸟挟带着风声冲向二人。
冯继升想也没想，大步跨上前，站在了那姑娘前面，握着弓柄的双手指节泛白。
巨鸟越来越近，二十米，十五米，十米……
生前能看到如此精妙绝伦的机关，他已死而无憾。
五米，三米……
……还是有点遗憾的。他的火箭还没研制出来，天下人也还没用上他造出来的弓箭。他还想去看看传闻中墨城的天工阁，田中的木牛……
正当他在心中默默与这一切作别时，巨鸟俯身掠他而过，一只木箭从它身上抖落，须臾间它又匿入黑夜。
或许方才哪只箭射中了它，这才惊动这只崖间巨鸟，冯继升如此想着，拾起了地上的箭。
紧盯靶心，分毫不移。
他没有犹豫，松开了弓弦。
大地颤动，崖内棘轮轰然转起，那颗差点停滞的心重新开始跳动。
还没待他反应过来，巨鸟便带着他飞上了山顶。
阳光从机关的裂隙洒向崖底，一只肖似巨鸟的机关小鸟轻轻落在了女子肩头。
她抬头看了看那崖上的身影。
“欢迎入山，冯师弟。”
en:
Only one arrow remained.

He had not flinched when he gambled away his travel money, nor had his resolve wavered when a stray arrow struck a hornet's nest and forced him to leap into a raging river.
But now, standing in the crushing dark of Gasping Cliff, Feng Jisheng's hand trembled with a slight, uncontrollable shudder as he gripped his bow.

Below the target before him lay a massive ratchet mechanism. A single hit might trigger the gears and hoist him and the stranger behind him out of this abyss. But if he missed...
Feng's gaze slipped downward. The rotating ratchet components around them seemed almost sentient, inhaling and exhaling the frigid mist of the ravine. The bottom of the cliff was invisible, leaving only the faint sound of flowing water.
He did not know where he was, who this girl was, or why she was trapped here with him. He only knew he could not abandon her to seek his own escape. Driven to action, he had scrambled to jam the gears and decipher the pivots. The result was dragging them both into an even deeper dead end.

The arrow flew.

A hair's breadth off. Feng heard the sound of the fletching being deflected. A few breaths later, a faint splash echoed from the abyss below.

"My apologies, Miss," Feng said. He was still frozen in his release stance, his voice dry. "It seems I have only succeeded in dragging you into my ruin."
"Why do you seek Mohist Hill?" The girl suddenly asked, catching him off guard.
"I am not afraid to make a fool of myself," he smiled bitterly. "Look at this place. The interlocking mechanisms form a natural stronghold. Even without the bite of cold steel, it has trapped us completely. That is exactly what I pursue."
"If I could apply such mechanics to archery, perhaps one day anyone could shoot true from a hundred paces and repel enemies from a thousand miles away..."

His voice trailed off into the dark. He had expected to be turned away by the Mohists, and he thought they might scoff at his unorthodox skills. Yet he never imagined he would end up buried alive in these sunless cliffs alongside his arrows.

"Do you think Mohist Hill would ever take in a disciple of the Inkbound Order?"
"Countless Ways all lead to the same Truth. Does where we start or how we walk truly matter so much?" Feng muttered, his eyes fixed on a thin thread of light seeping through the stone.
"I am no prodigy with a bow. When I first learned, barely a few out of a hundred arrows would hit the mark. But I would keep my eyes glued to the target and never look away. If I missed once, I would try again. If I missed a hundred times, I would try for the hundred and first."
"Alas, it seems my quiver is spent."

As soon as the words left his mouth, the faint light vanished. A deeper shadow swept through the darkness. A gargantuan bird lunged at them with the roar of a gale.
Without a second thought, Feng stepped forward. He placed himself between the girl and the creature, his knuckles turning white as he gripped the center of his bow.

The great bird drew closer. Twenty meters. Fifteen. Ten.
At least he had witnessed such an incredible mechanism before his death; he could die with no regrets.

Five. Three.

Well, perhaps one regret. His flaming arrows were not finished yet, and the world had not seen the bows he dreamed of making. He still longed to see the legendary Divinecraft Pavilion of Mohist City and the mechanical oxen tilling the fields.

Just as he was bidding a silent farewell to the world, the gargantuan bird swept over him. It shook loose a single wooden arrow from its body before vanishing back into the night.

Perhaps his stray arrow had struck the beast and roused this guardian of the cliffs. Thinking this, Feng retrieved the shaft from the ground. He fixed his gaze upon the heart of the target, not letting it waver by a hair's breadth.
He did not hesitate and released the bowstring.

The earth shuddered. Within the cliff, the ratchets roared to life with a thunderous grind, and his nearly stopped heart began to beat again. Before he could catch his breath, the great bird snatched him up and soared toward the summit.
Sunlight cascaded through the fissures of the mechanism, bathing the depths of the ravine. A small mechanical bird, resembling the giant guardian, landed gently on the woman's shoulder.
She looked up at the silhouette on the cliff.
"Welcome to the mountain, Feng."

清流既没，四海同悲。八司马者，义贯云霓。虽非同脉而肝胆照，纵存异志唯思言合。兼有支君雨檐，卓荦非常，世之瑰杰。其人也，正当壮年，筋骨若龙虎之健，神采如日月之华。虽处谪迁之困，而意气更凌霄汉。或运筹帷幄，可定乾坤之局；或挥毫泼墨，能醒混沌之世。每见其仗剑长啸，声震林樾，似鹏举九天之志未酬；抚琴高歌，音彻霄壤，若龙吟沧海之思不绝。笔锋未钝，犹能裂帛；文心长赤，岂畏秋霜？
同侪支翁怀远，胸怀济世之志，腹蕴经纶之才，然花甲已逾，鬓发尽凋，形神衰败，恐难胜苦辛。嗟乎！壮年犹可期鹏举，暮齿何堪瘴地劫？
呜呼！孤忠昭昭，可照千古；清流浩浩，足涤八荒。八君魂铸鼎彝，二支名镌星汉。昔阿房宫之烬，鉴秦骄奢；今八司马之谪，岂非天以警世耶？长风浩浩送君去——志若岿岳，岂湮瘴海？心比金石，终耀青史！后人哀之而鉴之，勿使忠魂长羁浊尘矣！
en:
Found in: Main Hall

With the virtuous fallen, all beneath heaven mourn. The righteousness of the Eight Exiled Officials pierces the clouds. Though not of one blood, their loyal hearts shine together; though their paths diverged, they sought accord through honest counsel.
Among them stands Lord Zhi Yuyan, peerless and transcendent, a jewel among men. In the prime of his years, his sinews hold the vigor of dragon and tiger, his spirit the radiance of sun and moon. Though cast into exile, his spirit only rose higher still. At times he could shape the fate of the realm from behind the curtain; at others, his brush could stir a world sunk in darkness. When he raises his sword and roars, the woods tremble, as if his ambition to soar into the Nine Heavens remains unfulfilled. When he plays the zither and sings, his song echoes between earth and sky, like a dragon's endless cry across the sea. His brush has not blunted, capable of tearing through silk; his noble heart burns steadfast, defying the autumn frost.
His companion, Elder Zhi Huaiyuan, holds the ambition to save the realm and the wisdom to govern. Yet past his sixtieth year, his temples frosted and his vitality waning, I fear he cannot endure this bitter hardship. Alas! A man in his prime may still hope to soar, but how can one in his twilight withstand the pestilent wilds?
Alas! Their pure loyalty shines through eternity; the surging righteous current purifies all lands. The souls of eight lords are cast in bronze; the names of the two Zhis are engraved among the stars. The ashes of Epang Palace once warned against Qin's extravagance. Does the exile of the Eight not serve as Heaven's warning to the world?
The great wind carries you onward. With resolve firm as mountains, how could you be swallowed by pestilent seas? With hearts forged like metal and stone, you shall forever shine in the annals of history! Let posterity mourn and take heed, never leaving loyal souls bound to sullied dust!

他在等谁共饮？又在期待些什么？思考许久，你决定拿出……
#Y【飞鸡图纸。】这是你和冯大哥的创新发明，你知道张万师没有见过，他一定会感兴趣的。#E
静静地将图纸放在了他的身边。张万师似醉似醒，似是捕捉到了封页上的字眼。他用手轻轻一勾，拿起整摞图纸，看了两眼，又丢到了一旁。他拍了拍手，桃靥剑姬优雅地将你请离了墨守之心。
“此路无知己，明珠莫暗投……你且去吧。”

今夜，他依然与明月对饮。
en:
Ever since witnessing Zhang Wanshi's Aquatic Spectacle, you have been haunted by the memory of his Swordsworn automaton.
Thus, you dive beneath the waves once more to pay him a visit. Zhang Wanshi remains in a stupor, lying drunk upon the ground. Yet, unlike before, two brimful wine cups now rest in front of him.
Who is he waiting to drink with? What is he longing for? After much thought, you decide to present...
#Y[Wooden chicken diagrams] This is an innovation from you and Feng Jisheng. Having never seen such a thing, Zhang Wanshi will definitely be interested.#E
You quietly place the diagrams by his side. Half-drunk and half-awake, Zhang Wanshi seems to catch a glimpse of the words upon the cover. With a casual flick of his finger, he lifts the stack of diagrams, spares them a glance, and casts them aside. He claps his hands, and the Rosy-Faced Swordsworn elegantly ushers you out from the Changeless Heart.
"There's no one here who truly understands you. Don't let your gifts go to waste... You should move on."

Tonight, he drinks with the bright moon once more.

zh:
在记忆中的家乡，每个人都能跳起舞来。
当姑娘们扬手起舞时，银铃叮当，欢笑不绝——那是永不褪色的声音。
阿依奴最喜欢铃铛手串了，带上了铃铛手串，想怎么跳舞就怎么跳，连脚底扬起的尘土都裹着蜜糖似的甜。

后来她遇见那位比明月还夺目的公主。可当公主行走时，鬓边的饰品轻晃的声响明明和铃铛一样悦耳，怎么戴着铃铛的公主却不开心呢？
"这叫步摇，不是自由起舞的银铃。"公主指尖拂过垂下的金穗，"它时刻提醒我身上的责任。" 

小阿依奴听不懂，她想着，既然公主不开心，那就把代表快乐的铃铛送给公主。
公主蹲下身，鎏金步摇与银铃在风中相撞。"你的快乐要自己攥在手心。"她将铃铛重新带回阿依奴的手腕。她喜欢这个小姑娘的笑容和舞步，她希望凉州的百姓都能安居乐业。

年少的阿依奴拿着铃铛，认真地答应公主，她会一直快乐，永远不会哭泣。
en:
In the memories of home, everyone could dance. 
When girls raised their hands, silver bells chimed, laughter unending—a sound that never faded. 
Aynur loved bell bracelets most. With them, she could dance freely, even the dust at her feet sweet like honey. 

Later, she met a princess even more dazzling than the moon. But when the princess walked, the ornaments at her temples swayed with the same pleasant sound as bells—why wasn't the princess happy? 
"These are step-shakers, not free-dancing silver bells." The princess touched the hanging golden tassels. "They remind me of my duty."

Little Aynur didn't understand. She thought: if the princess is unhappy, I'll give her my joyful bells. 
The princess knelt. Gilded step-shakers and silver bells chimed in the wind. "Your joy must stay in your own hands." She returned the bells to Aynur's wrist. She loved the girl's smile and dance, hoping all in Liangzhou could live in peace. 

Young Aynur took the bells and solemnly promised: she would always be happy, never cry.

en:
Years ago, a Mohist elder took five disciples. Because all five studied the art of precision mechanisms and created many strange objects, they were known as the "Five Wonders" by the other disciples. The last of them had escaped the war outside and happened to flee into Hidden Mountain. His heart was filled with unquenchable hatred, and he used his knowledge to create various venomous insects, intending to seek revenge once his studies were complete. Seeing his improper intent, the elder never taught him his full knowledge.
Before the four senior disciples left on their travels, they created venomous mechanism insects to lure and kill the venomous creatures in the mountains using special sounds. They did this to prove to their master that venomous mechanisms could also be used for good. While co-creating the Five Venoms, they quietly passed the final secrets of precision mechanisms to their junior brother.
The Inkpincer Scorpion was one of the Five Venoms, created by the senior brother, Su Yuandao.
Those with strength help others, those with wealth share with others, and those with wisdom teach others. Be content with simplicity, and stay true to the faith.

zh:
【儒行第四十一】

鲁哀公问于孔子曰：“夫子之服，其儒服与？”孔子对曰：“丘少居鲁，衣逢掖之衣，长居宋，冠章甫之冠。丘闻之也：君子之学也博，其服也乡；丘不知儒服。”
哀公曰：“敢问儒行。”孔子对曰：“遽数之不能终其物，悉数之乃留，更仆未可终也。”
哀公命席。孔子侍曰：“儒有席上之珍以待聘，夙夜强学以待问，怀忠信以待举，力行以待取，其自立有如此者。
儒有衣冠中，动作慎，其大让如慢，小让如伪，大则如威，小则如愧，其难进而易退也，粥粥若无能也。其容貌有如此者。
儒有居处齐难，其坐起恭敬，言必先信，行必中正，道涂不争险易之利，冬夏不争阴阳之和，爱其死以有待也，养其身以有为也。其备豫有如此者。
儒有不宝金玉，而忠信以为宝；不祈土地，立义以为土地；不祈多积，多文以为富。难得而易禄也，易禄而难畜也，非时不见，不亦难得乎？非义不合，不亦难畜乎？先劳而后禄，不亦易禄乎？其近人有如此者。
儒有委之以货财，淹之以乐好，见利不亏其义；劫之以众，沮之以兵，见死不更其守；鸷虫攫搏不程勇者，引重鼎不程其力；往者不悔，来者不豫；过言不再，流言不极；不断其威，不习其谋。其特立有如此者。
儒有可亲而不可劫也；可近而不可迫也；可杀而不可辱也。其居处不淫，其饮食不溽；其过失可微辨而不可面数也。其刚毅有如此者。
……
en:
【The Conduct of the Scholar (Chapter 41)】

Duke Ai of Lu asked Confucius, saying, "Is the dress you wear, Master, that of a scholar?" Confucius replied, "When I was young, I lived in Lu and wore a robe with wide sleeves; when I grew up, I lived in Song and wore a cap of Zhangfu. I have heard that a gentleman's learning is broad, and his dress follows the customs of his native place. I do not know what the dress of a scholar is."
Duke Ai said, "May I ask about the conduct of a scholar?" Confucius replied, "To enumerate them hastily, one cannot exhaust all their details; to recount them fully would require a long stay, and even with the attendants taking turns, it could not be finished."
Duke Ai ordered a mat to be spread. Confucius, attending him, said, "A scholar has treasures on his mat to await employment; he studies diligently day and night to await questioning; he cherishes loyalty and faithfulness to await recommendation; he exerts himself in practice to await selection. Such is his self-establishment.
A scholar is proper in his dress and demeanor, careful in his actions. In great concessions he appears as if indifferent; in small concessions, as if hypocritical. In great matters he seems awe-inspiring; in small matters, as if ashamed. He is hard to advance but easy to retire, appearing weak and as if without ability. Such is his appearance and manner.
A scholar is strict and solemn in his daily conduct. In sitting and rising, he is respectful. In speech, he must first be sincere; in action, he must be upright and correct. On the road, he does not contend for the advantage of easy or difficult paths; in winter and summer, he does not contend for the comforts of shade or warmth. He cherishes his death to await the right time, and nourishes his body to have something to accomplish. Such is his preparedness.
A scholar does not treasure gold and jade, but regards loyalty and faithfulness as treasures. He does not seek land, but establishes righteousness as his land. He does not seek great accumulation, but regards abundant learning as wealth. He is hard to obtain but easy to remunerate; easy to remunerate but hard to retain. If the time is not right, he does not appear—is this not being hard to obtain? If righteousness does not prevail, he does not associate—is this not being hard to retain? He labors first and then receives remuneration—is this not being easy to remunerate? Such is his approach to others.
A scholar may be entrusted with goods and wealth, or immersed in pleasures and likes, yet seeing profit, he does not impair his righteousness. He may be threatened by multitudes, or deterred by weapons, yet facing death, he does not change his principles. When fierce beasts attack, he does not measure his courage; when lifting heavy tripods, he does not measure his strength. He does not regret the past, nor anticipate the future. He does not repeat erroneous words, nor pursue rumors to the extreme. He does not relax his dignity, nor rehearse his schemes. Such is his singular standing.
A scholar may be approached with affection but cannot be coerced; may be drawn near but cannot be pressured; may be killed but cannot be humiliated. In his daily life, he is not extravagant; in his eating and drinking, he is not indulgent. His faults may be subtly pointed out but cannot be enumerated to his face. Such is his firmness and resoluteness.
……

zh: 锓木，雕版之工序也。上版既成，持刀循字迹刊刻。或铲地留墨，或剔空留白，使原稿字形凸显于版上，乃雕版印刷之精髓。古人执刀刻木，下刀需稳，进退有节。其法首在“发刀”，即初刻定边，然后“挑刀”去余屑，次以“打空”“锯边”收尾。一划刻成，万卷始生。
en:
Engraving was the core step of woodblock printing. Once the text had been transferred onto the block, the carver followed the written strokes with a knife, cutting away the blank areas and leaving the characters standing in relief.
A steady hand and precise control were essential. The process began with outlining the strokes, then clearing away the shavings, and finally hollowing out the larger blank spaces and trimming the edges. From a single carved block, countless copies could be printed.

zh:
小沙弥手记

疫气越来越重。
师父说，病不只会跟人走，也会跟水走。
江南井泉相通，沟渠暗连。
城外一口井坏了，城里一条渠也会坏。

师父请来镇水匠，下井寻水眼。
他们说，水脉像活物，有口，有眼，也有心。
水眼若开，污水便走。
水眼若压，疫气便困。
师父让我守住后山小门。

他说，不是拦人，是拦病。

我一直守着。

可现在，我也病了。
en:
Novice Monk's Note

The miasma grows heavier. Master said the sickness follows not only people, but also water.
In Jiangnan, all wells and springs are connected. The canals link in the dark. A tainted well outside the city will rot a canal inside it.
Master invited the Water Wardens to descend and find the water source. They said water is like a living being with a digestive system of its own.
If the water sources are left open, the foul water can leave. If the sources are sealed, the miasma is trapped.
Master told me to guard the small gate at the back mountain. He said it was not to keep people out, but to keep the sickness in.
I have kept watch the entire time.
But now, I am sick too.

Virtue is the foundation of nature, and music is the flower of virtue. Metal, stone, silk, and bamboo are the instruments of music. From the harmonious grand compositions of the Han Dynasty to the banquet music of the Tang, string and wind music have flourished for centuries. 
Many musicians skilled in these instruments roam the jianghu, playing both court music and village tunes. They express emotions through music and convey sentiments through melody. Should jianghu wanderers meet by chance and play a tune together, they might emulate Boya and Ziqi, becoming kindred spirits.

【有司第十七】

有司彻，扫堂。司宫摄酒。乃燅尸俎，卒燅，乃升羊、豕、鱼三鼎，无腊与肤，乃设扃鼏，陈鼎于门外，如初。
乃议侑于宾，以异姓。宗人戒侑。侑出，俟于庙门之外。司宫筵于户西，南面；又筵于西序，东面。尸与侑，北面于庙门之外，西上。主人出迎尸，宗人摈。主人拜，尸答拜。主人又拜侑，侑答拜。主人揖，先入门，右。尸入门，左；侑从，亦左。揖，乃让。主人先升自阼阶，尸、侑升自西阶，西楹西，北面东上。主人东楹东，北面拜至，尸答拜。主人又拜侑，侑答拜。
乃举，司马举羊鼎，司士举豕鼎、举鱼鼎，以入。陈鼎如初。雍正执一匕以从，雍府执二匕以从，司士合执二俎以从，司士赞者亦合执二俎以从。匕皆加于鼎，东枋。二俎设于羊鼎西，西缩。二俎皆于二鼎西，亦西缩。雍人合执二俎，陈于羊俎西，并皆西缩。覆二疏匕于其上，皆缩俎，西枋。
主人降，受宰几。尸、侑降，主人辞，尸对。宰授几，主人受，二手横执几，揖尸。主人升，尸、侑升，复位。主人西面，左手执几，缩之，以右袂推拂几三，二手横执几，进授尸于筵前。尸进，二手受于手间，主人退。尸还几，缩之，右手执外廉，北面奠于筵上，左之，南缩，不坐。主人东楹东，北面拜。尸复位，尸与侑皆北面答拜。主人降洗，尸、侑降，尸辞洗。主人对，卒洗，揖。主人升，尸、侑升，尸西楹西北面拜洗。主人东楹东北面奠爵答拜，降盥。尸、侑降，主人辞，尸对。卒盥。主人揖，升，尸、侑升。主人坐取爵，酌献尸。尸北面拜受爵，主人东楹东北面拜送爵。主妇自东房荐韭、菹、醢，坐奠于筵前，菹在西方。妇赞者执昌、苴、醢以授主妇。主妇不兴，受；陪设于南，昌在东方。兴，取笾于房，麷、蕡坐设于豆西，当外列，麷在东方。妇赞者执白、黑以授主妇。主妇不兴，受，设于初笾之南，白在西方；兴，退。乃升。司马朼羊，亦司马载。载右体，肩、臂、肫、胳、臑，正脊一、脡脊一、横脊一，短胁一、正胁一、代胁一，肠一、胃一、祭肺一，载于一俎。羊肉湆：臑折、正脊一、正胁一、肠一、胃一、哜肺一，载于南俎。司士朼豕，亦司士载，亦右体：肩、臂、肫、胳、臑，正脊一、脡脊一、横脊一，短胁一、正胁一、代胁一，肤五、哜肺一，载于一俎。侑俎：羊左肩、左肫、正脊一、胁一、肠一、胃一、切肺一，载于一俎。侑俎：豕左肩折、正脊一、胁一、肤三、切肺一，载于一俎。阼俎：羊肺一，祭肺一，载于一俎。羊肉湆：臂一、脊一、胁一、肠一、胃一、哜肺一，载于一俎。豕脀：臂一、脊一、胁一、肤三、哜肺一，载于一俎。主妇俎：羊左臑、脊一、胁一、肠一、胃一、肤一、哜羊肺一，载于一俎。司士朼鱼，亦司士载，尸俎五鱼，横载之，侑、主人皆一鱼，亦横载之，皆加膴祭于其上。卒升。宾长设羊俎于豆南，宾降。尸升筵自西方，坐，左执爵，右取韭、菹手耎于三豆，祭于豆间。尸取麷、蕡，宰夫赞者取白、黑以授尸。尸受，兼祭于豆祭。雍人授次宾疏匕与俎。受于鼎西，左手执俎左廉，缩之，却右手执匕枋，缩于俎上，以东面受于羊鼎之西。司马在羊鼎之东，二手执桃匕枋以挹湆，注于疏匕，若是者三。尸兴，左执爵，右取肺，坐祭之，祭酒，兴，左执爵。次宾缩执匕俎以升，若是以授尸。尸却手受匕枋，坐祭，哜之，兴，覆手以授宾。宾亦覆手以受，缩匕于俎上以降。尸席末坐啐酒，兴，坐奠爵，拜，告旨，执爵以兴。主人北面于东楹东，答拜。司马羞羊肉湆，缩执俎。尸坐奠爵，兴取肺，坐绝祭，哜之，兴，反加于俎。司马缩奠俎于羊湆俎南，乃载于羊俎，卒载俎，缩执俎以降。尸坐执爵以兴。次宾羞羊燔，缩执俎，缩一燔于俎上，盐在右。尸左执爵，受燔，手耎于盐，坐振祭，哜之，兴，加于羊俎。宾缩执俎以降。尸降筵，北面于西楹西，坐卒爵，执爵以兴，坐奠爵，拜，执爵以兴。主人北面于东楹东答拜。主人受爵。尸升筵，立于筵末。
……
en:
【Officers' Ceremony, Chapter Seventeen】

The officers clear away the offerings and sweep the hall. The palace steward adjusts the wine. Then the roasted meats on the stands are warmed; when done, the three tripods—lamb, pork, and fish—are brought up, without the dried meat or skin, and the crossbars and covers are set in place. The tripods are arranged outside the gate, as before.
Then the host consults with the guests about who shall assist the impersonator, choosing one of a different surname. The ancestral officer instructs the assistant. The assistant comes out and waits outside the temple gate. The palace steward lays out a mat to the west of the door, facing south; another mat is laid by the western wall, facing east. The impersonator and the assistant stand north of the temple gate, facing north, with the impersonator on the west. The host comes out to greet the impersonator, with the ancestral officer acting as usher. The host bows, and the impersonator returns the bow. The host then bows to the assistant, who returns the bow. The host makes a gesture of invitation and enters first, going to the right of the gate. The impersonator enters to the left of the gate; the assistant follows, also on the left. With a gesture, they yield precedence. The host ascends first by the eastern steps, while the impersonator and assistant ascend by the western steps, standing west of the western pillars, facing north, with the impersonator on the east. The host stands east of the eastern pillar, facing north, and bows in welcome; the impersonator returns the bow. The host again bows to the assistant, who returns the bow.
Then the offerings are lifted. The master of horses lifts the lamb tripod, the master of officers lifts the pork tripod and the fish tripod, and they enter. The tripods are arranged as before. The chief of the palace staff follows with one ladle, the palace steward follows with two ladles, and the master of officers follows carrying two stands together, while the assistant to the master of officers also follows carrying two stands together. The ladles are all placed on the tripods, with their handles pointing east. Two stands are set to the west of the lamb tripod, aligned north-south. Two stands are placed to the west of the other two tripods, also aligned north-south. The palace cook carries two stands together and sets them to the west of the lamb stand, all aligned north-south. Two open-work ladles are placed upside down on top, aligned with the stands, with handles pointing west.
The host descends to receive the armrest from the steward. The impersonator and assistant descend, and the host declines, but the impersonator responds. The steward hands the armrest to the host, who receives it with both hands, holding it horizontally, and bows to the impersonator. The host ascends, and the impersonator and assistant ascend, returning to their positions. The host, facing west, holds the armrest with his left hand, aligns it lengthwise, and with his right sleeve brushes it three times. Then, holding it horizontally with both hands, he advances and presents it to the impersonator before the mat. The impersonator advances, receives it with both hands between the host's hands, and the host withdraws. The impersonator turns the armrest, aligns it lengthwise, holds it by the outer edge with his right hand, and, facing north, places it on the mat, with the left side to the south, aligned north-south, without sitting. The host, east of the eastern pillar, faces north and bows. The impersonator returns to his position, and both the impersonator and assistant face north and return the bow. The host descends to wash, and the impersonator and assistant descend; the impersonator declines the washing. The host responds, finishes washing, and makes a gesture. The host ascends, and the impersonator and assistant ascend. The impersonator, west of the western pillar, faces north and bows for the washing. The host, east of the eastern pillar, faces north, sets down the goblet, returns the bow, and descends to wash his hands. The impersonator and assistant descend, the host declines, and the impersonator responds. When the washing is done, the host makes a gesture and ascends, and the impersonator and assistant ascend. The host sits, takes the goblet, and pours wine to offer to the impersonator. The impersonator, facing north, bows and receives the goblet, while the host, east of the eastern pillar, faces north and bows in sending it off. The host's wife, from the eastern chamber, presents chives, pickled vegetables, and sauces, sitting to place them before the mat, with the pickled vegetables to the west. The woman assistant holds the ginger, arrowroot, and sauce to give to the host's wife. The host's wife, without rising, receives them and sets them to the south, with the ginger to the east. Rising, she takes baskets from the chamber, and places the roasted wheat and hemp seeds, sitting, to the west of the bean dishes, aligned with the outer row, with the wheat to the east. The woman assistant holds the white and black offerings to give to the host's wife. The host's wife, without rising, receives them and sets them south of the first baskets, with the white to the west. Rising, she withdraws. Then the meats are brought up. The master of horses portions the lamb, and the master of horses also arranges it. The right side is arranged: shoulder, upper arm, rump, leg, and shank; one proper spine, one middle spine, one transverse spine; one short rib, one proper rib, one alternate rib; one intestine, one stomach, and one lung for offering—all arranged on one stand. The lamb in broth: the shank broken, one proper spine, one proper rib, one intestine, one stomach, and one lung for tasting—arranged on the southern stand. The master of officers portions the pork, and the master of officers also arranges it, also the right side: shoulder, upper arm, rump, leg, and shank; one proper spine, one middle spine, one transverse spine; one short rib, one proper rib, one alternate rib; five pieces of skin, and one lung for tasting—arranged on one stand. The assistant's stand: lamb left shoulder, left rump, one proper spine, one rib, one intestine, one stomach, and one sliced lung—arranged on one stand. The assistant's stand: pork left shoulder broken, one proper spine, one rib, three pieces of skin, and one sliced lung—arranged on one stand. The host's stand: one lamb lung and one offering lung—arranged on one stand. The lamb in broth: one upper arm, one spine, one rib, one intestine, one stomach, and one lung for tasting—arranged on one stand. The pork portion: one upper arm, one spine, one rib, three pieces of skin, and one lung for tasting—arranged on one stand. The host's wife's stand: lamb left shank, one spine, one rib, one intestine, one stomach, one piece of skin, and one lamb lung for tasting—arranged on one stand. The master of officers portions the fish, and the master of officers also arranges it. The impersonator's stand has five fish, arranged crosswise; the assistant and host each have one fish, also arranged crosswise, all with the belly meat placed on top as an offering. When the presentation is complete, the senior guest sets the lamb stand south of the bean dishes, and the guest descends. The impersonator ascends to the mat from the west, sits, holds the goblet with his left hand, and with his right hand takes the chives and pickled vegetables, rubs them in the three bean dishes, and offers them between the dishes. The impersonator takes the roasted wheat and hemp seeds, and the steward's assistant takes the white and black offerings to give to the impersonator. The impersonator receives them and offers them together with the bean offerings. The palace cook gives the open-work ladle and stand to the secondary guest. He receives them west of the tripod, holding the left edge of the stand with his left hand, aligning it lengthwise, and with his right hand holding the ladle handle, placing it lengthwise on the stand, and facing east, he receives them west of the lamb tripod. The master of horses, east of the lamb tripod, holds the handle of the skimmer with both hands to scoop the broth, pouring it into the open-work ladle, doing this three times. The impersonator rises, holds the goblet with his left hand, takes the lung with his right hand, sits, offers it, offers the wine, rises, and holds the goblet with his left hand. The secondary guest, holding the ladle and stand lengthwise, ascends and presents them to the impersonator in this manner. The impersonator, with the back of his hand, receives the ladle handle, sits, offers, tastes it, rises, and with the back of his hand hands it to the guest. The guest also receives it with the back of his hand, places the ladle lengthwise on the stand, and descends. The impersonator, at the end of the mat, sits, sips the wine, rises, sits, sets down the goblet, bows, announces that the wine is excellent, and rises holding the goblet. The host, facing north east of the eastern pillar, returns the bow. The secondary guest presents the lamb in broth, holding the stand lengthwise. The impersonator sits, sets down the goblet, rises, takes the lung, sits, tears it for the offering, tastes it, rises, and places it back on the stand. The secondary guest sets the stand lengthwise south of the lamb broth stand, then arranges it on the lamb stand, and when done, holds the stand lengthwise and descends. The impersonator sits, holds the goblet, and rises. The secondary guest presents the roasted lamb, holding the stand lengthwise, with one piece of roasted meat placed lengthwise on the stand, with salt on the right. The impersonator, holding the goblet with his left hand, receives the roasted meat, rubs it in the salt, sits, shakes it in offering, tastes it, rises, and places it on the lamb stand. The guest holds the stand lengthwise and descends. The impersonator descends from the mat, faces north west of the western pillar, sits, drains the goblet, rises holding it, sits, sets it down, bows, and rises holding it. The host, facing north east of the eastern pillar, returns the bow. The host receives the goblet. The impersonator ascends to the mat and stands at the end of the mat.

阿回和你在天水集里逛得很尽兴。你听着他像一只快乐的小鸟一样叽叽喳喳说个不停，多希望青史能为他停留一刻——不必征战沙场，不必骨肉分离，不必卷入波诡云谲的朝堂斗争，亦不必为了归唐大业献出自己的一生。此刻他就是阿回，那个勇敢的，开朗的，活泼的，有些小机灵的，装作小大人的，把你当做朋友的阿回。
en:
Under the lantern-lit splendor of Skybrim Market, the people remain lost in an endless celebration. Amid the bustling crowd, you spot Hui, who has sneaked out to play again. He sees you too, waves excitedly, and thanks you for helping him buy a lantern last time. This time, he pats his little pouch and invites you to stroll through the market together. It's hard to turn down such a gracious invitation, but where to next?...

You and Hui have a wonderful time strolling through Skybrim Market. Listening to him chatter away like a cheerful little bird, you can't help but wish the annals of history might pause for him just for a moment, sparing him the blood-soaked battlefields, the separation from his family, the treacherous storms of court intrigue, and the lifelong burden of restoring the Tang. In this moment, he is simply Hui, a brave, cheerful, lively, and clever boy who pretends to be a grown-up and treats you as a true friend.

zh:
二来来饼摊开张了，摊主是个冷脸的简师傅。
简师傅记得自己曾嘲笑衡儿，“张罗吃食比研究飞天简单多了”，如今看着面前一坨坨不成形的面糊糊，和摇摇欲坠的二来来招牌，简师傅开始怀念凿研的苦日子了。
但民以食为天，简师傅仍然记得过去每个熬夜的日子里，一张热乎乎的咸食就能让自己重拾干劲。于是简师傅拿出了研究飞天的热忱，开始钻研如何摊好一张咸食。
水多了加面，面多了加水……再来颗新鲜的鸡子。
终于，一张如月儿般圆满的饼子摊成了。简师傅擦了擦额间的汗水，饼摊的热火融化了那张冷脸。

轶儿喜欢荠菜，荣儿喜欢火腿，阿杜喜欢西葫芦，阿央喜欢鲜羊肉……简师傅搜罗了大家的喜好，变着花样地做了数十种咸食。
这儿的人需要些新鲜的盼头。
二来来饼摊的生意渐渐红火了起来，不仅因为这儿的咸食种类丰富，是无患崖难得的美食；更因为大家都想来瞧瞧曾经的孤僻先生是如何努力赚吆喝的。
“刚烙的咸食香得紧，保管您惦记着整个二来来！”
人生嘛……纵使往事消亡，有了盼头，便也能整个二来来。
en:
That was how the "Come-Again" pancake stall opened. The owner was Master Jian, still stern-faced, still scowling.
He remembered mocking Heng'er once, "Peddling snacks is child's play compared to the study of Flight!" Now, staring at lumpy batter and a crooked sign barely holding together, he found himself oddly nostalgic for those punishing days of study.
But people live on food. He remembered how a single hot, savory bite had been enough to steady his heart on countless sleepless nights. So he brought the same stubborn dedication he once poured into flight, and turned it toward a griddle.
Too much water? Add flour. Too thick? Add water... Then, one fresh egg.
At last, a pancake spread into a perfect, full circle, round as the moon. Master Jian wiped the sweat from his brow. The steam rising from the stall seemed to soften the hard lines of his face.

Yi'er liked shepherd's purse. Rong'er liked ham. Ah Du liked zucchini. Ah Yang liked fresh lamb... He memorized every preference, inventing dozens of savory fillings.
The people here needed something new to look forward to.
Before long, business at "Come-Again" picked up. Not just because the food was good, which was rarely good in Brighthale Cliff, but because people wanted to see it for themselves. To see how that once-lonely, aloof scholar now struggled earnestly to hawk his wares.
"Hot off the griddle! Savory and rich! One bite guarantees you'll be Coming Again!"
That's life, isn't it? Even if the past is dust... as long as you have something to look forward to, you can always start again.

曾经有一只歌声动听的小猫，所有听了它声音的人都会陶醉其中。猫咪的主人十分得意，每逢宴客，都会带上小猫让它一展歌喉。

哈吉咪再也无法唱歌了，曾夸耀它的歌喉是吉兆的主人也不在了。
它只能从喉咙里挤出嘶哑的声音，被一个又一个人嫌弃地赶走。然后它遇到了毛师傅，毛师傅眯着眼睛看着它，指了指脚边的草窝。
它钻进去住了，一住便住到了现在。
en:
There once was a little cat with a voice so enchanting that anyone who heard it was swept away. Its owner, proud as could be, brought the cat to every banquet just to let it sing. 
But at one such feast, the honeyed dishes on the table drew a swarm of bees from the trees. Guests scattered, yet the owner and the cat were not so fortunate. 
After that day, Gigi could no longer sing—and the owner who once called its voice a blessing was gone as well. 
All that remained was a hoarse rasp that made people wrinkle their noses and chase it off. Until it met Master Mao. He squinted down at the bedraggled cat, and then tapped a grass nest by his feet. 
Meow Meow slipped inside—and never left.

zh:
……娘的，上周门里结算，我又是倒数。长老看我的眼神就跟看茅房的臭石头一样。真纳闷了，一样都是耍人，为啥就我捞不到钱？
我觉得是我一开始就找错方向了。
老百姓都勒紧裤腰带过日子，兜比脸还干净，能有几个钱？我天天盯着他们，那不是瞎耽误工夫吗？
可是江湖人就不一样了！江湖上的各门派，各有手艺，有专长，那就是有赚钱的法子，钱袋子自然鼓。开封城里啥门派的人都有，我咋不早想到从他们手里捞钱？
就这么办，明日起，我就去开封城里挨个会会他们！

【青溪】
我今天一上街就瞅见个青溪的大夫，医箱就放在路边，诊金就放箱子上，她压根都没时间看，忙得脚打后脑勺。我过去摸了两个铜板，转身刚走，就听到她跟人说，一副药只收五文钱。
我一听就傻眼了。原来她忙前忙后就赚这点钱。兜里这俩铜板一下子就烫手了，我赶紧把钱扔了回去。
亏心钱我可不拿！

【狂澜】
气死我了！
狂澜的人是好找，酒馆里一抓一个准。我凑过去跟那孙子喝酒，给他酒里加了点料，想着等他倒了，钱袋就是我的了。谁知道他酒品烂成这样！几杯马尿下肚，手脚就不老实，居然往我身上乱摸！妈的，老子偷钱虽然不光彩，但也是堂堂正正的手艺，怎么能平白给他占了便宜！
最后我就一脚踹开他跑了。真亏，就顺了他一壶破酒，才换了十文钱！

【醉花阴】
我早知道醉花阴的都是人精，但都失败两次了，我说今天就得明知山有虎，偏向虎山行！
阿心师姐教我，要接近醉花阴的弟子就得搞身行头，去樊楼装大爷。我押了五文钱，向师姐借了身好衣裳。别说，我觉得我穿着还挺像模像样。一进樊楼，就有个醉花阴的美女，嘴跟抹了蜜似的，对我又夸又捧，夸得我晕头转向。唉，当有钱人的感觉就是爽！就是爽得我都忘了自己是去干嘛的……
喝完酒，看完美人跳舞，她就把我送出去了。但怪的是，她居然没收我酒钱？
难道她看出我其实是个穷光蛋了？那她费那么大劲捧我干嘛？想不通。
不过，美女身上可真香啊。

【梨园】
从樊楼出来一直想着美女，不知不觉就溜达到梨园的戏台了。一听吓一跳！我的天爷，人的嗓子咋能灵成这样？听得我骨头都酥了。跟她们比，我这嗓子就跟破锣似的。
唱完了，那个小妹妹下台来讨赏，一双眼睛水灵灵的，我脑子一热，把兜里剩下五文钱全赏出去了。
好嘛，折腾一圈，全白干！
en:
...Last week's accounting nearly drove me mad. Once again, I was at the very bottom. The elder looked at me as if I were a foul stone in an outhouse. I truly don't understand it—everyone else tricks people for a living, yet I'm the only one who never seems to earn a coin. 
I think I went wrong from the very beginning. 
Ordinary folk are tightening their belts just to survive. How much money could they possibly have? And I keep watching them day after day... What a complete waste of time. 
But people of the jianghu are different. Every sect has its own skill, its own specialty, which means its own way of making money. Their purses must be full. Kaifeng is full of wanderers from every school. How did I not think to make them my target? 
That's settled, then. Starting tomorrow, I'll visit them one by one. 

[Silver Needle] 
The moment I stepped onto the street today, I spotted a healer from Silver Needle. Her medical kit was set beside her, and the consultation fee sat on top, yet she was too busy to even look at it. So I slipped over, took two copper coins, and had just turned to leave when I heard her say to someone, "A full prescription only costs five wen." 
I stopped cold. All that hard work, all that running around—for so little? Those two coins felt unbearably heavy in my pocket. I dropped them into her box without a second thought. 
I will not take money my conscience cannot bear! 

[Raging Tides] 
I'm so angry! 
Finding someone from Raging Tides is easy—just walk into any tavern. I sat down with one of them, shared a drink, slipped a little something into his cup, planning to take his purse once he passed out. But who could have guessed he would drink himself into such disgrace? After only a few cups, he started getting handsy, reaching for me as though I were part of the furniture. Theft may not be an honorable trade, but it is at least a straightforward one. I will not let myself be taken advantage of by some drunken stranger! 
In the end, I kicked him aside and ran. What a loss—out of the whole ordeal, all I managed to take was a jug of cheap wine worth barely ten wen! 

[Velvet Shade] 
I've always known those at Velvet Shade were sharp, but having failed twice, I told myself that today I would try again, for I had nothing left to lose. 
Senior Sister A'xin taught me that if I wanted to get close to one of their disciples, I had to look the part—dress well and act like a man of means at Revelry Hall. I staked some money and borrowed a fine outfit from her. And honestly, once I put it on, I really did look respectable. 
The moment I stepped into Revelry Hall, a lovely woman from Velvet Shade greeted me with a voice sweet as honey. She showered me with compliments until I was completely dazzled. Ah... Being treated like a rich man felt wonderful—so wonderful I nearly forgot why I had come. 
After a few drinks and watching her dance, she even walked me out herself. Curiously, she didn't charge me for the wine. 
Had she realized I was actually penniless? Then why go to such lengths to flatter me? I couldn't make sense of it. 
Still... the fragrance she carried lingered even after she left. 

[The Masked Troupe] 
I left Revelry Hall thinking of her, and before I knew it, I had wandered to the stage at the Masked Troupe. And what a surprise—how can a human voice sound so beautiful? It felt like my bones softened amidst the voice. By comparison, mine is nothing but a broken gong. 
When she finished, a young girl came down to collect tips. Her bright eyes were impossible to refuse, and in a moment of impulse, I handed her the last few coins I had. 
So after an entire day of scheming... I ended up with nothing at all.
Has anything unusual happened lately?
HotsilentHeart

zh:
游侠，见字如面。
前些时日，老朽随府尹大人巡查蒙学，见学堂里的娃娃们一个个正襟危坐，埋首书卷，连我等走近了都未曾察觉。
老朽心下好奇，是何等妙文，能让这些上蹿下跳的娃娃们如此专心？一问才知，他们手中所读，竟是你前些时日所赠。
老朽又问，这些书好在何处？娃娃们七嘴八舌，老朽这才知道，原来你竟为每个孩子都择了不同的书，实在是费心了。而听闻老朽与你相熟，他们都央着我，定要代他们向你道声谢。
只是，真要问他们想说什么，这群小家伙却面露羞赧，讷讷而止了。最后，老朽想了个法子，让他们把想说的话都诉诸笔端，一并封在信里了。至于写了什么，老朽绝未偷看！
对了，娃娃们还托我转交几幅画作，说是读了书卷后的有感而发。他们都说，游侠你是他们见过最有眼光的人，定能欣赏他们的大作。
哈哈，看来往后若再有与孩子们打交道的差事，找游侠准是没错了。
<IMAGE id='im1' image_url='https://h72.fp.ps.netease.com/file/68ce4167b525ec4cab99739f6k18aLuG06' size='2198*1554' color='255;255;255')'></IMAGE>

en:
Dear Wanderer,

The other day, I accompanied the Prefect on an inspection of the village school. The children sat straight at their desks, noses buried in scrolls, so absorbed they didn't even notice us draw near.
Curious what could hold their attention so completely, I asked. Turns out, they were reading the very books you gifted them not long ago.
I inquired further: what made these books so special? The little ones burst into chatter, and that's when I learned you had chosen a different book for each child. What thoughtfulness.
When they heard I knew you, they begged me to pass along their thanks.
But when I asked what they wanted to say, shyness took over, and words failed them. So I suggested they write it down instead. Their letters are enclosed. And no, I did not peek!
Oh, and they also asked me to send you a few drawings. Inspired, they said, by your books. They all agreed you're the most discerning person they've ever met, and that you'd surely appreciate their masterpieces.
Seems to me, whenever there's a task involving children, you're the one to call.

zh:
张三在等一个人，只是今日日头实在太好，所以他好像不小心睡着了，而且错过了接头的时间。不过追魂引还是来了。

手边的暖茶已冷，一首《七友》循环了许久许久，是近来最喜欢的一首歌。临近年末了，大家开始忙着计划跨年和迎接新年的到来，在这半暖时光里，回想起即将结束的一年，一边感叹时间匆匆，一边写着记录，在过去的一年里看看都收获了些什么。

大概这一年是我最为充实的一年吧，边上学边兼职，时间不紧不慢。终于，不再伸手时时向家里要钱。终于，学着安排自己的生活。从前，知道把持柴米油盐的日子不易，可并不知道真正有多不易。现如今，成长的第一件事就是要学会咽的下苦和学会快乐，学会从容。
en:
Zhang San was waiting for someone, but the sun was so warm today that he accidentally dozed off and missed their meeting. Still, the Soul Pursuer showed up.

The tea beside him had gone cold, and his favorite song, "Seven Friends," had been playing on repeat for a long time. As the year winds down, everyone is busy making plans for New Year's Eve and the arrival of the new year. In this gentle warmth, he reflects on the past year, amazed at how quickly time has flown, and takes stock of everything he's accomplished.

This has probably been my most fulfilling year yet—balancing school and part-time work at a steady pace. I no longer have to constantly ask my family for money. I'm finally learning to take charge of my own life. I always knew managing the everyday stuff wasn't easy, but I didn't truly realize how tough it really is. Growing up means learning to swallow the bitter with the sweet, finding joy along the way, and learning to stay steady no matter what.

zh:
大个子：
我们坐上了大圆盘，小寿上去之前特别兴奋，上去之后反而不敢睁开眼睛，可飞起来就不怕啦！等我们回去要跟薛丑好好说说，他肯定没坐过。
对了，我们发现一个圆头圆脑、黄澄澄、看不见手脚的小玩意儿，它还会钻土呢！
后来遇上一个工匠大叔，说什么都能刻，我们想把那个圆家伙刻出来。他听了半天摇摇头说刻不了，还说那叫“五不像”……
大个子，你见识多，肯定知道那是什么，对吧？
en:
Big One,
We rode the giant spinning disk! Little Shou was thrilled before we got on, but once we were actually up there, she squeezed her eyes shut. But once we started flying, she wasn't scared at all! When we get back, we're definitely going to rub it in Xue Chou's face. I bet he's never ridden it!
Oh, yeah! We also found this weird little round, bright-yellow thing with no hands or feet, and it burrows into the dirt!
Later on, we ran into this middle-aged artisan who bragged he could "carve absolutely anything," so we asked him to carve that round guy for us. He listened to us describe it forever, then just shook his head and said he couldn't do it. He even called it a monster...
Big One, you know everything! You definitely know what that thing is, right?

少东家，新岁好呀。
方才外头在放爆竹，倒教我想起有一年除夕夜，师父说，守岁到天亮的娃娃，来年最有福气。我便拉着你陪我一起熬夜，等着天亮。谁知咱们连三更都没撑到，脑袋就像小鸡啄米，一下一下往桌上点……其实、其实当时我只是太害怕那震天的响声，非要你陪着，心里才踏实。
今年我守得久些了，窗外偶尔响起爆竹声，屋里倒显得格外静。也不知你那边热闹不热闹，心里总惦记着，就顺手给你备了点小东西，可要收好啦。
新岁平安，在外要照顾好自己。
en:
Young Master, a very happy New Year to you.
The firecrackers outside reminded me of Spring Festival's Eve long ago. My master said that children who keep the vigil until dawn will be the most blessed in the coming year. So I dragged you along to stay up all night with me, waiting for the light of day. Who knew we wouldn't even last until the third watch? Our heads were nodding like little chicks pecking for grain, thumping against the table... The truth is... I was simply terrified of those thunderous booms. I only insisted you stay so my heart could feel at ease.
I stayed awake longer this year. With the occasional crackle of firecrackers outside, the room feels strangely quiet. I wonder if it is lively where you are; you are always on my mind. I have prepared a little something for you. Keep it safe, now.
May the New Year bring you peace. Take good care of yourself on your travels.

zh:
正月初一
一年过去，差事如水井不波。新岁新气象，今年定要寻到转机！

二月十六
近两月来主要观察宣徽院的同僚行事，从开年祭礼到年节宴会到长春节，每日都只见他们急匆匆入官署，却从不见他们离开。如此忙碌恐怕伤身，不妥，不妥。

三月十八
幸甚幸甚！原本意图谋求三司之职，幸甚未成，否则昨日失火，恐怕便要遭灾。
如此想来，我于数算一道也不甚精通，恐怕难当每月每年的账本盘算之职。不妥，不妥。

五月初九
司天监每日装忙，实则甚为清闲，但若逢天象有异、贵人患病、灾祸连绵，恐要沦为担责的弃子。不妥，不妥。

六月廿二
罗问之啊罗问之，你不能再挑挑拣拣了，难道还要如此蹉跎下去吗？

八月初三
听闻昭文馆有意补缺，但只缺一人，岂能弃齐祥在此？不妥，不妥。
en:
First Month, Day 1

Another year has gone by, and my post is as still as a well with no ripples.

New year, new prospects. This year, I must find a way forward.



Second Month, Day 16

For nearly two months now, I have mainly been watching my colleagues at the Ceremonial Office.

From the opening rites of the year to the seasonal banquets to the Changchun Festival, I see them hurrying in day after day, yet never once do I see them leave.

That kind of workload is bound to wear a person down. No good. No good.



Third Month, Day 18

A blessing indeed, a blessing indeed.

I had originally hoped to secure a post in the Commission of the Three Fiscal Bureaus. Luckily, it did not work out, or yesterday's fire might well have caught me up in it.

Come to think of it, I am not much good at figures either. Month after month, year after year, all that balancing of books would finish me. No good. No good.



Fifth Month, Day 9

The Observatory looks busy every day, but in truth, it is a rather easy post.

Still, the moment strange omens appear in the sky, or some important person falls ill, or disaster strikes again and again, the people there are liable to end up taking the blame.

No good. No good.



Sixth Month, Day 22

Luo Wenzhi, Luo Wenzhi, you cannot keep picking and choosing like this. Are you really going to let your days slip away?



Eighth Month, Day 3

I hear Brightlore Hall is looking to fill a vacancy, but there is room for only one. How could I leave Qi Xiang behind here?

No good. No good.

zh:
【聘礼第八】

聘礼。君与卿图事，遂命使者，使者再拜稽首辞，君不许，乃退。既图事，戒上介，亦如之。宰命司马戒众介，众介皆逆命，不辞。
宰书币，命宰夫官具。及期，夕币。使者朝服，帅众介夕。管人布幕于寝门外。官陈币，皮北首，西上，加其奉于左皮上；马则北面，奠币于其前。使者北面，众介立于其左，东上。卿、大夫在幕东，西面北上。宰入，告具于君。君朝服出门左，南乡。史读书展币。宰执书，告备具于君，授使者。使者受书，授上介。公揖入。官载其币，舍于朝。上介视载者、所受书以行。
厥明，宾朝服释币于祢。有司筵几于室中。祝先入，主人从入。主人在右，再拜，祝告，又再拜。释币，制玄纁束，奠于几下，出。主人立于户东。祝立于牖西，又入，取币，降，卷币，实于笲，埋于西阶东。又释币于行。遂受命。上介释币亦如之。
上介及众介俟于使者之门外。使者载旃，帅以受命于朝。君朝服，南乡。卿、大夫西面北上。君使卿进使者。使者入，及众介随入，北面东上。君揖使者，进之，上介立于其左，接闻命。贾人西面坐启椟，取圭垂缫，不起而授宰。宰执圭屈缫，自公左授使者。使者受圭，同面，垂缫以受命。既述命，同面授上介。上介受圭屈缫，出，授贾人，众介不从。受享束帛加璧，受夫人之聘璋，享玄纁束帛加琮，皆如初。遂行，舍于郊，敛旃。
若过邦，至于竟，使次介假道，束帛将命于朝，曰：“请帅。”奠币。下大夫取以入告，出许，遂受币。饩之以其礼，上宾大牢，积唯刍禾，介皆有饩。士没其竟。誓于其竟，宾南面，上介西面，众介北面东上，史读书，司马执策立于其后。
未入竟，壹肄。为壝坛，画阶，帷其北，无宫。朝服无主，无执也。介皆与，北面西上。习享，士执庭实习夫人聘享，亦如之。习公事，不习私事。
及竟，张旃，誓。乃谒关人。关人问从者几人，以介对。君使士请事，遂以入竟。
入竟，敛旃，乃展。布幕，宾朝服立于幕东，西面，介皆北面东上。贾人北面，坐拭圭，遂执展之。上介北面视之，退复位。退圭。陈皮，北首，西上，又拭璧，展之，会诸其币，加于左皮上。上介视之，退。马则幕南、北面，奠币于其前。展夫人之聘享，亦如之，贾人告于上介，上介告于宾。有司展群币以告。及郊，又展，如初。及馆，展币于贾人之馆，如初。
……
en:
【The Rites of Betrothal, Eighth】

The Rites of Betrothal. The ruler consults with his high ministers on the matter, and then dispatches an envoy. The envoy bows twice with his head to the ground and declines, but the ruler does not permit it, and so he withdraws. After the matter is decided, the chief assistant is instructed in the same manner. The steward commands the marshal to instruct the other assistants, and all of them accept the command without declining.
The steward records the gifts, and orders the steward of the household to prepare them according to regulations. When the day arrives, the gifts are displayed in the evening. The envoy, in court robes, leads the assistants to the evening display. The steward spreads a curtain outside the bedchamber gate. The officers lay out the gifts: the skins are placed with their heads to the north, arranged from the west upward, and the offerings are placed on the left skin; the horses face north, and the gifts are set before them. The envoy faces north, and the assistants stand to his left, arranged from the east upward. The high ministers and great officers stand to the east of the curtain, facing west, arranged from the north upward. The steward enters and reports to the ruler that all is prepared. The ruler, in court robes, comes out through the left side of the gate and faces south. The recorder reads the document and checks the gifts. The steward holds the document, reports to the ruler that everything is complete, and hands it to the envoy. The envoy receives the document and passes it to the chief assistant. The ruler bows and withdraws. The officers load the gifts and store them at the court. The chief assistant inspects the loaded goods and the document received, and then sets out.
The next morning, the guest, in court robes, offers silk to the shrine of his father. The officer in charge spreads mats and a low table in the chamber. The invocator enters first, and the host follows him in. The host stands on the right, bows twice, the invocator makes the announcement, and he bows twice again. He offers the silk—a bundle of dark and light colored fabric—placing it beneath the low table, and then exits. The host stands to the east of the door. The invocator stands to the west of the window, then enters again, takes the silk, descends, rolls it up, places it in a basket, and buries it to the east of the western steps. He also offers silk to the deity of the road. Then he receives the command. The chief assistant offers silk in the same manner.
The chief assistant and the other assistants wait outside the envoy's gate. The envoy, with his banner displayed, leads them to receive the command at the court. The ruler, in court robes, faces south. The high ministers and great officers face west, arranged from the north upward. The ruler sends a high minister to summon the envoy forward. The envoy enters, and the assistants follow him in, facing north, arranged from the east upward. The ruler bows to the envoy and motions him forward. The chief assistant stands to his left, close enough to hear the command. The merchant, facing west, sits and opens the case, takes out the jade tablet with the cord hanging down, and without rising, hands it to the steward. The steward holds the jade tablet, coils the cord, and from the left of the ruler hands it to the envoy. The envoy receives the jade tablet, facing the same direction, with the cord hanging down, and receives the command. After reciting the command, he faces the same direction and hands it to the chief assistant. The chief assistant receives the jade tablet, coils the cord, exits, and hands it to the merchant; the other assistants do not follow. He receives the bundle of silk with a jade disc for the audience gift, receives the jade tablet for the lady's betrothal gift, and the dark and light silk with a jade cong for the lady's audience gift—all in the same manner as before. Then they set out and lodge in the suburbs, furling the banner.
If they pass through another state, upon reaching its border, the envoy sends the second assistant to request passage, presenting a bundle of silk with a message at the court, saying: "We request to lead [our party through]." He presents the gifts. A lower great officer takes them and goes in to report, comes out and grants permission, and then receives the gifts. He provides them with provisions according to the rites: the principal guest receives a grand offering of ox, sheep, and pig, and the provisions consist only of fodder and grain; each assistant also receives provisions. The officers escort them to the border. They take an oath at the border: the guest faces south, the chief assistant faces west, and the other assistants face north, arranged from the east upward. The recorder reads the document, and the marshal stands behind them holding the tally.
Before entering the border, they rehearse once. They build an earthen altar, mark out the steps, and screen the north side with a curtain, but there is no enclosing wall. They wear court robes, but there is no host, and no gifts are held. All the assistants participate, facing north, arranged from the west upward. They rehearse the audience ceremony, with officers holding the courtyard gifts. They rehearse the lady's betrothal and audience ceremonies in the same manner. They rehearse the public ceremonies, but not the private ones.
Upon reaching the border, they display the banner and take an oath. Then they announce themselves to the border official. The border official asks how many followers there are, and they answer with the number of assistants. The ruler sends an officer to inquire about their business, and then they are allowed to enter the border.
After entering the border, they furl the banner and then conduct an inspection. A curtain is spread, and the guest, in court robes, stands to the east of the curtain, facing west. All the assistants face north, arranged from the east upward. The merchant, facing north, sits and wipes the jade tablet, then holds it up for inspection. The chief assistant, facing north, inspects it, then withdraws to his position. The jade tablet is put away. The skins are laid out, heads to the north, arranged from the west upward. Then the jade disc is wiped and inspected, and placed together with the other gifts, on top of the left skin. The chief assistant inspects them and withdraws. The horses are placed to the south of the curtain, facing north, with the gifts set before them. The lady's betrothal and audience gifts are inspected in the same manner. The merchant reports to the chief assistant, and the chief assistant reports to the guest. The officers inspect all the gifts and report. Upon reaching the suburbs, they inspect again, as before. Upon reaching the lodging, they inspect the gifts at the merchant's lodging, as before.
……

Study Tokens are exclusive points for Inkbound Order classes. All Wanderers can earn them by attending classes such as Scripture Recitation, Calligraphy Practice, and Mounted Archery while meeting their requirements. Study Tokens are reset #Hevery Monday#E with no upper limit.

The amount of Study Tokens earned varies depending on the teacher. Classes taught by both Jianghu Sect teachers and Inkbound Order players grant Study Tokens, but classes taught by players offer greater rewards: classes taught by players at #HMaster#E rank grant a #H1.25x#E Study Tokens bonus, while classes taught by players at #HDean#E rank grant a #H2x#E bonus.

Study Tokens also determine #Hadvancement#E within the Inkbound Order. Mentor Disciples need to earn enough Study Tokens to promote to Master, while Masters need to keep earning Study Tokens to qualify for election as Dean.

zh:
最美味的果子，生长在采撷者的梦里。
这是从岭南快马加鞭进献上来的珍果，普通人看上一眼亦是难事。
同行的教坊乐师剥开了雪白的果肉，而三娘只想将它留下。

之后天子和贵妃喜爱她唱江南吉州小调，又赞“喉转一声，响传九陌”。
在御前畏畏缩缩的小娃儿，成了闻名长安的永新娘子。
她唱“北斗酌美酒，劝龙各一觞”，唱高台郎月，喜者闻之气勇，愁者闻之肠绝。
春日得赐的那枚荔枝，被她收在枕边，直到腐坏枯萎。
王朝的腐坏，并不比荔枝来得晚。
洎渔阳之乱，六宫星散。她流落广陵，江上唱“平沙落日大荒西，陇上明星高复低”，却听得有人泣泪相和。
金吾将军也好，绝世名伶也罢，今夜不过飘摇孤舟。

离人忆长安，言谈中她恍然想起梨花散坠的那个春日。
那位女子已成了马嵬坡一缕芳魂。
三娘再也无缘问她，这首曲子，你是否真心喜爱？
en:
The choicest fruit grows only in the dreams of those who gather it. 
Rushed from Lingnan by swift horses, this rare delicacy was so precious that even a mere glance was a privilege denied to ordinary folk. 
While the troupe's musicians eagerly peeled back its snow-white flesh, Sanniang only wished she could keep it a secret, a treasure all her own. 

Later, the Emperor and the Noble Consort delighted in her singing—a tender folk tune from the southern lands. They praised her voice, saying, "Her clear voice sends echoes weaving through every street and alleyway." 
That timid child who once trembled before the imperial throne blossomed into Lady Eternal Renewal, a name on the lips of all Chang'an. 
Her song echoes beneath the bright moon atop the lofty pavilion, stirring courage in the joyful and wrenching sorrow in the broken-hearted. 
That lychee, gifted on a spring day, lay beside her pillow—cherished until it withered and decayed. 
The rot of the dynasty came no slower than that of the fruit. 
When the rebellion shattered the palace and scattered the sovereignty, she found herself adrift in distant lands. Her sorrowful melodies were met by tearful echoes in kind. 
Whether mighty generals or performers unmatched in skill, that night all were but solitary boats adrift on a stormy sea. 

The exiled soul carried memories of Chang'an close, and in quiet moments recalled a spring day, when pear blossoms fell like drifting snow. 
The woman from that day had become nothing more than a lingering fragrance on a barren slope. 
Sanniang would never again have the chance to ask her: "Did you truly love this song?"

zh: “华岳峨峨，冈峦参差。神木灵草，朱实离离。总会仙倡，戏豹舞罴。白虎鼓瑟，苍龙吹篪。女娥坐而长歌，声清畅而蜲蛇。洪涯立而指麾，被毛羽之襳襹。度曲未终，云起雪飞。初若飘飘，后遂霏霏。复陆重阁，转石成雷。礔砺激而增响，磅盖象乎天威。巨兽百寻，是为曼延。”
en:
"Lofty Hua Mountain, with its undulating ridges, 
Divine trees and sacred grass, bright fruits aglow. 
Immortal performers gather, leopards and bears dance, 
White tigers strum guqins, azure dragons blow pipes. 
The goddess Chang'e sits singing, her voice pure and lingering, 
While Hong Ya stands directing, clad in feathered robes. 
Before the music ends, clouds rise and snow swirls. 
First drifting lightly, then falling thickly. 
From towers and terraces, rolling stones mimic thunder, 
Echoing like the wrath of heaven. 
A colossal beast, a hundred spans long, and this is the'Manyan.'"

zh:
显德二年……月……日
妙善禅师御前答辩，受封佛子，执掌法华禅院。这禅院近在慈心镇之畔，有佛子庇佑，镇上佛雕生意想必不会受到灭佛之事影响。
我等向佛之心，佛祖定会有知。只管安心择石雕佛便是。
……
显德三年……月……日
不孝子一先整日耍滑偷懒，不思进取，我杨氏家传佛雕手艺怕是后继无人。不过近日来镇上买佛雕的商船越来越少，或许也该换个营生……罢了，罢了，儿孙自有儿孙福。
……
显德六年……月……日
两年来入不敷出，镇上人心惶惶。阿槐他们总念叨着要找佛子说理，可这灭佛之令是官家下的，佛子又能做些什么？
……
显德六年……月……日
佛子来信，请我前去菩提苦海罪业塔开石。到时方知，他请我破开的竟是一块稀世璞玉，玉中隐约可见佛影一尊，绝非凡品。如此美玉当打磨赏玩为上，佛子却令我将它一剖为二，真是可惜……此玉坚硬无匹，须得小心下手才是。
……
显德六年……月……日
暮鼓……怎会在白日响起？还是来自罪业塔的方向。难道禅师……不行，我得去看看。
（记录在此戛然而止）
en:
...Day...Month, Second Year of the Xiande Era
Master Miaoshan defended his thesis before the throne and was honored as the Enlightened One, entrusted with the Fahua Temple. This temple stands near Mercyheart Town, and with the Enlightened One's protection, the town's Buddha statue trade should remain untouched by the anti-buddist movement.
Our devotion will surely be known to the Buddha. Let us carve statues in peace....

...Day...Month, Third Year of the Xiande Era
My worthless son, Yixian, idles all day, lazy and unambitious. It seems the Yang family's Buddha-carving heritage will die with me. Lately, fewer merchant ships come to town for statues... perhaps it's time to change trades. Ah, never mind. Kids must find their own way....

...Day...Month, Sixth Year of the Xiande Era
Two years of dwindling earnings. The town grows uneasy. A'huai and others mutter about demanding answers from the Enlightened One. But the purge decree comes from the court. What can he do?...

...Day...Month, Sixth Year of the Xiande Era
A letter from the Enlightened One summoned me to the Pagoda of Karma at the Bodhi Sea to cleave stone. Only upon arrival did I learn the task, to split a rare jade boulder. Within its depths, the shadow of a Buddha faintly gleamed. Such jade ought to be polished and treasured, yet he ordered it halved. What waste... The stone resists all tools; I must work carefully....

...Day...Month, Sixth Year of the Xiande Era
The evening drum... why does it sound at noon? And from the Pagoda's direction. Could the master...? No, I must check it out.(The record ends abruptly here.)
1 Mohist Tally = 1 Song Coin

zh:
又到一年上元节，陇州各处张灯结彩，行人如织，热闹非凡。
魏芷昔不甘人后，大清早的，就开始风风火火张罗宅里的装扮，把屋子里早起的儿子忘了个一干二净。
这可正好遂了赵承宗的愿。
还没到大人半身高的小娃娃，悄悄从床底下扒拉出早前便收拾好的包裹，踮着脚，穿过宅子里管家和丫鬟的裙角和裤腿，而后钻过院子角落的狗洞，溜了。
他谋划这事好久了。娘亲总催他念书，而爹爹老是不着家，也没个人能帮他。他反抗过，无果，争取过，无用。于是他决定，就今天，他要用这场离家出走，来让娘亲看到他一天只愿看一个时辰而不是两个时辰的书的决心！
但是前头走过的那几个黑衣人，哎哎哎，这个巨大的麻袋，怎么就对着他罩过来了？

入夜后的陇州，万籁俱静。赵家上下忙里忙慌把整个城翻了个底朝天，都没找着他们的小少爷。然后一天过去了，两天过去了，魏夫人日夜在外奔波寻人，赵老爷也从千里之外赶了回来，赵家上下没一个过得安生……就在大家伙都开始绝望的时候，一个麻袋被扔在了大门口，然后他们的小少爷毫发无伤的，生龙活虎的，扑闪着一双大眼睛钻了出来。
“好帅！好帅的大侠！”“他这样，再那样，哗哗哗！全给打趴下了！”“他们说什么，我这样的娃娃，最值钱！”“然后大侠又这么一拳，那么一脚，再伸手一捞！就把我救出来了！”“名字？大侠说他没有名字！”“我说外面的世界怎么这么可怕，大侠说，不怕不怕，有很多像他这样的大侠，会保护我们的。”
叽叽喳喳的，几个时辰后，赵承宗终于累了。他乖乖躺下，在被窝迷迷糊糊地想，最后那大侠说的什么……为侠者，如星火燎原。
那是什么意思，他不懂。但是他，赵承宗，从明日起，就要做那颗最最最闪耀的星！
en:
It was Lantern Festival again, and Longzhou was ablaze with colored lights, throngs of people, and festive chaos. 
Wei Zhixi, never one to be outdone, spent the dawn bustling about the mansion, decorating every corner, and entirely forgetting her young son, who'd just woken up.
This suited Zhao Chengzong perfectly.
The boy, barely half an adult's height, quietly retrieved a pre-packed bundle from under his bed. On tiptoe, he wove through the steward's robes and maid's skirts, slipped through the dog hole in the courtyard corner, and escaped.
He'd been plotting this for weeks. His mother constantly nagged him to study, his father was always away, and no one listened to his protests. Enough was enough! Today, he'd prove his resolve by running away, all to show he only wanted to study one hour a day, not two!
But those black-clad figures ahead... hey, why was that gunny sack suddenly being thrown over his head?

By nightfall, Longzhou had fallen silent, but the Zhao household was in chaos. They scoured the entire city for their young master, to no avail. A day passed, then two. Madam Wei searched day and night, while Lord Zhao rushed back from thousands of miles away. Hope was fading when a gunny sack was dumped at the front gate, and their son popped out, unharmed, wide-eyed, and very excited.
"So cool! The hero was so cool!" he babbled. "He moved like this, then that...whoosh! ... and knocked everyone down! They said kids like me are worth money, but the hero punched here, kicked there, and grabbed me right out!" "His name? He said he doesn't have one!" "I said the world's so scary! He said don't worry, there are lots of heroes like him!"
After hours of chattering, Zhao Chengzong finally grew tired. As he drifted off under his blanket, he puzzled over the hero's last words: "A hero is but a spark... yet sparks can set the plains ablaze."
What did it mean? He wasn't sure. But tomorrow, he, Zhao Chengzong, would become the brightest star of all.
Zhu Yue
Like a Stream's Tide

zh:
【学记第十八】

发虑宪，求善良，足以謏闻，不足以动众；就贤体远，足以动众，未足以化民。君子如欲化民成俗，其必由学乎！
玉不琢，不成器；人不学，不知道。是故古之王者建国君民，教学为先。《兑命》曰：“念终始典于学。”其此之谓乎！
虽有嘉肴，弗食，不知其旨也；虽有至道，弗学，不知其善也。是故学然后知不足，教然后知困。知不足，然后能自反也；知困，然后能自强也，故曰：教学相长也。《兑命》曰：“学学半。”其此之谓乎！
古之教者，家有塾，党有庠，术有序，国有学。比年入学，中年考校。一年视离经辨志，三年视敬业乐群，五年视博习亲师，七年视论学取友，谓之小成；九年知类通达，强立而不反，谓之大成。夫然后足以化民易俗，近者说服，而远者怀之，此大学之道也。《记》曰：“蛾子时术之。”其此之谓乎！
大学始教，皮弁祭菜，示敬道也；《宵雅》肄三，官其始也；入学鼓箧，孙其业也；夏楚二物，收其威也；未卜禘不视学，游其志也；时观而弗语，存其心也；幼者听而弗问，学不躐等也。此七者，教之大伦也。《记》曰：“凡学官先事，士先志。”其此之谓乎！
大学之教也，时教必有正业，退息必有居学。不学操缦，不能安弦；不学博依，不能安《诗》；不学杂服，不能安礼；不兴其艺，不能乐学。故君子之于学也，藏焉，修焉，息焉，游焉。夫然，故安其学而亲其师，乐其友而信其道。是以虽离师辅而不反也。《兑命》曰：“敬孙务时敏，厥修乃来。”其此之谓乎！
今之教者，呻其佔毕，多其讯言，及于数进，而不顾其安。使人不由其诚，教人不尽其材；其施之也悖，其求之也佛。夫然，故隐其学而疾其师，苦其难而不知其益也，虽终其业，其去之必速。教之不刑，其此之由乎！
大学之法，禁于未发之谓豫，当其可之谓时，不陵节而施之谓孙，相观而善之谓摩。此四者，教之所由兴也。
……
en:
【Record on the Subject of Education XVIII】

When plans are laid and good sought, it suffices to gain a small reputation, but not to move the masses. To draw near the worthy and embrace the distant suffices to move the masses, but not to transform the people. If a gentleman wishes to transform the people and perfect their customs, must he not proceed through learning?
Jade uncut does not become a vessel; a person unlearned does not know the Dao. Therefore, the ancient kings, when establishing states and ruling the people, placed teaching and learning first. The "Charge to Yue" says: "Keep in mind from beginning to end the constant dedication to learning." Is this not what is meant?
Though there be fine dishes, if one does not eat them, one does not know their flavor; though there be the utmost Dao, if one does not learn it, one does not know its goodness. Therefore, after learning, one knows one's deficiencies; after teaching, one knows one's perplexities. Knowing deficiencies, one can then reflect upon oneself; knowing perplexities, one can then strengthen oneself. Hence it is said: Teaching and learning promote each other. The "Charge to Yue" says: "Teaching is half of learning." Is this not what is meant?
In ancient times, those who taught had schools in every home, academies in every district, institutions in every province, and universities in the capital. Students entered school every year, and examinations were held every other year. In the first year, they were examined on their ability to parse texts and discern aspirations; in the third year, on their diligence in study and harmony with peers; in the fifth year, on their broad learning and closeness to teachers; in the seventh year, on their discussion of learning and choice of friends—this was called minor attainment. In the ninth year, they knew categories and achieved comprehensive understanding, stood firm without wavering—this was called major attainment. Only then could they transform the people and improve customs; those nearby were delighted and persuaded, and those afar cherished them. This is the way of the great learning. The "Record" says: "The ant larvae constantly learn by example." Is this not what is meant?
At the commencement of great learning, one dons the leather cap and offers sacrificial vegetables, showing reverence for the Dao; one practices three pieces of the "Lesser Odes of Majesty," beginning with official duties; upon entering school, one drums and opens the book boxes, showing respect for one's studies; the cane and the rod are two instruments, used to maintain authority; before the great sacrifice, no inspections of learning are made, to allow students to roam freely in their aspirations; one observes at times but does not speak, to keep their minds focused; the young listen but do not question, for learning does not skip levels. These seven are the great principles of teaching. The "Record" says: "In all learning, officials first attend to their duties, and scholars first attend to their aspirations." Is this not what is meant?
In the teaching of great learning, timely instruction must have proper subjects, and periods of rest must have supplementary studies. Without learning to strum, one cannot settle the strings; without learning broad analogies, one cannot settle the "Odes"; without learning various duties, one cannot settle the rites; without cultivating one's arts, one cannot delight in learning. Therefore, the gentleman in his learning stores it, cultivates it, rests in it, and roams in it. In this way, he is at ease in his studies and close to his teacher, delights in his friends and trusts in the Dao. Thus, even when separated from teacher and companions, he does not turn back. The "Charge to Yue" says: "Respectfully and reverently, be ever diligent and timely; then your cultivation will come." Is this not what is meant?
Nowadays, teachers drone over their texts, multiply their questions, rush through advancement, without regard for what students can absorb. They cause people to act without sincerity, and teach without fully developing their abilities; their methods are contrary, and their demands are unreasonable. In this way, students conceal their learning and resent their teachers, suffer the difficulty and do not know its benefits. Though they complete their studies, they will quickly abandon them. Is not the failure of teaching due to this?
The methods of great learning: preventing before it occurs is called preparation; acting at the opportune moment is called timeliness; not overstepping stages in instruction is called order; mutual observation and emulation of goodness is called polishing. 结果，进了宅院门，却见那人把门一关，手一摊。哪有什么肉？明明是个草编的玩意儿。
在一片哄笑声中，大壮难过地叫了起来。
可恶啊，九流门，连狗都不放过。
等笑够了，这人才在大壮可怜巴巴的眼神中拿出真肉，一边喂一边说：“好啦好啦，逗你玩的。喏，给你肉。看你皮包骨头的，以后就跟我们九流门混吧，包你吃香喝辣的。至于吃的怎么来的，你就别问了，好不？”
en:
A Nine Mortal Ways disciple tricks Strong into guarding their gate.
Lured by the smell of meat, Strong follows the figure in black robes with a gourd at his waist, eyes fixed on the meat in his hand.
But once through the gate, the man closes the door and holds out empty hands. There's no meat, just a woven grass toy.
Amidst the laughter, Strong whines in dismay.
How cruel! Even a dog isn't safe from the Nine Mortal Ways!
When they've had their laugh, the man finally produces real meat for Strong's pitiful gaze.
"Alright, alright, just teasing. Here's your meat. Look at you, skin and bones. From now on, stick with us; we'll feed you well. Where does the food come from? Don't ask, okay?"

To the heroes of Well of Heaven,

I have heard that three hundred disciples are making for Zhongdu Bridge, and I am ashamed beyond words. Bearing the stain of one who betrayed the sect, how could I deserve such loyalty?
I know well that to lay down one's life in the cause of righteousness is the way by which Well of Heaven brings salvation to the world. I therefore earnestly beg you, heroes, to hasten to the front at once, and with this blade and this body, guard the realm from falling.

zh: 齐鲁民间小吃，以整猪焖烤肉切片，夹入现烤火烧而成。据《章丘县志》载，此焖烤之法距今近四百年，其艺已入非遗。明代邢侗《章丘茅令君去思碑记》已有“卖浆割炙，栉比鳞列”之述，可见当时烤肉售卖之盛。火烧一脉，可溯至汉代西域传入之“胡饼”，唐时已“面脆油香”。齐鲁为小麦主产区，面食烤制之风自古有之。当地百姓合二为一，以新出炉烤肉夹入剖开火烧，佐以大葱甜酱，皮酥肉嫩，肥而不腻。
en: A traditional Shandong snack made with roast pork tucked into freshly baked flatbread. The roasting technique dates back nearly 400 years and is now recognized as intangible cultural heritage, while the flatbread traces its roots to the Han dynasty. 此处修缮，无法使用。墙壁上有前人奋力刻字：

予疾行入城，突感腹中万马奔腾，雷霆激荡，汗如雨下，疾趋此圊溷。

及至门前，翘首以盼，不意大门紧闭，如铜墙铁壁，竟无通路可入。任予叩关百遍，终是求门不得。

予伫立良久，方寸大乱。欲转投他处，奈何乾坤一气已至关要，进退失据。

俄而风雷大作，防线尽溃。刹那间，泥石俱下，万物尽染。

悲乎！天下之痛，莫过于临门一脚；世间之惨，无出于黄衣之灾。泣作此文，以告后人。
en:
This place is under repair and cannot be used. Upon the wall, someone before you carved these words with great effort:

I hastened into the city, when suddenly I felt ten thousand horses galloping in my belly, thunder crashing within, sweat pouring down like rain, and I rushed swiftly toward this privy.

Upon reaching the door, I craned my neck in anticipation, only to find the gate shut tight, like a wall of bronze and iron, with no path through. Though I knocked upon it a hundred times, in the end my plea for entry went unanswered.

I stood there long, my composure scattered to the winds. I wished to seek another place, but alas, the great turning of heaven and earth had reached its critical juncture, and I could neither advance nor retreat.

Then suddenly wind and thunder erupted, and my final defenses collapsed entirely. In an instant, mud came pouring down, and all things were stained.

Alas! No pain surpasses that of failing at the final step; no tragedy in this world exceeds the calamity of the yellow robe. Weeping, I write this account, to warn those who come after.

zh:
范撒小时候住在南门大街，家里开着一间包子铺。
她年幼时用铺子里的食材边角料练习着如何做成一个馒头，后来又在宫里用别人不要的边角料摸索着馒头的老味道，日复一日。
宫墙里的天地是四方的，实在太小，离家又那么远。要是想家，范撒就会找些边角料包上一个馒头，只要馒头还热着，家就不会永远在梦里。
宫墙小，天地却很大，有很多人在这世间留下自己的痕迹，可范撒不知道自己的意义在哪里。
日子像风一样，走了又来，一生是蒸一屉馒头的工夫，眨眼间便到了。范撒总是想，等出宫就回家，用这些年攒的钱过上好日子，但什么是好日子，她还没想明白，光阴就擦肩而过了。
en:
Fan Sa grew up on South Gate Avenue, helping at her family's little steamed bun stall.
As a child, she learned to turn scraps of dough and leftover fillings into flawless steamed buns. Later, inside the palace, she kept at it, salvaging what others discarded and coaxing from those scraps the old, comforting flavors she remembered.
The palace was a small, square world far from home. When longing hit, she'd find some scraps to make a steamed bun. As long as the bun was still warm, home wouldn't just be a dream forever.
The court was cramped, but the world beyond its walls was vast, and Fan Sa never knew what mark she might leave on it.
Life passed like steam from a tray of buns, one day folding into the next, and she kept promising herself she'd leave the palace, return home, and spend her savings on a "good life." She never got around to defining what that meant before the years slipped away.

zh:
被汗浸湿的纸条，拿着它来赴约的人，心情十分忐忑。

他一直在和女儿说等等。
等爹爹名扬江湖，就回来看你。
等爹爹求到方丈给你看病，就不会痛了。
等爹爹当上大官，就让全江湖的人都…… 都怎么样来着……
他忘了。

当他收到女儿相约的纸条时，他正好被上官嫌弃不能赴宴。
他想这是天意吧，今天他累了，累到不想再爬起来。
他可以退隐了，回乡吧，带着愿意回家的女儿一起。

于是他来了。
他雀跃地穿上随纸条附上的新鞋子，即使有点宽松。
他轻巧地朝着仓库奔来，比从城门擂台上滚下来更快，像一条重新开始蹦跳的老狗。
这次他不会让女儿再等了。
他对自己说，回家吧兰守持，牵着女儿的手，快乐地回家去吧。
en:
The sweat-stained note, trembled in the hand of the man on his way to the meeting, his heart heavy with anxiety. 

He kept telling his daughter to wait a little longer. 
Wait until Father's name echoes through the jianghu; then I'll return for you. 
Wait until Father persuades the abbot to ease your pain, so it no longer aches. 
Wait until Father rises to high office; then everyone in the jianghu will... will what again? 
He had forgotten. 

When he received her invitation, he was just being chastised by his superior for missing a banquet. 
He thought maybe it was fate—today he was too weary, too worn to get back on his feet. 
He could retire, go home, and bring his willing daughter along. 

So he came. 
He slipped on the new shoes that came with the letter, a little loose but cherished nonetheless. 
Light on his feet, he hurried toward the warehouse, quicker than falling down the city gate's arena—like an old dog learning to leap anew. 
This time, he vowed, he would never make his daughter wait again. 
Go home, Lan Shouchi. He whispered in his heart. Take her hand and go home, happily together.

离乡西行，已过旬月。一路所见，令石某颇多感慨。

金明池畔，见官家战船巍峨如山，本觉振奋，怎料转至隐雾林，竟又闻老幼泣诉毒雾为祸，致村落十室九空。
种种情状反差之巨，令石某一时心绪难平……只叹这盛世光华之下，犹有疮痍暗涌。石某习武多年，恨不能以手中陌刀荡清毒瘴，与其他江湖同道共解此厄。
如是心绪，提笔欲言，却不知所云。
本想早日归来，与你煮酒畅谈。奈何途经鸿沟古渠，见官兵鞭挞役夫，出手相阻，竟惹上官非。
为免祸连你，今且暂避风头，归期……恐将延后（笔迹至此，陡然潦草，似是换手仓促写就）。
待风波平息，石某定回不羡仙，与你畅饮一场，不醉不归。

en:
To the Wanderer:
It has been over a month since I left home and headed west. All that I have seen along the way has left me with profound mixed feelings.
In Kaifeng, Revelry Hall is brightly lit all night, echoing with endless songs. Yet, just around Forsaken Quarter, starving people with barely enough clothes to cover themselves huddle in the freezing wind.
By Jinming Pool, seeing the majestic imperial warships filled me with inspiration. But upon reaching the Mistveil Forest, I heard the young and old weeping over the poisonous mist that has left most homes empty.
The stark contrast of these scenes has left my mind deeply unsettled... I can only sigh that beneath the glory of this prosperous age, hidden wounds still fester. Having practiced martial arts for years, I wish I could use the Mo Blade in my hands to clear away this poisonous miasma and solve this crisis alongside other heroes of the martial world.
With such thoughts weighing on me, I picked up my pen to write, yet I know not what to say.
I originally intended to return early and talk freely with you over warm wine. Unfortunately, while passing the Grand Canal, I saw imperial soldiers whipping the laborers. I intervened, and consequently, ran into trouble with the authorities.
To avoid bringing disaster upon you, I will lay low for now. My return... I fear will be delayed. (The handwriting suddenly becomes sloppy here, as if written in a frantic rush with the other hand.)
Once the storm passes, I will definitely return to Blissful Retreat and drink with you until we drop.
Separated by a great distance, I hope you take care.
Shi Jingtian

en:
"Where fish and salt gather, a market grows; where cooking fires rise, a village forms."
West Lake is rich with fish and other aquatic bounty. Tao Gu's Records of Strange Things recounts how Mao Sheng, a man of the Wuyue Region, once wrote a joking Register of Honors for the Water Folk, praising the local fish and shrimp as something "found nowhere else under heaven."
Wuyue cuisine favors fresh, clean tastes, and fish is never cooked with heavy seasoning. Over time, the sweet-and-sour method came into favor, and by Southern Song, the Millet Dream Record lists it among Lin'an's schools of fish cookery.
The dish demands the most exacting ingredients. The fish must be kept alive in clean water until every trace of grit is purged, then poached in boiling water until just done. The art lies in the timing and heat, and the balance of sweet and sour.
