考盘在阿，硕人之薖。独寐寤歌，永矢弗过。
考盘在陆，硕人之轴。独寐寤宿，永矢弗告。

硕人

硕人其颀，衣锦褧衣。齐侯之子，卫侯之妻。东宫之妹，邢侯之姨，谭公维私。
手如柔荑，肤如凝脂。领如蝤蛴，齿如瓠犀，螓首蛾眉。巧笑倩兮，美目盻兮。
硕人敖敖，说于农郊。四牡有骄，朱𪩸镳镳，翟茀以朝。大夫宿退，无使君劳。
河水洋洋，北流活活。施罛濊濊，鳣鲔发发，葭菼揭揭。庶姜孽孽，庶士有朅。
氓
氓之蚩蚩，抱布贸丝。匪来贸丝，来即我谋。送子涉淇，至于顿丘。匪我愆期，子无良媒。将子无怒，秋以为期。
乘彼垝垣，以望复关。不见复关，泣涕涟涟。既见复关，载笑载言。尔卜尔筮，体无咎言。以尔车来，以我贿迁。
桑之未落，其叶沃若。于嗟鸠兮，无食桑葚。于嗟女兮，无与士耽。士之耽兮，犹可说也。女之耽兮，不可说也。
桑之落矣，其黄而陨。自我徂尔，三岁食贫。淇水汤汤，渐车帷裳。女也不爽，士贰其行。士也罔极，二三其德。
三岁为妇，靡室劳矣。夙兴夜寐，靡有朝矣。言既遂矣，至于暴矣。兄弟不知，咥其笑矣。静言思之，躬自悼矣。
及尔偕老，老使我怨。淇则有岸，隰则有泮。总角之宴，言笑晏晏。信誓旦旦，不思其反。反是不思，亦已焉哉。
……
en:
【Odes of the States · Odes of Wei】

The Odes of Qi Ao

Look at that bend in the Qi River, where green bamboos grow lush and fair. There is a noble gentleman, refined as if carved and polished, like jade ground smooth. Solemn and dignified, resplendent and bright. This noble gentleman, forever unforgettable.
Look at that bend in the Qi River, where green bamboos grow thick and green. There is a noble gentleman, with ear-plugs of precious jade, and a cap-buckle shining like stars. Solemn and dignified, resplendent and bright. This noble gentleman, forever unforgettable.
Look at that bend in the Qi River, where green bamboos grow dense as a mat. There is a noble gentleman, precious as gold and tin, pure as a jade tablet or disc. Broad-minded and generous, leaning on his chariot's rails. Skilled in jest and banter, yet never cruel or harsh.

The Odes of Kao Pan

My hut is by the stream, the great man's heart is broad. Alone I sleep and wake and speak, my vow I'll never break.
My hut is on the hill, the great man's heart is free. Alone I sleep and wake and sing, my vow I'll never stray.
My hut is on the plain, the great man's heart is firm. Alone I sleep and wake and rest, my vow I'll never tell.

The Odes of the Great Lady

Tall and stately is the great lady, in broidered robes with plain over-garment. Daughter of the Marquis of Qi, wife of the Marquis of Wei. Sister of the Crown Prince, aunt to the Marquis of Xing, and sister-in-law to the Duke of Tan.
Her hands are like soft blades of grass, her skin like congealed cream. Her neck is like the tree-grub, her teeth like melon seeds. A broad forehead and fine eyebrows. Her lovely smile dimples her cheeks, her beautiful eyes sparkle.
Stately and tall is the great lady, halting in the suburban fields. Four stallions prance proudly, red trappings fluttering, her pheasant-feathered carriage comes to court. The officers retire early, lest they weary their lord.
The river waters surge vast, flowing northward with a gurgle. Casting nets with a splash, sturgeon and carp leap, reeds and rushes stand tall. The many bridesmaids are splendid, the many escorts are stalwart.
The Odes of Mang
A simple fellow, Mang, came with cloth to barter for silk. Not truly to barter for silk, but to seek me for marriage. I saw you across the Qi River, as far as Dunqiu. It was not I who delayed the date, you had no proper matchmaker. Pray do not be angry, let autumn be our time.
I climbed that ruined wall, to gaze towards Fuguan. Not seeing Fuguan, my tears fell streaming. When I saw Fuguan, I laughed and talked. You consulted tortoise and yarrow stalks, no ill omens were found. You came with your carriage, to take me and my dowry away.
When the mulberry leaves are fresh, lush and glossy. Ah, turtledove, do not eat the mulberries! Ah, young maiden, do not dally with men! A man who dallies can still break free. A maiden who dallies cannot be freed.
When the mulberry leaves fall, yellow and dropping. Since I came to you, three years of hardship. The Qi River's waters swell, soaking the carriage curtains. I have not erred, but you have changed your ways. A man's heart is fickle, his virtue inconstant.
For three years as your wife, I toiled without rest. Rising early and sleeping late, never a morning of ease. My purpose once achieved, you turned to cruelty. My brothers do not know, they laugh at me. In silence I ponder, and grieve for myself.
We vowed to grow old together, but growing old brings me only bitterness. The Qi River has its banks, the marsh its bounds. In the innocence of childhood, we talked and laughed joyfully. Our vows were sincere, never thinking they'd be broken. Since they are broken, let it be so, and be done with it.
...

zh:
大葱多以分株之法繁殖。欲育其苗，可先于室内培育，择土质松软、排灌便宜、三年未植葱蒜韭类之沃土为苗床。
葱苗于室内育成后，可于早夏移栽至田。起苗时，择去病、虫、弱、伤、杂及抽苔者，按苗之大小分三等，分别栽植。
定植时，先于沟中灌水，待水尽渗，将葱苗垂直插入土中。须令葱苗上齐下不齐，不得掩埋心叶。
采收时，取窄条镢，距葱株约一寸半处下镢，掀起培土，使葱白显露。取出后晾晒半日，继而拣选分等，剔除病残弱小之棵，以稻草捆作七斤之束，束腰扎三道，即可待售。
en:
These plants were commonly propagated by division. To raise seedlings, they could first be started indoors in a seedbed of loose, fertile soil with good drainage and irrigation, preferably on land where no allium crops (such as garlic, onions, or chives) had been grown in the previous three years.
Once the seedlings were ready, they were transplanted to the fields in early summer. When lifting them, any that were diseased, insect-damaged, weak, injured, mixed, or already bolting were discarded. The rest were sorted into three grades by size and planted separately.
Before transplanting, water was first poured into the furrow. Once it had fully soaked in, the seedlings were set upright in the soil. Their tops were to be kept level while the lower portions sat at varying depths, and the heart leaves were not to be buried.
At harvest, a narrow hoe was used about one and a half inches from the plant to loosen the ridged soil and expose the white stalk. After lifting, the crop was left out to dry for half a day, then sorted by grade. Any diseased, damaged, weak, or undersized plants were removed. The remainder were tied with rice straw into bundles of seven jin, fastened in three places around the middle, and made ready for sale.

zh:
任小平永远也搞不懂郑然，很多小孩子都是笨瓜，郑然不是笨瓜，但比笨瓜更奇怪。
今儿又有一个笨瓜问了一个傻问题：“咱们能看见树，看见河，那瞎子眼前都是黑乎乎的，那算是能看见什么？”
任小平瞧瞧问这话的娃娃，又瞧了瞧郑然，这是天大的傻问题：“你说瞎娃娃吗？瞎子啥也看不见呗。”
“我看得见！”
“瞎娃娃又说谎！瞎子能看见什么？”
“我、我看得见，我、能看见——”
“看见梦！”
“大伙睡的时候都会闭着眼睛做梦，我问过了，这时候大家眼前都是黑乎乎的，但那些人只是在、在做梦。”

任小平愣了一下，没搞明白这一套，但是不妨碍他习惯性地哈哈大笑——“瞎娃娃说她做梦，瞎娃——”他的话还没有说完，就被他娘一巴掌拍在了背上，像是拎着小鸡仔一样拎了起来，以至于郑然听他叫救命的声音，都比刚刚说话的位置高了一截。
任小平她娘的左手拎着儿子，右手牵着郑然，走回自己的家里，这个女人利落地问他们刚刚吵了什么，任小平说了一通，不知道他娘到底听懂没，但如往常一般，他娘最后下了结论，阿然说得对，她闭上眼睛，看见的就是梦。
“是梦！”
“对对对，阿然能看见梦的。”

于是，阿然会活在一辈子的梦里。
那又如何，只要她能一辈子活在漂亮的梦里，只要有人愿意让她一辈子活在漂亮的梦里，世上总得有人活在漂亮的梦里。
而阿然是个好孩子，阿然可以活在漂亮的梦里。

但阿然也有一个梦，阿然不要看见这条街上的人一个一个消失，阿然长大之后，想要站在每一个喜欢的人身前。
只是，那些算命的道士说，梦是和现实总是相反的。
但没关系的，阿然，如果世间是一个循环往复的故事，那么梦和现实也许会拥有，同一个终点。
en:
Ren Xiaoping would never understand Zheng Ran. Many children were fools, but Zheng Ran wasn't a fool. She was something stranger than a fool.
That day, another fool asked a stupid question: "We can see trees and rivers, but blind people only see darkness, so what do they actually see?"
Ren Xiaoping glanced at the child who asked, then at Zheng Ran. What an idiotic question.
"You mean blind kids? They see nothing, obviously."
"I can see!"
"Blind kid lies! What could you possibly see?"
"I... I can see... I can see—"
"Dreams!"
"When everyone sleeps, they close their eyes and dream. I asked before, and when that happens, people see darkness too, but they're just... dreaming."

Ren Xiaoping froze, unable to make sense of this logic, but that didn't stop him from bursting into laughter. "Blind kid says she sees dreams! Blind kid..." Before he could finish, his mother's palm smacked his back, lifting him like a chick by the scruff. Zheng Ran heard his "Help!" from a much higher position than before.
Ren Xiaoping's mother carried her son in one hand and held Zheng Ran's hand in the other, leading them home. The woman briskly asked what they'd been arguing about. Ren Xiaoping babbled an explanation—who knew if she understood? But as always, she delivered her verdict: "Ran is right. When she closes her eyes, she sees dreams."
"Dreams!"
"Yes, yes, Ran can see dreams." And so, Ran would live in dreams her whole life.

So what? 
As long as she could live in beautiful dreams forever, 
as long as someone was willing to let her live in beautiful dreams forever, then this world ought to have people who dwell in beautiful dreams. 
And Ran was a good child. Ran deserved to live in beautiful dreams. 

But Ran had one dream of her own. She didn't want to watch the people on this street disappear one by one. When she grew up, she wanted to stand in front of everyone she loved. 
Only... the fortune telling Daoists said dreams were always the opposite of reality.
But it didn't matter, Ran. If the world is a story that cycles endlessly, then perhaps dreams and reality share the same ending.
Run! I... I can't keep up...
Tang Xuan Yi Shao
Ground Sichuan Peppercorn

Whether it's a major event or a trivial matter, Bu Jiujie always struggles to make up his mind. From choosing what to eat to deciding whether to go out, he spends a lot of time weighing the pros and cons repeatedly. For example, choosing what to have for lunch can take him until dinner time. He wonders whether to have milk with his pancake, if he doesn't, his throat will be dry, but he's too lazy to go elsewhere to get milk. In fact, for such trivial matters, there is no loss no matter which choice he makes, but Bu Jiujie always gets stuck on minor details. Sometimes his indecision leads to missed opportunities, and he ultimately suffers the consequences. 
He is very dependent on the advice of friends or family. Even after people around him analyze the pros and cons comprehensively and give him suggestions, he still nitpicks at their advice as if looking for faults. In contrast, when his friends face choices, he can provide surprisingly clear suggestions.

zh:
汤念念最烦别人说她嘴硬心软。
“我的心可比嘴硬多了！”
路过的流民蹲在摊子前喝汤，她嘟囔着“又来了又来了”，盛汤的手却始终没停下过。
猫儿狗儿在她脚边转悠，她嘴上骂骂咧咧，可到最后，猫儿狗儿的嘴里都塞满了丸子。
摊子上忙活一天，范芗芗算算账，叹气说今天又没赚钱。
汤念念把抹布往案板上一摔，没好气道：“俺早就说了别这么干！恁耳朵长哪儿去了？”
可第二天天没亮，她比范芗芗起得还早，蹲在灶台前头烧火。
范芗芗起来看见她，笑她不是说不干了？
汤念念脸一红，瓮声瓮气道：“俺……俺就是睡不着。”
她没说的是，每天晚上一闭眼，都能想起那碗鱼汤。白花花的，泛着油光，烫得她眼泪直流。
那时候她以为自己要死了，是娘亲用一碗鱼汤，向阎罗王讨回了自己的命。
所以她嘴上再凶，手里的活却从来没停过。
流民来了，她照样端菜上桌，照样给每个碗里多添一勺。
流民喝光了鱼汤，捧着空碗，又摸了摸空空的口袋，小心翼翼地觑了觑汤念念。
四目相对时，汤念念忽然觉得心里头有点愧意，于是她急忙瞅向别处，装作不在意。
“没、没啥大不了的，先吃饱饭最要紧……别的事，吃饱了再说。”
en:
Tang Niannian absolutely hated it when people said she was all bark and no bite.
"My heart is a lot harder than my mouth!" she'd snap.
Yet, whenever starving refugees huddled around their stall, she'd groan, "Not this again," even as her hands kept steadily ladling out oversized portions.
Stray cats and dogs would weave between her ankles while she cursed them out, but somehow, every single one of them always trotted away stuffed with meatballs.
At the end of another exhausting day, Fan Xiangxiang would tally up the ledger and sigh over the lack of profit.
Niannian would slam her rag down onto the counter. "I told you we can't keep giving food away! Do you ever listen to me?"
But the very next morning, long before the sun came up, she'd be out of bed before her mother, squatting by the stove to stoke the fire. When Xiangxiang woke up and caught her, teasingly asking if she hadn't just threatened to quit, Niannian's face would turn beet red.
"I... I just couldn't sleep, okay?" she'd grumble.
What she kept to herself was that every night, when she closed her eyes, she still saw that bowl of fish soup. Milky, glistening with broth, and so scalding hot it had brought tears to her eyes.
She had been so sure she was dying back then. It was her mother who had bargained with King Yama, buying her life back with a single bowl of soup.
So, no matter how much she complained, her hands never stopped working. When hungry refugees showed up, she served them just the same, always sneaking an extra ladle into their bowls.
After scraping their plates clean, the refugees would pat their empty pockets and shoot her nervous, apologetic looks. Whenever she caught them staring, a weird pang of guilt would hit her. She'd quickly look away, pretending to be busy with something else.
"It's fine, whatever... Getting a hot meal in your belly is what matters. We can worry about the rest later."

en:
Traveling north from Verdant Wilds and crossing Xiu River, the plains stretch vast for a thousand miles, home to countless steeds galloping freely—this is Wildmane Ranch. North of the pasture lies Finesteed Hamlet, nestled against North Ridge with a stone cliff rising behind it. Both the village and ranch belong to the Qi family of horse tamers. Legend has it their ancestors were horse merchants from Youzhou; after the Sixteen Prefectures of Yanyun fell, the family migrated to Qinghe. Seeing the lush pastures here, they established the ranch and built the village. It's also said that during the Xiande era of the previous dynasty, Finesteed Hamlet presented a thousand fine horses to aid Emperor Shizong's northern expedition. 
Arriving at Wildmane Ranch today, the village buildings still stand, and a few horse tamers tend horses in the wild. Yet the village is no longer what it once was—how lamentable.

他说拿着这根弦，去到岱山九幽洞的人，可得道真之传承。
垂垂老矣的道真掌教在他的后半生，第一次当众提到了雩真。

有人说，他想到的是雩真要还在，能与之并肩作战，该是如何光景？
也有人说，他终于突破了功法的最后一重。
天地困窘，牢笼都是虚妄。他想告诉雩真他胜了自己，胜了时间。

此弦被取出，是因为李昭雪曾亲眼见证了它“切开”镇冠珏的一幕。
李昭雪想，那它也定然能“切开”九幽洞，放她出来。
en:
Li Zhaoxue drew the artifact before the bloodstained gates of Chang'an amidst a relentless tide of rebel forces and a sea of the fallen.
He knew not how much longer the city could hold.
To the survivors, he made a vow: whoever carried this single string to the Abyssal Cavern of Mount Tai would inherit the true legacy of the Daozhen Sect. It was the first time in his twilight years that the aging patriarch had spoken the name Yuzhen aloud.

Some whispered he was dreaming of what could have been, of how it would feel to have her fighting by his side once more.
Others claimed he had finally pierced the ultimate veil of his martial cultivation, realizing that the confines of heaven and earth were mere illusions. Perhaps he simply wanted to tell Yuzhen that he had finally conquered himself and time.
But the true secret of the string remained his alone.
Li Zhaoxue had unsheathed it for one reason: he had once seen it cleave the impenetrable Zhenguan Jade. If it could sever the jade, he reasoned, it could surely sever the bindings of the Abyssal Cavern and finally set her free.

The atmosphere here is eerie. Wearing a helmet, I stepped inside and received a hero's welcome from the soldiers—they must have mistaken me for a general.
Then, as I beat the war drum, I accidentally knocked the helmet off. Was that it? Was that the moment everything changed? Because suddenly, their warmth turned to steel, and every sword was drawn.

What secret does that helmet hide? I couldn't grab it in the confusion.
With such elite troops inside, I could investigate no further and was forced to return with nothing.

My investigation suggests this was an old Anxi Army garrison. An army base wouldn't have legendary treasures or martial arts.
And it certainly wouldn't be filled with beauties. That letter had to be a vicious lie!

A warning to the next soul fated to find this: Run.

zh:
午夜的寒风吹谢了灯花，但开封府尹赵光义仍未入眠。
他的耳中有太多声音了。自唐钱收缴之策推行，反对的，嘲讽的，乞怜的声音总是时时刻刻地在他的耳畔响起。
可他绝不会后退一步，兄长青年时的考验在沙场之上，而他的考验，就在这看似风平浪静的开封城之中。
人人都说兄长胸怀宽阔，只有他知道兄长也睡不着。
这天下群狼环伺，一统之前，谁又能卧榻安眠？
他不怕天下人拿自己和兄长比较，他坚信他们本质上都是一样的人。因此兄长没有反对他，没有反对，已是足够的支持。
就让兄长去做天下人心中那个仁慈的英雄吧，他不怕去扮演那个冷血的角色。
这是他的第一步。他相信自己将拥有自己的功业，自己的千秋，来日史家回看之时，他不会被埋没在兄长的光辉中，他将以自己毕生的光芒，与其……并肩同辉。
en:
The midnight wind snuffed out the lanterns, but Zhao Guangyi, Governor of Kaifeng Prefecture, remained awake.
The voices wouldn't stop. Since implementing the Tang Coin confiscation reform, his ears rang with protests, mockery, and pleas.
Yet he wouldn't yield. Where his elder brother proved himself on battlefields, his trial was this deceptively calm Kaifeng City.
They call his brother magnanimous. Only he knows the Emperor sleeps no better.
How can any ruler rest with wolves at the gates?
He wasn't afraid of the world comparing him to his elder brother - he firmly believed they were fundamentally the same. That's why his brother never opposed him. And that absence of opposition was support enough.
Let history remember his brother as the benevolent hero. He'd gladly be the ruthless one.
This was merely his opening move. There'd be more, his own legacy, his own glory. When historians wrote of this era, his light wouldn't be overshadowed. It would burn alongside his brother's.

zh:
周显德六年，十二仙遇到了改变他一生的人。那人青睐他的书画，赏识他的手艺，告诉他，他的天赋是何等宝贵，而这样的天赋应该用到正确的地方。这年年末，他用家传的蜀锦技艺织造了一件黄袍。从此，他成了大宋开国皇帝眼前的红人。

十二仙，世故了然也天真。他当然不知，所谓”正确“也不过是任人打扮的小姑娘，只是这次，他足够幸运。这些年，十二仙以白衣之身帮朝廷做了不少事。三年前，他献上了五牙大舰的图纸，如今又开始探查杀神出庙一事。

不久前，十二仙得知江南人手中有唐宫羽衣所余原缎一尺，而天下竟无一人能将其风华复原。十二仙动了心思，“天赋应该用到正确的地方”。也许有一天，他能得见羽衣风华。
en:
In the sixth year of the Zhou Xiande era, Twelve Immortals met the person who would change his life forever. That man admired his calligraphy and painting, and praised his craftsmanship. He told him his talent was a treasure, a gift that ought to be used in the "right" way. At the end of that year, Twelve Immortals wove a yellow robe using the family's ancient Shu brocade technique. From then on, he became a favored figure before the founding emperor of the Song dynasty.

Worldly-wise yet still a little naive, Twelve Immortals did not understand then that "the right way" merely meant being dressed up and used like a pretty little girl. This time, he was simply lucky enough to be favored. Over the years, dressed always in white, Twelve Immortals quietly undertook many tasks for the court. Three years ago, he presented the blueprints for the Quintadent Warship. Now, he had turned his attention to investigating the mystery of the God of Killing.

Not long ago, he learned that someone in Jiangnan still possessed a surviving scrap of silk from the Beauty's Garment. Yet no one in the world could replicate its former brilliance. Twelve Immortals felt a stir in his heart.

"Talent ought to be used in the right way."

Perhaps, one day, he would be the one to restore the glory of the Beauty's Garment.

墨城有一奇匠，醉心机巧，无妻无女，独自过活。
某日得闲制人偶，历经艰难终制成。这人偶真叫一个栩栩如生，风情万种。奇匠日渐迷恋，将其起名为巧姬，更对外称其为自家娘子。
一日，奇匠外出为之寻材。一迷路书生误入其室，见巧姬，惊为天人，遂与之相伴。
时光荏苒，书生与巧姬情愫暗生，誓结连理。
然奇匠终归，二人正情深共浴，呀呀呀，好一对痴男浪女！
奇匠见私有之巧姬竟被他人所夺，怒而斩下书生头颅。
巧姬裸身出浴，顷刻泪如雨下，屋外忽而风起。须臾间，巧姬关节尽裂，肝肠木落成灰，只留下一地骇人心碎。

世人皆言，人偶无情，却不知此中情深似海，爱逾生死。
奇匠日夜思念，曾几番试图重制复活巧姬，皆无效也，终成一痴。
巧姬之影，再难寻觅，空余奇匠一人度过漫长余生……
en:
In Mohist City lived a master artisan, devoted to his intricate mechanisms and living a solitary life. One day, he poured his skill into crafting a puppet so lifelike and enchanting that he named her Qiao and called her his wife.
While he was away gathering materials, a lost scholar wandered into the workshop, entranced by Qiao's beauty. The two quietly fell in love and pledged their hearts to one another.
But when the artisan returned and found them together, jealousy consumed him. Enraged to see his "property" stolen, the artisan severed the scholar's head in a single stroke.
Heartbroken, Qiao was weeping. The wind stirred. Her wooden joints splintered; her clockwork heart crumbled to ash. All that remained was a wreckage of heartbreak.

Though many say puppets lack feeling, her love was deeper than life itself.
After Qiao vanished, the artisan lived out his days alone, forever mourning the love he lost.

Because the harvesting window is so incredibly short and yields are tiny, an old saying claims: "Pre-Qingming tea is worth its weight in gold." Pre-Grain Rain tea is picked a bit later. zh:
【离娄章句下】

孟子曰：舜生于诸冯，迁于负夏，卒于鸣条，东夷之人也。文王生于岐周，卒于毕郢，西夷之人也。地之相去也，千有余里；世之相后也，千有余岁。得志行乎中国，若合符节。先圣后圣，其揆一也。
子产听郑国之政，以其乘舆济人于溱洧。孟子曰：惠而不知为政。岁十一月，徒杠成，十二月，舆梁成。民未病涉也。君子平其政，行辟人可也，焉得人人而济之？故为政者，每人而悦之，日亦不足矣。
孟子告齐宣王曰：君之视臣如手足，则臣视君如腹心；君之视臣如犬马，则臣视君如国人；君之视臣如土芥，则臣视君如寇雠。
王曰：礼，为旧君有服，何如斯可为服矣？
曰：谏行言听，膏泽下于民；有故而去，则君使人导之出疆，又先于其所往；去三年不反，然后收其田里，此之谓三有礼焉。如此则为之服矣。今也为臣，谏则不行，言则不听，膏泽不下于民；有故而去，则君搏执之，又极之于其所往。去之日，遂收其田里，此之谓寇雠。寇雠何服之有？
孟子曰：无罪而杀士，则大夫可以去；无罪而戮民，则士可以徙。
孟子曰：君仁莫不仁，君义莫不义。
孟子曰：非礼之礼，非义之义，大人弗为。
孟子曰：中也养不中，才也养不才，故人乐有贤父兄也。如中也弃不中，才也弃不才，则贤不肖之相去，其间不能以寸。
孟子曰：人有不为也，而后可以有为。
孟子曰：言人之不善，当如后患何？
孟子曰：仲尼不为已甚者！
孟子曰：大人者，言不必信，行不必果，惟义所在。
孟子曰：大人者，不失其赤子之心者也。
孟子曰：养生者不足以当大事，惟送死可以当大事。
孟子曰：君子深造之以道，欲其自得之也。自得之，则居之安；居之安，则资之深；资之深，则取之左右逢其原。故君子欲其自得之也。
孟子曰：博学而详说之，将以反说约也。
孟子曰：以善服人者，未有能服人者也。以善养人，然后能服天下。天下不心服而王者，未之有也。
孟子曰：言无实不祥，不祥之实，蔽贤者当之。
徐子曰：仲尼亟称于水，曰：水哉，水哉！何取于水也？
孟子曰：原泉混混，不舍昼夜，盈科而后进，放乎四海。有本者如是，是之取尔。苟为无本，七八月之间雨集，沟浍皆盈，其涸也，可立而待也。故声闻过情，君子耻之。
孟子曰：人之所以异于禽兽者几希，庶民去之，君子存之。舜明于庶物，察于人伦，由仁义行，非行仁义也。

en:
【Lilou Chapter II】

Mencius said: Shun was born in Zhufeng, moved to Fuxia, and died in Mingtiao—a man of the Eastern Yi tribes. King Wen was born in Qizhou and died in Biying—a man of the Western Yi tribes. The distance between their lands was more than a thousand li, and the time between their eras was more than a thousand years. Yet when they realized their ambitions and practiced their ways in the Central Kingdoms, their actions matched like the two halves of a tally. The earlier sage and the later sage, their principles were one and the same.
Zichan, in administering the government of the state of Zheng, would use his own carriage to ferry people across the Zhen and Wei rivers. Mencius said: "This shows kindness but ignorance of governance. By the eleventh month, footbridges are completed; by the twelfth month, carriage bridges are finished. The people are not troubled by crossing. A gentleman, when his governance is equitable, may have his path cleared as he travels—how can he ferry every single person across? Thus, if a ruler tries to please each individual, his days would not suffice."
Mencius said to King Xuan of Qi: "If a ruler regards his ministers as his hands and feet, then the ministers will regard him as their heart and mind. If a ruler regards his ministers as dogs and horses, then the ministers will regard him as a mere fellow countryman. If a ruler regards his ministers as dirt and grass, then the ministers will regard him as a bandit and an enemy."
The King said: "According to ritual, there is mourning prescribed for a former ruler. Under what circumstances should one observe mourning for him?"
Mencius replied: "When remonstrances are heeded and advice is followed, so that benefits flow down to the people; when a minister leaves for a reason, the ruler sends someone to guide him out of the borders and makes arrangements ahead at his destination; and if he does not return after three years, only then does the ruler reclaim his fields and residence—this is called the threefold courtesy. In such a case, mourning is observed. But nowadays, when a minister's remonstrances are not implemented and his words are not heeded, so that benefits do not reach the people; when he leaves for a reason, the ruler seizes and detains him, and does his utmost to hinder him at his destination; and on the very day he leaves, his fields and residence are confiscated—this is called treating him as a bandit and enemy. What mourning is there for a bandit and enemy?"
Mencius said: "If scholars are killed without crime, then the high officials may leave. If the people are slaughtered without crime, then the scholars may move away."
Mencius said: "If the ruler is benevolent, none will be unbenevolent. If the ruler is righteous, none will be unrighteous."
Mencius said: "The great man does not practice rituals that are not truly ritual, nor righteousness that is not truly righteous."
Mencius said: "The balanced nurture the unbalanced; the talented nurture the untalented. Therefore, people delight in having worthy fathers and elder brothers. If the balanced were to abandon the unbalanced, and the talented were to abandon the untalented, then the gap between the worthy and the unworthy would be less than an inch."
Mencius said: "A man must have what he will not do, before he can have what he will do."
Mencius said: "To speak of others' faults—what about the future troubles?"
Mencius said: "Confucius did not do things to excess!"
Mencius said: "The great man does not necessarily keep his word, nor necessarily accomplish his deeds; he only follows where righteousness lies."
Mencius said: "The great man is one who does not lose the heart of a newborn child."
Mencius said: "Nourishing the living is not enough to be considered a great affair; only sending off the dead can be considered a great affair."
Mencius said: "The gentleman advances deeply in the Way, desiring to acquire it for himself. Having acquired it for himself, he dwells in it peacefully. Dwelling in it peacefully, he draws from it deeply. Drawing from it deeply, he finds its source wherever he turns. Therefore, the gentleman desires to acquire it for himself."
Mencius said: "Learn broadly and explain in detail, so as to return to simplicity in speech."
Mencius said: "He who tries to subdue others with goodness has never been able to subdue them. He who nourishes others with goodness can then subdue the world. There has never been one who became king without winning the hearts of the world."
Mencius said: "Words without substance are inauspicious. The substance of inauspiciousness falls upon those who obstruct the worthy."
Xu Zi said: "Confucius repeatedly praised water, saying, 'Water! Oh, water!' What did he find in water?"
Mencius said: "Water from a spring gushes forth, never ceasing day or night. It fills the hollows and then moves on, until it reaches the four seas. Such is the nature of that which has a source. This is what he valued. If it were without a source, like the rain that collects in the seventh and eighth months, filling the ditches and channels, its drying up can be waited for standing. Therefore, a reputation that exceeds reality is a disgrace to the gentleman."
Mencius said: "That whereby man differs from the birds and beasts is but slight. The common people discard it, while the gentleman preserves it. Shun understood the nature of things and discerned human relations. He acted from benevolence and righteousness; he did not just perform acts of benevolence and righteousness."
…

zh:
横江吾徒鉴之：
淮深归葬凉州，与万千归义英魂同饮霜雪。尘障已破，执念俱消。今为师弥留之际，留此铁血二誓：
其一：狂澜一门，誓与庙堂绝涉。自今而后，鹰扬不奉诏，龙战岂承恩！
其二：狂澜弟子，死后不留金玉满堂，不留青史虚名，不留残骨累世，酒葫满盛米油酒，黄泉路上无冻馁。
若见腰悬“一葫不归”之客，务必以礼相待。此子侠肝义胆，颇有我狂澜风骨，若愿共饮，当归入门下。
诀矣，珍重。
en:
To my disciple: 
Let my bones be interred in Liangzhou, to share the eternal frost with the myriad righteous spirits gathered there. The mortal veil is torn, and my worldly obsessions have vanished. As I lie dying, I leave for our clan two vows, sworn in iron and blood. 
The First Vow: The sect of Raging Tides will cut all ties with the throne. From this day on, our eagles answer no summons, and our dragons seek no grace! 
The Second Vow: Our disciples shall not pass from this world leaving fortunes, false glory, or even their bones to trouble the living. Their gourds shall be full of rice, oil, and wine, to ensure no soul goes hungry or cold on the journey beyond. 
Should you encounter one who wears the "Gourd of Remembrance," show him honor. That man possesses a hero's heart and our Raging Tides spirit. If he is willing to drink with you, welcome him into our fold. 
Farewell, and be well.

zh:
游侠，见字如面。
前些时日，老朽随府尹大人巡查蒙学，见学堂里的娃娃们一个个正襟危坐，埋首书卷，连我等走近了都未曾察觉。
老朽心下好奇，是何等妙文，能让这些上蹿下跳的娃娃们如此专心？一问才知，他们手中所读，竟是你前些时日所赠。
老朽又问，这些书好在何处？娃娃们七嘴八舌，老朽这才知道，原来你竟为每个孩子都择了不同的书，实在是费心了。而听闻老朽与你相熟，他们都央着我，定要代他们向你道声谢。
只是，真要问他们想说什么，这群小家伙却面露羞赧，讷讷而止了。最后，老朽想了个法子，让他们把想说的话都诉诸笔端，一并封在信里了。至于写了什么，老朽绝未偷看！
对了，娃娃们还托我转交几幅画作，说是读了书卷后的有感而发。他们都说，游侠你是他们见过最有眼光的人，定能欣赏他们的大作。
哈哈，看来往后若再有与孩子们打交道的差事，找游侠准是没错了。

en:
Dear Wanderer,

The other day, I accompanied the Prefect on an inspection of the village school. The children sat straight at their desks, noses buried in scrolls, so absorbed they didn't even notice us draw near.
Curious what could hold their attention so completely, I asked. Turns out, they were reading the very books you gifted them not long ago.
I inquired further: what made these books so special? The little ones burst into chatter, and that's when I learned you had chosen a different book for each child. What thoughtfulness.
When they heard I knew you, they begged me to pass along their thanks.
But when I asked what they wanted to say, shyness took over, and words failed them. So I suggested they write it down instead. Their letters are enclosed. And no, I did not peek!
Oh, and they also asked me to send you a few drawings. Inspired, they said, by your books. They all agreed you're the most discerning person they've ever met, and that you'd surely appreciate their masterpieces.
Seems to me, whenever there's a task involving children, you're the one to call.

zh:
阿婆过世后，江湖人寻到这里，说外面四处打仗，遍地都是食腐虫，求我出手救人，于是我跟着他们走了。
我用一年时间驱赶了各处食腐虫，江湖人却跟着我回了村子，要我交出长生虫。
这话惹恼了鹿神娘娘，山裂出一道大口子，我和村里的人都掉了进去。
我们呼喊求救，却没人理会，我决定为大家种下长生虫，等着返回地上的那一天。
长生之后，我不再像我了，我不会因为大家的逝去而悲伤，也不再想离开这里。
陈怀卿带着一身伤来了这里，说他听到长生仙人于此飞升的江湖传言。我知道他撑不了多久，问他要不要长生，他说不，说生如岁华，一世一荣，说人有寿限的好处在于不断轮回，变为男人女人，白鹿毒虫。一旦长生，便被定在了同一个身份里。
我没法体会他的大道理，我说我对他已没有利用价值，他还给我那盏灯就走了。
灯里放着他研制的丹方，它能让长生者变回普通人。如果他真是我的弟子，这便是汉人话里的“青出于蓝”了。
多年前给出去的善意，最后又传回了我手中。望着这点灯火，我记起了一点点常人的情感。
等丹药炼成，解了大家的长生，我就要离开这里，将我的所学都传给他。
如果我没等到丹药炼成，这张丹方也能帮助后世想摆脱长生的人。
送我长生虫时，阿婆说长生既是无价之宝，也一文不值，我终于明白了她的意思。
生如岁华，一世一荣。
en:
After Granny's death, the wanderers found me. War raged outside, they said. Carrion-devouring insects swarmed the land. They pleaded for my help. So I went.

For a year, I drove back the swarms. But instead of gratitude, those men followed me home, demanding the Everlasting Parasite.

Their greed angered the Deer Goddess. The mountain split open, and our village plunged into the abyss.

We screamed for help. No one came. So I planted the Everlasting Parasite within us all, waiting for the day we might return to the surface.

But immortality changed me. I no longer mourned the dead. I no longer cared to leave this place.

Then Chen Huaiqing came, battered and bleeding. He'd heard rumors that the Immortal of Longevity had ascended from this very abyss. I knew he wouldn't last. "Do you want to live forever?" I asked.

"No," he said. "Life is like the seasons—bloom once, fade once. The mercy of death is rebirth, to return as man or woman, as a white deer or venomous insect. But immortality? It traps you in one shape, unchanging."

I could not grasp his wisdom then. "I was of no more use to you," I told him. He left me the lamp and walked away. Inside was his life's work. A formula to undo immortality. If he truly was my disciple, then perhaps this was what the Han call "outshining the mentor."

The kindness I'd given long ago had returned to me. Holding that faint light, I felt something, flickers of a mortal heart. Once the pill is ready and our endless life is broken, I'll leave this abyss. I'll pass on all I've learned to him. And if I don't live to see the dawn? Well, this formula will remain for those who someday wish to shed eternity.

When Granny gave me the Everlasting Parasite, she said, "Immortality is both priceless and worthless." Now, at last, I understand. Life is like the seasons, which bloom once, fade once.

那眼神胡扒皮很熟悉，他和他养的狗——馒头也是这样长大。神使鬼差地，胡扒皮朝它招了招手，决定把它捡回家。
en:
Bun was the second stray dog Hu Bapi had taken in.
He was walking down the street one day when this dog came darting out of nowhere and scurried into a corner. The dog dropped a meat bun, god knows where it found one, and sat there panting like crazy.
Startled, Hu Bapi started cussing up a storm. The dog was shaking all over, but it kept its front paws firmly on that bun, staring up at Hu Bapi with pure vigilance.
That look hit close to home. It was the same look Mantou, his first dog, had when he was a pup. Something tugged at Hu Bapi. He gave a little wave and decided right then to bring the dog home.

鬼街十四煞中，七煞鬼公子姜隗，最令人闻风丧胆。
他似人似鬼，似正似邪。有时他是最慈悲的公子，吟诵佛经，为那些被世道所害的无辜女子送行。有时他又是最可怕的凶煞，轻晃纸伞，将那些挡在面前的人尽数斩杀。

旁人敬他，也惧他。但没人懂他。

姜隗也不在意。这许多年里，他着旧嫁衣，等一个不归人。日日夜夜，由着那些愧疚钻心蚀骨，过得浑浑噩噩不辨晨昏。而在得知隐雾林兴许有起死人肉白骨之药时，他感到了从未有过的清醒。

阿姐，纵是妄想，阿夔也要走这一遭。
en:
Among the Fourteen Fiends of Ghost Street, none inspire more fear than the Seventh—Ghost Master Jiang Kui. 
Man or ghost? Virtue or vice? No one knows for sure. At times, he is the gentlest of princes, reciting sutras and bidding farewell to innocent women crushed by a cruel world. Other times, he becomes a nightmare cloaked in flesh, spinning his paper umbrella as he cuts down all who stand before him. 

They respect him. They fear him. But none understand him. 

And Jiang Kui doesn't care. For years, he has wandered in a faded wedding robe, waiting for one who will never return. Day and night blur into a haze of remorse that gnaws through the soul. And when he heard rumors of a remedy hidden deep in the Mistveil Forest, a drug that could raise the dead, restore flesh to bone. For the first time in years, he felt truly awake. 

Sis... even if it's a fool's errand, A'kui must take this path.

zh:
第七十五条，不要把热汤放在她能够到的地方。

第三百一十条，有黄瓜的菜不吃，有葱的菜不吃，但只要不告诉她，或者骗她一骗，偶尔也能含糊过去。
……
鸥大匠长叹一声，这样的笔记，他已经写了十二本了。
机巧美食可以按图索骥，可养孩子，便没有现成的图纸给鸥大匠参考了。
机巧若是出了毛病，用力拍拍，或者拆下来检查一番，总能把问题修好。饭菜要是没把握好火候，也不过吃到夹生的米，糊掉的饼，最多肚子疼个两三天，也就过去了。

可养孩子半点也马虎不得，没人告诉他抱孩子要用多大的力气，喂饭要喂到几岁，每日该给她几句安慰、几句训斥、多少零花钱……

天底下哪有如此麻烦的机巧！鸥大匠不信了，他教了这么多年书，上能解墨道经文，下能造各类巧物，还会治不了一个挑食的小娃娃？他怒而搜罗了十几本古方，从止夜啼的汤水，到养胃口的补剂，只要是古籍上有的，他都学着熬煮给晓晓喝。

于是，原本堆满了机巧部件的屋子，堆满了各种稀奇古怪的食材。
墨山道钻研机巧的大匠，就此走上了研究古方的不归之途。
做研究嘛，本来就是他擅长的事。只要理顺了笔记，再照着养孩子，又有何难？

到那时，全墨城将再没有人比他更懂养孩子了——鸥大匠无不得意地想着，又埋首钻进古方中。

……只是这孩子怎么一点也没按书上的长呢？口味会变，脾气也会变。还学会了哄骗父亲，借计使计，暗渡陈仓……可看着晓晓抡起比手臂还长的饭铲，熟练地为锅里的鱼翻身，那些因这小娃儿升起的骄傲、欣慰、惭愧……涌上心间的，竟是天下食方里从没记载过的滋味。

鸥大匠决定把这些都放到笔记里去，这是一张从没有人写过的新方子。或许只要付出一些时间，一些陪伴，再加上一点点的耐心。然后啊，这些说不清道不明的心绪，便会自然而然地从孩子身上生长出来，悄悄爬满父亲的心间。
en:
Rule No. 75: Do not leave hot soup anywhere she can reach it.
Rule No. 160: Milk should only be made into pastries. If she drinks it as is, she will end up with an upset stomach.
Rule No. 310: No cucumbers. No scallions. Still, if no one tells her, or if she is fooled a little, she can sometimes be coaxed into eating them.

...

Grand Artisan Gull lets out a long sigh. He has already filled twelve notebooks with notes like these.

Mechanisms and fine food can both be worked out by following plans and recipes. Raising a child, though, comes with no ready-made blueprint for him to consult.

If a mechanism goes wrong, a few firm pats or a careful dismantling will usually fix it. If a dish goes wrong, at worst you get half-cooked rice or a burnt cake and a stomachache for two or three days. That passes soon enough.

But raising a child does not allow for carelessness. No one ever told him how tightly to hold a baby, how many years he ought to keep feeding her, how many words of comfort she needs each day, how many words of scolding, or how much pocket money to give her...

What kind of troublesome mechanism is this? Grand Artisan Gull refuses to believe he cannot handle it. He has taught for years, can interpret Mohist texts from the highest principles down, can build all kinds of ingenious devices. How could he possibly lose to one picky little girl?

So, in a fit of determination, he gathers more than a dozen old recipe books. Remedies for crying at night, tonics to improve the appetite, anything the old texts mention, he learns to cook up for Xiaoxiao.

Before long, the room that used to be piled high with mechanism parts is filled instead with all manner of strange ingredients. And just like that, the great artisan of Mohist Hill finds himself on a one-way road into the study of ancient recipes.

Research, after all, is what he does best. Once he straightens out his notes, surely raising a child by the book cannot be that hard.

By then, he thinks to himself with no small satisfaction, no one in all Mohist City will understand child-rearing better than he does. And with that, he buries his head in the old recipes once more.

...

Only, this child has not grown up the way the books said she would. Her tastes change, her temper changes too. She has even learned how to coax and outwit her father, borrowing one trick to set up another and slipping past him when he least expects it.

And yet, when he sees Xiaoxiao lifting a rice paddle longer than her arm and deftly turning the fish in the pan, all the pride, relief, and quiet guilt this child has stirred in him rise at once into his heart. It is a taste no recipe in the world has ever recorded.

Grand Artisan Gull decides to write all of it into his notes. This is a brand-new recipe, one no one has ever written before.

Perhaps all it takes is some time, some companionship, and a little patience. Then those feelings that are so hard to name will simply grow, little by little, out of the child herself, and quietly spread through her father's heart.

zh:
【公孙丑章句】

公孙丑问曰：夫子当路于齐，管仲、晏子之功，可复许乎？
孟子曰：子诚齐人也，知管仲、晏子而已矣。或问乎曾西曰：吾子与子路孰贤？曾西蹴然曰：吾先子之所畏也。曰：然则吾子与管仲孰贤？曾西艴然不悦，曰：尔何曾比予于管仲？管仲得君如彼其专也，行乎国政如彼其久也，功烈如彼其卑也，尔何曾比予于是？曰：管仲，曾西之所不为也，而子为我愿之乎？
曰：管仲以其君霸，晏子以其君显，管仲、晏子犹不足为与？
曰：以齐王，由反手也。
曰：若是，则弟子之惑滋甚。且以文王之德，百年而后崩，犹未洽于天下；武王、周公继之，然后大行。今言王若易然，则文王不足法与？
曰：文王何可当也？由汤至于武丁，贤圣之君六七作，天下归殷久矣，久则难变也。武丁朝诸侯，有天下，犹运之掌也。纣之去武丁未久也，其故家遗俗，流风善政，犹有存者。又有微子、微仲、王子比干、箕子、胶鬲，皆贤人也，相与辅相之，故久而后失之也，尺地莫非其有也，一民莫非其臣也，然而文王犹方百里起，是以难也。齐人有言曰：虽有智慧，不如乘势；虽有镃基，不如待时。今时则易然也。夏后、殷、周之盛，地未有过千里者也，而齐有其地矣。鸡鸣狗吠相闻，而达乎四境，而齐有其民矣。地不改辟矣，民不改聚矣，行仁政而王，莫之能御也。且王者之不作，未有疏于此时者也；民之憔悴于虐政，未有甚于此时者也。饥者易为食，渴者易为饮。孔子曰：德之流行，速于置邮而传命。当今之时，万乘之国行仁政，民之悦之，犹解倒悬也。故事半古之人，功必倍之，惟此时为然。
公孙丑问曰：夫子加齐之卿相，得行道焉，虽由此霸王，不异矣。如此，则动心否乎？
孟子曰：否，我四十不动心。
曰：若是，则夫子过孟贲远矣。
曰：是不难，告子先我不动心。曰：不动心有道乎？
曰：有。北宫黝之养勇也，不肤挠，不目逃，思以一豪挫于人，若挞之于市朝，不受于褐宽博，亦不受于万乘之君；视刺万乘之君，若刺褐夫，无严诸侯，恶声至，必反之。孟施舍之所养勇也，曰：视不胜犹胜也。量敌而后进，虑胜而后会，是畏三军者也。舍岂能为必胜哉？能无惧而已矣。孟施舍似曾子，北宫黝似子夏。夫二子之勇，未知其孰贤，然而孟施舍守约也。昔者曾子谓子襄曰：子好勇乎？吾尝闻大勇于夫子矣。自反而不缩，虽褐宽博，吾不惴焉；自反而缩，虽千万人，吾往矣。孟施舍之守气，又不如曾子之守约也。
曰：敢问夫子之不动心，与告子之不动心，可得闻与？
告子曰：不得于言，勿求于心；不得于心，勿求于气。不得于心，勿求于气，可；不得于言，勿求于心，不可。夫志，气之帅也；气，体之充也。夫志至焉，气次焉。故曰持其志，无暴其气。
既曰志至焉，气次焉，又曰持其志，无暴其气者，何也？
曰：志壹则动气，气壹则动志也。今夫蹶者趋者，是气也，而反动其心。敢问夫子恶乎长？
曰：我知言，我善养吾浩然之气。
敢问何谓浩然之气？
曰：难言也。其为气也，至大至刚，以直养而无害，则塞于天地之间。其为气也，配义与道，无是，馁也。是集义所生者，非义袭而取之也。行有不慊于心，则馁矣。我故曰：告子未尝知义，以其外之也。必有事焉而勿正，心勿忘，勿助长也。无若宋人然：宋人有闵其苗之不长而揠之者，芒芒然归，谓其人曰：今日病矣，予助苗长矣。其子趋而往视之，苗则槁矣。天下之不助苗长者寡矣。以为无益而舍之者，不耘苗者也；助之长者，揠苗者也。非徒无益，而又害之。何谓知言？
曰：诐辞知其所蔽，淫辞知其所陷，邪辞知其所离，遁辞知其所穷。生于其心，害于其政；发于其政，害于其事。圣人复起，必从吾言矣。
宰我、子贡善为说辞，冉牛、闵子、颜渊善言德行，孔子兼之，曰：我于辞命，则不能也。然则夫子既圣矣乎？
曰：恶。是何言也。昔者子贡问于孔子曰：夫子圣矣乎？孔子曰：圣则吾不能，我学不厌而教不倦也。子贡曰：学不厌，智也；教不倦，仁也。仁且智，夫子既圣矣。夫圣，孔子不居。是何言也？
昔者窃闻之：子夏、子游、子张皆有圣人之一体，冉牛、闵子、颜渊则具体而微。敢问所安？曰：姑舍是。曰：伯夷、伊尹何如？非其君不事，非其民不使，治则进，乱则退，伯夷也，何事非君，何使非民，治亦进，乱亦进，伊尹也。可以仕则仕，可以止则止，可以久则久，可以速则速，孔子也。皆古圣人也，吾未能有行焉，乃所愿，则学孔子也。
伯夷、伊尹于孔子，若是班乎？
曰：否。自有生民以来，未有孔子也。然则有同与？
曰：有。得百里之地而君之，皆能以朝诸侯，有天下；行一不义，杀一不辜，而得天下，皆不为也，是则同。曰：敢问其所以异？
……
en:
[Part of Gongsun Chou]

Gongsun Chou asked Mencius, saying, "Master, if you were to obtain the ordering of the government in Qi, could you promise yourself to accomplish anew such results as those realized by Guan Zhong and Yan?"
Mencius said, "You are indeed a true person of Qi. You know about Guan Zhong and Yan, and nothing more. Someone asked Zeng Xi, saying, 'Sir, to which do you give the superiority—to yourself or to Zilu?' Zeng Xi looked uneasy, and said, 'He was an object of veneration to my grandfather.' 'Then,' pursued the other, 'do you give the superiority to yourself or to Guan Zhong?' Zeng Xi, flushed with anger and displeased, said, 'How dare you compare me with Guan Zhong? Considering how entirely Guan Zhong possessed the confidence of his prince, how long he enjoyed the direction of the government of the State, and how low, after all, was what he accomplished—how is it that you liken me to him?' Thus concluded Mencius, Zeng Xi would not be Guan Zhong, and is it what you desire for me that I should do so?"
Gongsun Chou said, "Guan Zhong raised his prince to be the leader of all the other princes, and Yan made his prince illustrious, and do you still think it would not be enough for you to do what they did?"
Mencius answered, "To raise Qi to the royal dignity would be as easy as it is to turn round the hand."
"So!" returned the other. "The perplexity of your disciple is hereby very much increased. There was King Wen, moreover, with all the virtue which belonged to him; and who did not die till he had reached a hundred years: and still his influence had not penetrated throughout the kingdom. It required King Wu and the Duke of Zhou to continue his course, before that influence greatly prevailed. Now you say that the royal dignity might be so easily obtained—is King Wen then not a sufficient object for imitation?"
Mencius said, "How can King Wen be matched? From Tang to Wu Ding there had appeared six or seven worthy and sage sovereigns. The kingdom had been attached to Yin for a long time, and this length of time made a change difficult. Wu Ding had all the princes coming to his court, and possessed the kingdom as if it had been a thing which he moved round in his palm. Then, Zhou was removed from Wu Ding by no great interval of time. There were still remaining some of the ancient families and of the old manners, of the influence also which had emanated from the earlier sovereigns, and of their good government. Moreover, there were the Viscount of Wei and his second son, their Royal Highnesses Bi Gan and the Viscount of Ji, and Jiao Ge, all people of ability and virtue, who gave their joint assistance to Zhou in his government. In consequence of these things, it took a long time for him to lose the throne. There was not a foot of ground which he did not possess. There was not one of all the people who was not his subject. So it was on his side, and King Wen at his beginning had only a territory of one hundred square li. On all these accounts, it was difficult for him immediately to attain to the royal dignity. The people of Qi have a saying—'A person may have wisdom and discernment, but that is not like embracing the favourable opportunity. A person may have instruments of husbandry, but that is not like waiting for the farming seasons.' The present time is one in which the royal dignity may be easily attained. In the flourishing periods of the Xia, Yin, and Zhou dynasties, the royal domain did not exceed a thousand li, and Qi embraces so much territory. Cocks crow and dogs bark to one another, all the way to the four borders of the State: Qi possesses the people. No change is needed for the enlarging of its territory: no change is needed for the collecting of a population. If its ruler will put in practice a benevolent government, no power will be able to prevent his becoming sovereign. Moreover, never was there a time farther removed than the present from the rise of a true sovereign: never was there a time when the sufferings of the people from tyrannical government were more intense than the present. The hungry readily partake of any food, and the thirsty of any drink. Confucius said, 'The flowing progress of virtue is more rapid than the transmission of royal orders by stages and couriers.' At the present time, in a country of ten thousand chariots, let benevolent government be put in practice, and the people will be delighted with it, as if they were relieved from hanging by the heels. With half the merit of the ancients, double their achievements is sure to be realized. It is only at this time that such could be the case."
Gongsun Chou asked Mencius, saying, "Master, if you were to be appointed a high noble and the prime minister of Qi, so as to be able to carry your principles into practice, though you should thereupon raise the ruler to the headship of all the other princes, or even to the royal dignity, it would not be to be wondered at—In such a position would your mind be perturbed or not?"
Mencius replied, "No. At forty, I attained to an unperturbed mind."
Chou said, "Since it is so with you, my Master, you are far beyond Meng Ben."
"The mere attainment," said Mencius, "is not difficult. The scholar Gao had attained to an unperturbed mind at an earlier period of life than I did." Chou asked, "Is there any way to an unperturbed mind?"
The answer was, "Yes. Beigong You had this way of nourishing his valour: He did not flinch from any strokes at his body. He did not turn his eyes aside from any thrusts at them. He considered that the slightest push from anyone was the same as if he were beaten before the crowds in the market-place, and that what he would not receive from a common person in his loose large garments of hair, neither should he receive from a prince of ten thousand chariots. He viewed stabbing a prince of ten thousand chariots just as stabbing a fellow dressed in cloth of hair. He feared not any of all the princes. A bad word addressed to him he always returned. Meng Shishe had this way of nourishing his valour: He said, 'I look upon not conquering and conquering in the same way. To measure the enemy and then advance; to calculate the chances of victory and then engage—this is to stand in awe of the opposing force. How can I make certain of conquering! I can only rise superior to all fear.' Meng Shishe resembled the philosopher Zeng. Beigong You resembled Zixia. I do not know to the valour of which of the two the superiority should be ascribed, but yet Meng Shishe attended to what was of the greater importance. Formerly, the philosopher Zeng said to Zixiang, 'Do you love valour? I heard an account of great valour from the Master. It speaks thus: If, on self-examination, I find that I am not upright, shall I not be in fear even of a poor person in his loose garments of hair-cloth? If, on self-examination, I find that I am upright, I will go forward against thousands and tens of thousands.' Yet, what Meng Shishe maintained, being merely his physical energy, was after all inferior to what the philosopher Zeng maintained, which was indeed of the most importance."
Gongsun Chou said, "May I venture to ask an explanation from you, Master, of how you maintain an unperturbed mind, and how the philosopher Gao does the same?" Mencius answered,
"Gao says, 'What is not attained in words is not to be sought for in the mind; what produces dissatisfaction in the mind, is not to be helped by passion-effort.' This last, when there is unrest in the mind, not to seek for relief from passion-effort, may be conceded. But not to seek in the mind for what is not attained in words cannot be conceded. The will is the leader of the passion-nature. The passion-nature pervades and animates the body. The will is first and chief, and the passion-nature is subordinate to it. Therefore I say, Maintain firm the will, and do no violence to the passion-nature."
Chou observed, "Since you say—'The will is chief, and the passion-nature is subordinate,' how do you also say, 'Maintain firm the will, and do no violence to the passion-nature?'" Mencius replied,
"When it is the will alone which is active, it moves the passion-nature. When it is the passion-nature alone which is active, it moves the will. For instance now, in the case of a person falling or running, that is from the passion-nature, and yet it moves the mind." "I venture to ask," said Chou again, "wherein you, Master, surpass Gao."
Mencius told him, "I understand words. I am skilful in nourishing my vast, flowing passion-nature."
Chou pursued, "I venture to ask what you mean by your vast, flowing passion-nature?"
"The reply was, 'It is difficult to describe it. This is the passion-nature: It is exceedingly great, and exceedingly strong. Being nourished by rectitude, and sustaining no injury, it fills up all between heaven and earth. This is the passion-nature: It is the mate and assistant of righteousness and reason. Without it, one is in a state of starvation. It is produced by the accumulation of righteous deeds; it is not to be obtained by incidental acts of righteousness. If the mind does not feel complacency in the conduct, the nature becomes starved. I therefore said, Gao has never understood righteousness, because he makes it something external. There must be the constant practice of this righteousness, but without the object of thereby nourishing the passion-nature. Let not the mind forget its work, but let there be no assisting the growth of that nature. Let us not be like the person of Song. There was a person of Song, who was grieved that his growing corn was not longer, and so he pulled it up. Having done this, he returned home, looking very stupid, and said to his people, "I am tired to-day. I have been helping the corn to grow long." His son ran to look at it, and found the corn all withered. There are few in the world, who do not deal with their passion-nature, as if they were assisting the corn to grow long. Some indeed consider it of no benefit to them, and let it alone—they do not weed their corn. They who assist it to grow long, pull out their corn. What they do is not only of no benefit to the nature, but it also injures it.'" Gongsun Chou further asked, "What do you mean by saying that you understand whatever words you hear?"
Mencius replied, "When words are one-sided, I know how the mind of the speaker is clouded over. When words are extravagant, I know how the mind is fallen and sunk. When words are all-depraved, I know how the mind has departed from principle. When words are evasive, I know how the mind is at its wit's end. These evils growing in the mind, do injury to government, and, displayed in the government, are hurtful to the conduct of affairs. When a Sage shall again arise, one will certainly follow my words."
On this Chou observed, "Zai Wo and Zigong were skilful in speaking. Ran Niu, the disciple Min, and Yan Yuan, while their words were good, were distinguished for their virtuous conduct. Confucius united the qualities of the disciples in himself, but still he said, 'In the matter of speeches, I am not competent'—Then, Master, have you attained to be a Sage?"
Mencius said, "Oh! what words are these? Formerly Zigong asked Confucius, saying, 'Master, are you a Sage?' Confucius answered him, 'A Sage is what I cannot rise to. I learn without satiety, and teach without being tired.' Zigong said, 'You learn without satiety—that shows your wisdom. You teach without being tired—that shows your benevolence. Benevolent and wise—Master, you ARE a Sage.' Now, since Confucius would not allow himself to be regarded as a Sage, what words were those?"
Chou said, "Formerly, I once heard this: Zixia, Ziyou, and Zizhang had each one member of the Sage. Ran Niu, the disciple Min, and Yan Yuan had all the members, but in small proportions. I venture to ask: With which of these are you pleased to rank yourself?" Mencius replied, "Let us drop speaking about these, if you please." Chou then asked, "What do you say of Boyi and Yi Yin?" "Their ways were different from mine," said Mencius. "Not to serve a prince whom he did not esteem, nor command a people whom he did not approve; in a time of good government to take office, and on the occurrence of confusion to retire—this was the way of Boyi. To say 'Whom may I not serve? My serving him makes him my ruler. What people may I not command? My commanding them makes them my people.' In a time of good government to take office, and when disorder prevailed, also to take office—that was the way of Yi Yin. When it was proper to go into office, then to go into it; when it was proper to keep retired from office, then to keep retired from it; when it was proper to continue in it long, then to continue in it long; when it was proper to withdraw from it quickly, then to withdraw quickly—that was the way of Confucius. These were all sages of antiquity, and I have not attained to do what they did. But what I wish to do is to learn to be like Confucius."
Chou said, "Comparing Boyi and Yi Yin with Confucius, are they to be placed in the same rank?"
Mencius replied, "No. Since there were living people until now, there never was another Confucius." Chou said, "Then, did they have any points of agreement with him?"
The reply was, "Yes. If they had been sovereigns over a hundred li of territory, they would, all of them, have brought all the princes to attend in their court, and have obtained the throne. And none of them, in order to obtain the throne, would have committed one act of unrighteousness, or put to death one innocent person. In those things they agreed with him." Chou said, "I venture to ask wherein he differed from them."

她关心雩真想要那把无量剑，却不关心雩真对李无量的敬仰。

当然，她无须关心任何人，因为她是天下最有权势的公主。
也自认为即将是天下的主人。
在她骄横的作风之下，无人敢指出——
她有她母亲一样的野心，却在才能上相差太远。
所有人沉默不语，他们都看到了，公主对雩真，爱之拉拢之，则赏赐之。而当雩真身败名裂，又将她抛于马后。
en:
To show how much she cared about presenting the sword, the Princess selected many fine silks to line the Wuliang Blade's case. But the moment she heard that Daozhen had tried to dissuade her, she simply ordered his shrine smashed.
She cared that Yuzhen wanted the Wuliang Blade, but not that Yuzhen revered Li Wuliang himself. Then again, she had no need to care about anyone. She was the most powerful princess under heaven, and in her own mind, the future ruler of it as well.
Under her overbearing rule, no one dared point out the truth: she had inherited her mother's ambition, but not her ability.
So everyone kept silent. They all saw how she treated Yuzhen. When she wanted to win her over, she lavished her with favor and rewards. And when Yuzhen's name was ruined, she cast her aside without a second thought.

zh:
《入阵》下
时值暮秋，苦风萧瑟。
他单衫草鞋，走在不熟悉的山路上，瑟缩慢步。
“家”已经不能回了。而远亲收留他的那间柴棚，甚至不能遮风避雨。
远处山下的灯火隔着雾，愈发飘渺。离得更远再看，像从水底仰望人间。

他想起那位戏台上的覆面将军，孤身一人，在千军万马中突围。
歌声无法驱散黑暗。更糟的是招来山间走兽，抑或不怀好意的流寇。
但他顾不上这许多。
心跳声如那日的重鼓，将军一往无前，声犹激越。

他奔跑着，朝向灯火的方向。
火光映映，渐渐能听见琵琶声声缭绕，喝彩声不绝。
这是他第二次来到戏台。
明明是草木凋萎的时节，他闭上双眼之前，却看见千树万树，梨雪飘坠。

“我等胡儿，吐气如电。
我采顶雷，踏石如泥。右得士力，
左得鞭回。日光西没，东西若月。
舞乐打去，录录长曲。”

顾秋华，湖州人氏，生具音律之才。
幼年为梨园弟子程肃所救，后拜入回雪舫。其天赋卓绝，音色清越，《兰陵王入阵曲》尤佳。
en:
Formation Entry II 
It was late autumn, and the wind had turned sharp and bitter. 
Dressed in a thin shirt and straw sandals, he made his way down an unfamiliar mountain path, shivering as he walked. 
There was no "home" left to return to. And the shed his distant relatives had given him wasn't even enough to keep out the rain, let alone the wind. 
Down below, the lights of the valley flickered through the mist, growing fainter the farther he went—as if he were looking up at the world from the bottom of a lake. 

He thought of the masked general on the stage, alone in a sea of soldiers, carving a path through countless foes. 
A song could not keep the darkness at bay. Worse, it might draw the attention of mountain beasts or passing bandits. 
But none of that mattered to him now. 
His heartbeat pounded like the war drums from that day, the general surging forward, fearless and unshaken. 

He ran—toward the distant glow of firelight. 
As the glow deepened, he began to hear it: the spiraling notes of a pipa, the cheers and cries of the crowd. 
It was his second time standing before the stage. 
Though the season was one of withered grass and falling leaves, the moment before he closed his eyes, he saw pear blossoms—thousands of them—snowing down from unseen branches. 

"We breathe lightning. 
I grasp thunder above my head, grind stone soft beneath my feet. Strength in my right hand, 
command in my left. When the sun sets in the west, the east rises silver as the moon. 
Beat the drums—let the long song roll." 

Gu Qiuhua, a native of Huzhou, was born with music in his bones. 
As a child, he was saved by Cheng Su of the Masked Troupe and later joined the Pavilion of Returning Snow. His talent was unmatched, his voice clear and bright—
and of all his performances, none surpassed The Prince Enters the Formation.

Ding Xiao,

This venture into the Central Army Camp to steal military supplies is no small matter. Your life may well hang upon it. Though you have known Du Qiyin, the storeroom clerk, for many years, getting the storeroom key from him will still demand the utmost care.

I have already made arrangements with Lin and Xiao of the Inkbound Order. Once the key is in your hands, seek out Xiao Heyi in secret. He will help move the supplies out through the hidden passage beneath that cur Du's storeroom. He is a cautious and reliable man, so you may trust him.

Enclosed with this letter is a pair of Mohist Trickshot Gauntlets. It may prove useful.

I will keep this brief. Act with care. We meet by the Hutuo River at the fifth quarter of the Mao Hour.

zh:
【特牲馈食礼第十五】

特牲馈食之礼。不诹日。及筮日，主人冠端玄，即位于门外，西面。子姓兄弟如主人之服，立于主人之南，西面北上。有司群执事，如兄弟服，东面北上。席于门中，闑西阈外。筮人取筮于西塾，执之，东面受命主人。宰自主人之左赞命，命曰：“孝孙某，筮来日某，诹此某事，适其皇祖某子。尚飨！”筮者许诺，还，即席，西面坐。卦者在左。卒筮，写卦。筮者执以示主人。主人受视，反之，筮者还，东面。长占，卒，告于主人：“占曰迹攥则筮远日，如初仪。宗人告事毕。
前期三日之朝，筮尸，如求日之仪。命筮曰：“孝孙某，诹此某事，适其皇祖某子，筮某之某为尸。尚飨！”
乃宿尸。主人立于尸外门外。子姓兄弟立主人之后，北面东上。尸如主人服，出门左，西面。主人辟，皆东面，北上。主人再拜。尸答拜。宗人摈辞如初，卒曰：“筮子为某尸，占曰吉，敢宿！”祝许诺，致命。尸许诺，主人再拜稽首。尸入主人退。
宿宾。宾如主人服，出门左，西面再拜。主人东面，答再拜。宗人摈，曰：“某荐岁事，吾子将莅之，敢宿！”宾曰：“某敢不敬从！”主人再拜，宾答拜，主人退，宾拜送。
厥明夕，陈鼎于门外，北面北上，有鼏。棜在其南，南顺实兽于其上，东首。牲在其西，北首，东足。设洗于降阶东南，壶、禁在东序，豆、笾、鉶在东房，南上。几、席、两敦在西堂。主人及子姓兄弟即位于门东，如初。宾及众宾即位于门西，东面北上。宗人、祝立于宾西北，东面南上。主人再拜，宾答再拜。三拜众宾，众宾答再拜。主人揖入，兄弟从，宾及众宾从，即位于堂下，如外位。宗人升自西阶，视壶濯及豆笾，反降，东北面告濯、具。宾出，主人出，皆复外位。宗人视牲，告充。雍正作豕。宗人举兽尾，告备；举鼎鼏。请期，曰“羹饪”。告事毕，宾出，主人拜送。
……
en:
【The Fifteenth Ceremony of the Special Sacrifice】

The rite of the special sacrifice. The day is not consulted. When the day is divined, the host, wearing a dark ceremonial cap and robes, takes his position outside the gate, facing west. The sons and grandsons, dressed like the host, stand to the south of the host, facing west, with the north as the place of honor. The officers and various attendants, dressed like the brothers, stand facing east, with the north as the place of honor. Mats are spread in the middle of the gate, outside the threshold to the west of the central pillar. The diviner takes the divining stalks from the western study, holds them, and facing east, receives the command from the host. The steward, standing to the left of the host, assists in proclaiming the command, saying: "The filial grandson, so-and-so, divines for a coming day, so-and-so, for this particular matter, to offer to his august ancestor, so-and-so. May he deign to enjoy this offering!" The diviner assents, turns around, and takes his seat on the mat, facing west. The hexagram recorder sits to his left. When the divination is complete, the hexagram is written down. The diviner holds it up to show the host. The host receives it, examines it, and returns it. The diviner turns around, facing east. The elders interpret the divination. When finished, they report to the host: "The divination says auspicious." If it is inauspicious, then they divine for a later day, following the same procedure. The ancestral officer announces that the matter is concluded.
On the morning of the third day before the ceremony, the person to serve as the impersonator of the deceased is divined, following the same procedure as for choosing the day. The command for divination says: "The filial grandson, so-and-so, for this particular matter, to offer to his august ancestor, so-and-so, divines whether so-and-so, son of so-and-so, shall serve as the impersonator. May he deign to enjoy this offering!"
Then the impersonator is invited. The host stands outside the gate of the impersonator's residence. The sons and grandsons stand behind the host, facing north, with the east as the place of honor. The impersonator, dressed like the host, comes out from the left side of the gate, facing west. The host steps aside, and all face east, with the north as the place of honor. The host bows twice. The impersonator returns the bow. The ancestral officer announces the invitation as before, concluding: "We have divined that you shall serve as the impersonator for so-and-so, and the divination says auspicious. We presume to invite you!" The invocator assents and conveys the message. The impersonator assents. The host bows twice, touching his head to the ground. The impersonator enters, and the host withdraws.
The guests are invited. The guest, dressed like the host, comes out from the left side of the gate, facing west, and bows twice. The host, facing east, returns the bow twice. The ancestral officer announces, saying: "So-and-so will present the annual sacrifice, and I presume you will honor it with your presence. I presume to invite you!" The guest says: "How dare I not respectfully follow!" The host bows twice, and the guest returns the bow. The host withdraws, and the guest bows to see him off.
On the evening of the following day, the cauldrons are set up outside the gate, facing north, with the north as the place of honor, covered with lids. The stand is placed to their south, aligned north-south, with game placed upon it, head facing east. The sacrificial animal is to its west, head facing north, feet facing east. The washing basin is set up to the southeast of the steps for descending, and the jars and stands are placed at the eastern wall. The dishes, baskets, and tripods are placed in the eastern chamber, with the south as the place of honor. The low tables, mats, and two round baskets are placed in the western hall. The host, sons, and grandsons take their positions east of the gate, as before. The guest and the other guests take their positions west of the gate, facing east, with the north as the place of honor. When the king established the capital, he determined the directions and rectified the positions, divided the land into fields and surveyed the wilderness, set up officials and assigned duties, all to serve as the ultimate standard for the people. Thereupon he established the Earth Officials with the Minister of Education at their head, commanding his subordinates to manage the state's education, assisting the king in bringing peace and stability to the states.

“一命一价，你要救的人太多，这样的价，没人出得起。”
“师傅……我们总说‘一命一价’，‘一命一命’，咱们盘算的总是旁人的命。“
“可为何不能是我自己的？”
“师傅，徒儿有一问——徒儿的命， 何价？”
“……”
“此问，徒儿也想问问世间人。”
辞别之际，孙愿赠以软甲。
朱鱼跪，稽首三拜，出青溪门，再不回头。
至此，青溪山头少了一位常带师兄妹采朱萸的师姐。
开封城中多了一位悬壶济世，力抗北敌的红袖仙。
en:
Zhu Yu bids farewell to her master. The moment she lifts her backpack and leaves Silver Needle, she looks back.
 By the bamboo grove stands Sun Yuan, watching his disciple go.
 "One life, one price. But there are too many lives you must save, and the price is too high for anyone to pay."
 "Master, we always say one life, one price, always thinking of others' lives."
 "Why can't the life be my own?"
 "Tell me, Master, what is the price of my life?"
 "..."
 "Master, this is the question I wish to ask the world."
 As they part, Sun Yuan gifts her a soft armor.
 Zhu Yu kneels, kowtows three times, and never looks back after leaving Silver Needle.
 From then on, Silver Needle is missing one senior sister who led disciples to gather cornus plants.
 Yet in Kaifeng, there appears a Red-Sleeved Immortal, who heals the people and fights northern enemies.

zh:
雩真的心里装着剑和三个人。
教养之师、援手之恩和……唯一的朋友。
她答应过爷爷要去攀天下第一的山峰，她发誓要报答武皇的恩情，
而对于谢尧——
这世上的春夏秋冬，无论是怎生情景，他们定是要一起度过的。
后来，雩真被困在九幽洞里的岁月，
阳春，酷暑，残秋，都不再来临。
她只有冬天。
冬天来了，河上定然结了冰。
她在山上，在这片冰天雪地里。
谢尧在山下，在茫茫然的风雪中。
但无论相隔多远，无论这冬天是寒冷还是和煦，
他们总是要在一起度过的。
en:
Yuzhen's heart held only her sword and three people: the master who raised her, the sovereign who saved her, and... her only friend.
She had promised her grandfather she would conquer the world's highest peak, and she had sworn her life to repay Emperor Wu's grace.
Yet with Xie Yao, there were no vows, but a quiet certainty.
No matter how the seasons turned, they were simply meant to weather them together.
Yet, in the long years Yuzhen spent imprisoned within the Abyssal Cavern,
the thaw of spring, the fire of summer, and the fading gold of autumn ceased to exist.
She was left with nothing but winter.
When the rivers froze solid, she remained trapped at the summit, entombed in a desolate expanse of ice and snow.
Far below, Xie Yao wandered through blinding blizzards.
But across the vast, bitter divide, whether the winter winds were cruel or kind,
they were still spending the seasons together.

zh:
沈宁是沈家旁支的小女儿，为了给家中病重的长辈祈福，来到孤山礼佛清修。
来孤山的那天，旁人都说她可怜，小小年纪就要在这冷清的山上待着。
她却觉得山上的日子惬意极了，与鹤为伴，以梅为友，寻一僻静处摆下棋盘，等有缘人来，自己与自己也能下一天。
“娘子不觉得这闷吗？”
“闷？这里有梅树三百株，鹤二十四只，棋一副，阿爹还不时送书来，怎会闷呢？”
其他礼佛清修的娘子听了只觉得她古怪，继续怀念杭州城内的繁华热闹。
沈宁坐回了她的小棋桌前，看着不远处振翅的仙鹤笑道：
“你们真是自在，想飞便飞，想停便停，从不用问旁人许不许这样做。”
“我如今也和你们一样，想下棋便下棋，想发呆便发呆。没人催我议亲，没人管我规矩。”
这哪里是困她在山上？明明是她的天高地阔！
en:
As the youngest daughter of a cadet branch of the Shen family, Shen Ning had come to Lone Hill for a quiet Buddhist retreat, praying for a gravely ill elder at home.
Everyone had felt sorry for her when she arrived. Such a young girl, stuck on this lonely mountain.
She loved life on the mountain. With cranes and plum trees for company, she'd set out her board in a quiet spot and wait for someone to join her. Playing both sides could keep her happy all day.
"Don't you get bored up here?"
"Bored? There are three hundred plum trees here, twenty-four cranes, and a board to play on. Father sends me books now and then, too. How could I be bored?"
The other women on retreat found her odd and went back to longing for the bustle of Hangzhou.
Shen Ning settled back at her little game table, smiling at the cranes beating their wings nearby.
"You fly when you please and rest when you please. You never have to ask anyone's permission."
"And now I can do the same. I can play when I want or just sit and daydream. No one pushing me to marry, no one telling me how to behave."
Trapped on the mountain? Up here, she was free!

zh:
一日，庞妙在街边遇上个泼皮无赖。
说是无赖，其实也是庞妙自找的。

那无赖名唤高二。那日高二在街头追鸡撵狗，引得一阵喧闹。只是因为庞妙在人群中多看了高二一眼，恰好看到高二一个鹞子翻身从几丈高的墙头翻下来。
就这一眼，他便认定这是他的新师傅。

高二不耐烦地叼着草棍，听着庞妙絮絮叨叨。本来高二想啐一口就走，却听庞妙说允诺十两白银。于是他眼睛一转，便开口说道：“要说你这平庸之辈，怎能配得上我高二足下之名……”
庞妙涨红了脸。“是，是，师傅说的是。”
“不过看你心善，那这样，你且完成我的三项考验，我就收你为徒。”
庞妙喜出望外，连连答应。
接下来，庞妙帮高二修了房顶，挑了粪桶，又买了十多只烧鸡。
可等待他的，却是翻脸不认人的一记窝心脚，和扬长而去的嘲笑声。

高二从没觉得这么好笑。正当他放肆嘲笑庞妙是个傻子的时候，一只木锤重重砸在了他的肩膀。
木匠李怒吼一声。“敢欺负我老李的徒弟！”
“还有我！”绣花的沈三娘操起剪刀就往高二身上戳。
“我钱德要的徒弟也是你能消遣的！”巨大的算盘拍在门面上，高二只觉得眼冒金星。
颠勺的，算卦的，走镖的……高二被打得趴在地上，不住求饶。

“来，好徒儿，快起来。让师傅看看！”
“伤着没！上师傅药房去，师傅有的是药。”
“我的傻徒儿，可不能再这么实心眼了！”
看着围在自己身边的十几个师傅，庞妙痴痴笑了。这一刻他才明白，“名师满天下”到底是什么滋味。
en:
One day, Pang Miao ran into a local ruffian on the street. 
To call him a ruffian was partly Pang Miao's own fault. 

The ruffian's name was Gao Er. That day, Gao Er was chasing chickens and dogs down the street, causing quite a racket. Only because Pang Miao glanced at Gao Er in the crowd did he happen to see Gao Er execute a perfect hawk flip down from a wall several yards high. 
That one glance convinced him: this was his new master. 

Gao Er impatiently chewed on a grass stalk, listening to Pang Miao's rambling. Gao Er had initially wanted to spit and leave, but then he heard Pang Miao promise ten taels of silver. So his eyes shifted, and he said, "For someone as mediocre as you, how could you be worthy of the name 'disciple of Gao Er'..." 
Pang Miao flushed red. "Yes, yes... Master, you are right." 
"But seeing your kind heart... fine. Complete three trials for me, and I'll accept you as my disciple." 
Overjoyed, Pang Miao agreed repeatedly. 
Next, Pang Miao repaired Gao Er's roof for him, carried his manure buckets, and bought over ten roast chickens. 
What awaited him, however, was a sudden kick to the chest from a now-hostile Gao Er, and the sound of mocking laughter fading into the distance. 

Gao Er had never found anything so funny. Just as he was heartily laughing at Pang Miao for being an idiot, a wooden mallet slammed hard into his shoulder. 
The carpenter, Old Li, roared, "How dare you bully my apprentice!" 
"And me!" The embroiderer, Third Lady Shen, grabbed her scissors and jabbed at Gao Er. 
"My apprentice is not someone you can make a fool of!" A huge abacus smacked him in the face. Gao Er saw stars. 
The wok-tosser, the fortune-teller, the bodyguard... Gao Er was beaten until he lay on the ground, begging for mercy. 

"Come, good disciple, get up. Let me have a look!" 
"Are you hurt? Come to my pharmacy. I have plenty of medicine." 
"My silly disciple, you mustn't be so trusting again!" 
Looking at the dozen or so masters gathered around him, Pang Miao smiled foolishly. In that moment, he finally understood what it truly meant to have "masters all under heaven."

zh:
金叶之案·其二
  陈员外府仆妇刘氏，晨起洗衣，又见府中井口一草编金叶，观之，见一男子死于井中，查证为陈员外其人。仆妇刘氏言陈员外欺男霸女，曾多有年轻女子入府后不堪受辱，跃入井中而死，此为侠客杀人，女鬼索命，言辞激动，已送回西坊近角门里其子家中。
  依刘氏所言探寻，寻出井下白骨数具，且于府中后院假山树后见一低矮小门，土层松动，似有人往来其间。
（笔记备注：此嫌犯身形奇特，似从小门而入，如此瘦弱矮小之人如何杀人，莫不是先进府内，再接应同伙？金叶……金叶……近来一听金叶，颇为头疼。）
en:
The Gold Leaf Case, Chapter II 
Liu, Landlord Chen's housekeeper, woke up one morning to wash clothes and found a grass-woven gold leaf in the manor's well. When she looked closer, she spotted the body of a dead man, which turned out to be the Landlord himself. Liu said that Chen was a bully who was violent toward women, and many young women were assaulted in the manor before jumping into the well from the shame and guilt. She also claimed that the Gold Leaf Warrior did this to avenge the women, before she became extremely agitated and was sent home. 
According to Liu's testimony, several skeletons were exhumed from the well. A small gate was also found behind the feigned landscape of the garden, indicating that someone had been coming and going through this gate. 
(Note: The suspect had to have been small enough to come through this door. How can someone so small and possibly weak kill another? Did they come in to open the door for their accomplice to enter? Gold Leaf... Gold Leaf... This word is giving me a headache...)

“周阿哥，侬看我们配不配？”
周洪郎无奈地抓头发：“我是帮你寻伴的，不是把自己送你作伴的！”
好说歹说把这位姑娘送走，下一个生意就上门了。
“这位郎君，您身后这些是……”
周洪郎数了数，男子身后跟了有足足九个人，莫非这都是他的生意？
“伊拉家小子年纪小，自己搞不灵清，都是亲戚来帮他把把关。”
“伊拉家小子年纪都快能当我爹了！”周洪郎拍桌而起，他觉得自己在这地方要待不下去了。下完棋看上他的、要求太特别的、打听他家底的……挣的钱少了，日子也远不如过去逍遥自在，还得花钱请朋友喝酒倾诉，自己活成了个笑话！
周洪郎深深吸了口气，这都是自己招摇撞骗造的孽。他又看了眼自己那计数的小木板，算了算了，还剩下十七对！
马上自己这双眼睛就能重见光明了。
en:
"Miss, you go straight for the kill when you play. I'd pair you with someone..."
"Honglang, don't you think you and I would make a good match?"
Zhou Honglang scratched his head in exasperation. "I'm here to find you a partner, not volunteer for the job!"
It took some persuading to send her on her way. Then his next customer arrived.
"Sir, all these people behind you..."
He counted a full nine people trailing behind the man. Could they all be customers?
"The boy's still young. He can't be expected to handle all this himself. We're his relatives, here to help him choose."
"That 'boy' is almost old enough to be my father!" Zhou Honglang slapped the table and sprang to his feet. He couldn't stay in this place much longer. Clients who fell for him after a game, clients with absurd demands, clients prying into his finances... Less money, less freedom, and now he was buying his friends drinks just to have someone to complain to. What a joke he'd become!
Zhou Honglang took a deep breath. This was what he got for swindling people. He glanced at his little wooden tally board. All right, all right. Just seventeen couples to go!
Soon he'd be able to see again.

zh:
窗外草长莺飞，正是春深时节。屋内祁小舟挑剔地检点行囊：银两，足矣。换洗衣衫，叠作两套。干粮，可撑半月。短刀……在身侧。最要紧的，是向叔父讨来的那匹乌蹄！此刻正闲闲啃着檐下草皮，等她动身。
自小长在马群中的少女，行动如风，性亦如风。家中景色已然看腻，十六岁的祁小舟，包袱一甩，就此辞亲闯荡江湖去了。
江湖就是外头，外头就是江湖。可出门多日，方知话本里那些快意恩仇的新鲜事，终究是纸上云烟。景致虽时时翻新，新鲜劲儿却去得飞快。每日入眼的，最多的，还是那乌泱泱的流民，自北面逃来，一双双惶恐麻木的眼睛，看得人心里不好受。
小舟勒马沉吟片刻，少年人的决断本就下得飞快。于是这一叶孤舟，转道逆流而上。
时值契丹人南下进犯中原，祁小舟一路自清河往北，途径魏州、济州，沿途看到无数手无寸铁的百姓死在胡骑之下……她捧着一颗年轻无畏的心，一路向前走去……杀过兵卒，救过难民，宿过野渡，吃过生肉。她想，她找到自己最想干的事了。这么多人的人要帮，她就作大侠，多帮些人好了！
行侠第一年，她在魏州古道上救下了双生子阿执和阿破……路遇胜乐门老门主，相中了二人的绝佳根骨，向她讨人。
她自小便听过胜乐门的侠名。授人以鱼不如授人以渔，若是二人能学一身武艺傍身，他日双剑出，可救苍生万！
安顿好二人，小舟起身告辞……胜乐门的少主韦一渡追出来，递给她一个包裹，里面不仅有一枚崭新的火折子，还有一张丝帕，几盒面脂。
“祁女侠的火折子旧了，脸上也有些皴痕，北地苦寒，韦某略备薄礼，还请笑纳。”
良夜迢迢，君子如玉，一派光风霁月。
小舟接过包裹，道了声谢，却头也不回地策马而去了。
再至魏州，驿馆案头早候书函。韦字题封，字迹浓丽妍媚，随信附赠芙蓉酥一匣。小舟把信随手扔到了一边，拈了块糕点尝，糖放多了，太腻。
她又摸出韦一渡所赠的包裹，只留下了火折子，将丝帕和面脂送给了驿站的厨娘。
此后数月，她马蹄踏处，必有书信追云而至。信上所写，无外乎是各地吃食、坊间新诗，落款处总有关切之语……小舟明白对方的心思，可此等雕虫求凰技，怎配让她丢掉手里的剑？她第一次回信，惜字如金：吾志在行侠，岂耽风月？
信件断了月余。
待到她再收信时，落款虽仍是同一人，字迹却变了不少。
这一次，信中没有诗词也不谈珍馐，只简单交待了阿执阿破兄弟的近况，并且向她请教了些驯马的诀窍。信中还说，此前所临之帖，骨弱形靡，所以自己最近改临魏碑了。
鬼使神差地，小舟回了第二封信……问候了两兄弟，教授了驯马诀，也称赞了新字。……慢慢地，他们无话不谈，从驯马临帖聊到剑法招式，从前朝旧闻聊到武林新事……小舟渐渐觉得，信的那头，似乎有一个贴着她的心长出来的人，吾志彼洞明，吾怀彼尽承，似同魂，如共魄。

鱼雁往还，忽焉六载。
廿二岁生辰的前夕，韦一渡的信再次翩然而至，这一回，素笺无字，上面画着一只孤舟，岸边有个人正翘首等待它靠岸。信封里还夹着一片雁羽。
小舟拿着信，神色淡淡地望向窗外：落脚的村子民风淳朴，有少女在水边浣衣，有孩童在田边放牧，有文弱的少年举着一把弓，吃力地挽起，准备射天上的大雁。身旁的猎户想要上前帮忙，那执拗的少年却言辞谢绝：向心上人提亲用的聘雁必须自己来打，方显心意，即使箭术不精，亦要亲力亲为。
彼时风过莲塘，正有双雁掠水南飞。
小舟捏着那根雁羽，忽然有些想家。
en:
Outside the window, the grass grew tall and orioles took to the wing; it was the height of spring. Inside, Qi Xiaozhou critically inspected her travel pack: Silver, sufficient. Two sets of folded clothes for a change. Dry rations to last half a month. A short blade, kept close at her side. But the most crucial of all was that horse, Ebon Hoof, which she had coaxed from her uncle! At this moment, it was leisurely grazing on the turf beneath the eaves, waiting for her to set forth.
Having grown up among herds of horses, the young girl moved like the wind, and her temper was just as breezy. Tired of the overly familiar scenery of her home, the sixteen-year-old Qi Xiaozhou slung her bundle over her shoulder, bid her family farewell, and ventured out into the martial world.
The Jianghu was the world outside, and the world outside was the Jianghu. Yet, after being away from home for many days, she realized that those thrilling tales of swift vengeance and freely given gratitude in the storybooks were, in the end, nothing but ink and smoke. The scenery constantly changed, but the novelty wore off rapidly. What filled her eyes day after day was the endless, dark tide of refugees fleeing from the north. The fear and numbness in their eyes made her heart ache.
Xiaozhou reined in her horse and pondered for a moment. The decisions of the young are always made in a heartbeat. Thus, this solitary little boat turned her course against the current.
It was the time when the Khitans were invading the Central Plains from the north. Traveling north from Qinghe, passing through Weizhou and Jizhou, Qi Xiaozhou witnessed countless unarmed commoners slaughtered beneath the hooves of barbarian cavalry. Holding onto her young and fearless heart, she kept marching forward. She had killed soldiers, saved refugees, slept at desolate ferry crossings, and eaten raw meat. She thought she had finally found what she truly wanted to do in life. Since there were so many people needing help, she would simply become a great hero and help as many as she could!
In her first year of chivalry, she rescued the twin brothers Zhi and Po on the ancient roads of Weizhou. They happened upon the old master of the Shengle Sect, who, seeing the exceptional martial potential in the twins, asked her for them.
She had heard of the chivalrous reputation of the Shengle Sect since childhood. Giving a man a fish is not as good as teaching him to fish. If the two brothers could learn martial arts to protect themselves, the day their twin swords were drawn, they might save thousands of lives!
Having settled the twins, Xiaozhou rose to take her leave. Wei Yidu, the young master of the Shengle Sect, chased after her and handed her a parcel. Inside was not only a brand-new fire starter but also a silk handkerchief and several boxes of face cream.
"Your fire starter has grown old, and the bitter cold of the north has left your face somewhat chapped. I have prepared this meager gift; please do not laugh at its inadequacy."
The night was long and profound, and the young gentleman stood like flawless jade, his demeanor as bright as a clear breeze and the moon after rain.
Xiaozhou accepted the parcel, offered a word of thanks, and spurred her horse away without a single backward glance.
When she returned to Weizhou again, a letter was already waiting on her desk at the posthouse. The envelope bore the character "Wei," and the handwriting was thick, graceful, and charming. Accompanying the letter was a box of lotus pastries. Xiaozhou casually tossed the letter aside and picked up a pastry to taste. Too much sugar; it was too cloying.
She then dug out the parcel Wei Yidu had given her, kept only the fire starter, and gave the silk handkerchief and face cream to the posthouse cook.
For the next several months, wherever her horse's hooves tread, letters would chase the clouds to reach her. The contents were nothing more than local delicacies, new poems from the towns, and the signatures were always followed by words of deep concern. Xiaozhou understood the man's intentions, but how could such trivial tricks of courtship make her drop the sword in her hand? Her first reply cherished words like gold: "My ambition lies in chivalry; how could I indulge in romance?"
The letters stopped for over a month.
When she finally received another letter, though the signature remained the same, the handwriting had drastically changed. This time, there were no poems or talks of delicacies. It simply gave an update on the brothers Zhi and Po, and humbly asked her for some tips on horse taming. The letter also mentioned that the calligraphy style he previously copied was weak in structure and languid in form, so he had recently switched to studying the vigorous stele inscriptions of the Wei dynasty.
As if possessed by ghosts and gods, Xiaozhou wrote her second reply. She inquired about the brothers, taught him the secrets of horse taming, and praised his new handwriting. Slowly, they began to talk about everything, from horse taming and calligraphy to sword techniques and stances, from the old rumors of the previous dynasty to the new affairs of the martial world. Gradually, Xiaozhou felt that at the other end of the letters, there was someone growing close to her very heart. He understands my ambitions entirely, and embraces my feelings completely; it is as if we share the same soul and spirit.
Messages flew back and forth like migrating geese, and in a flash, six years had passed.
On the eve of her twenty-second birthday, Wei Yidu's letter fluttered in once again. This time, the plain paper bore no words, only a drawing of a lone boat, and a person standing on the shore, craning his neck in anticipation of its docking. Tucked inside the envelope was a single goose feather.
Holding the letter, Xiaozhou gazed out the window with a gentle expression. The village where she rested had simple and honest customs: a young girl was washing clothes by the water, a child was herding cattle by the fields, and a frail-looking youth was struggling to draw a bow, aiming at the wild geese in the sky. A nearby hunter wanted to step forward and help, but the stubborn youth politely declined: The betrothal goose used to propose to one's beloved must be hunted by one's own hands to show true sincerity; even if his archery was poor, he had to do it himself.
At that moment, the wind swept over the lotus pond, and a pair of wild geese skimmed the water, flying south.
Rolling that single goose feather between her fingers, Xiaozhou suddenly felt a little homesick.

The first time I came to Skybrim Market, I was astonished by its prosperity and joy.

As soon as I stepped onto the long bridge, I was swept along by the crowd. The deity competition before the market tower was truly lively, with gongs and drums... I heard that the general was inside that great market tower. 
What did they add to the lanterns? As I walked, I grew dizzy... Well then, I'll follow their lead and scoop wine with a cup to drink! Anyway, I've given the map to Brother Eagle, so I'll just take it easy, whoa...!

zh:
剑会因为失去主人而哀鸣吗？
很多江湖人怀疑着，老马，老友都有情，但一把剑？
而看到这把似无量之剑的人，都会动摇自己的想法。

这是一把失去主人的剑。
它没有断，没有锈。它凌冽的寒光还在，它耿直的剑身还在。但它不再让人视之生畏了。
现在的它，是一把平平无奇的剑。
世上没有人相信它是那把无量剑，连它两任主人的传说都很少再提起。
这世界上，即使是最强大的印记，也会被带走。
而那呼啸过去的，带走一切的，是时间。
en:
Does a sword weep for its master?
The jianghu would scoff at the thought. An old horse or a lifelong friend might mourn, but a length of cold steel?
Yet, anyone who cast their eyes upon this legendary blade would feel their certainties crumble.

For it is a masterless thing now.
Neither broken nor rusted, its icy gleam and flawless edge remain untouched. But the terror it once inspired has vanished.
It sits now as a mundane, unremarkable weapon.
No one believes it to be the mythical Wuliang Blade, and the epics of the two masters who once wielded it have drifted into obscurity.
In this world, even the deepest scars and the most indelible marks are ultimately worn away.
And the howling wind that erodes it all, sweeping everything into oblivion, is time.
