zh:
余与庄周与濠梁坐而论道，言及鱼之乐，偶得一新道，著不可言之书。
此书仅言一字，不以诗书为基，以偏为全，似有理实则无理，凡有所言皆可为错。然字甚毒，不以礼仪为界，贩夫走卒皆可为之，若用之不慎或有奇灾，慎之，慎之。
此字曰，杠。
杠之道其一，言必非。天地万物，必分阴阳，有是必有非。杠之道，在非其言而非非其理，以其言之非非之，更无需明其言之理。
杠之道其二，言其独。众人皆醉，醒者为尊，假弱以胜强。杠之道，在言其异而引众情，以众情而压其道，愚者必从之。
杠之道其三，言生言。凡有所言，定有所失，以其失攻其实。杠之道，在以虚盖实化虚为实，以其言之失换其言之理，甚者以失为理。
en:
Once, I was discussing the joy of fish with Zhuangzi by the river, a sudden insight struck me—this gave rise to The Unspoken.
This book centers on one word. It draws on no classics or teachings and mistakes fragments for wholes—plausible yet absurd, possibly all wrong. But this word is dangerous: it defies etiquette, easily wielded by anyone, and if carelessly used, it invites unexpected trouble—beware.
That word is "argue."
Firstly, deny whatever is said. Just target the statement, not its logic—attacking words without regard for truth.
Secondly, stand apart. By adopting a weaker stance, you can defeat the strong—offer a contrary view, stir emotions, and let the crowd's passion silence reason. The foolish will follow.
Thirdly, let words feed on words. Every utterance has flaws—find and exploit them. Use emptiness to mask reality and turn mistakes into principles.

zh:
问秋的爹娘早已退居幕后，但偶尔也会来点心铺，帮问秋招揽下生意。
秋天五色糕卖得最好，其他季节虽然也有稳定的客人，可总归还得叫喊两句宣传一下。
冬天的时候，他们就喊这五色糕藏阳养阴，冬天吃是最有益的。
在春天，他们的说法是五色糕滋养肝气，春天吃能强身健体，保客人一年都少生几场病。
到夏天，他们又换了套说辞，说这五色糕是去火气的。

谷问秋听到这话没忍住，把他们拉到一旁，让他们少看一点没有来由的医药方子。
她不说还好，这样一来，二人就冲她来了，说她火气太旺，最好也吃一点五色糕。
谷问秋拦不住，也就由着他们去了。

小时候谷问秋也好奇，一年也就一个重阳节，可怎么一年到头，爹娘都不见得有休息的时候。
“因为总会有人想吃啊。”
不是重阳节，也有人想要吃五色糕吗？
问秋想不通。上元节过了她就不想玩花灯了，五月五过了五彩缕就不知道扔哪里去了。
怎么会有人天天想要过重阳呢？

直到她自己接手了这间铺子，她发现那些重阳一起约着来买五色糕的人，平日里都是独自来的。
不是天天都是重阳节，但每天都会有人想起，一块过重阳的朋友们。
没有相聚的日子里，他们也在惦记着彼此。
en:
Wenqiu's parents had long since stepped out of the spotlight, but every so often they would still drift back into the pastry shop, lending a hand and a voice to help her pull in customers.
The Five-colored cakes sold best in autumn. The rest of the year wasn't bad either, though it never hurt to shout a few extra lines.
In winter, they swore the cakes "stored warmth and nourished the body," the perfect thing to eat against the cold.
Come spring, the story changed: now the cakes were said to restore vital energy, strengthen the body, and keep illness at bay for the year ahead.
By summer, they had a new claim ready: Five-colored Cakes, apparently, could cool the blood and drive off excess heat.

Wenqiu finally couldn't take it anymore. She pulled them aside and told them to stop reading those half-baked medical pamphlets.
That only made things worse. Her parents turned on her instead, declaring that her own temper ran too hot and that she ought to eat more Five-colored Cakes herself.
In the end, she gave up and let them carry on.

When she was young, she had often wondered about it. The Double Ninth Festival came only once a year, but why did her parents seem busy all year long, never taking a break?
"Because someone always wants to eat them," they told her.
But that made no sense to her. Outside the Double Ninth Festival, who would want Five-colored Cakes?
After the Lantern Festival, she lost all interest in lanterns. After the fifth day of the fifth month, the Five Color Threads were tossed aside and forgotten.
Who, she wondered, would want to celebrate the Double Ninth every single day?

Only after she inherited the shop did she begin to understand. The people who once came in groups on the Double Ninth now came alone, on ordinary days.
It wasn't always the festival—but every day, someone remembered the friends they used to celebrate with.
Even apart, they are still together in thought.

zh:
放排翁，本名黄止水。

少历世事，阅历丰赡。既能操刀精雕，复可执杆放排，刚柔并济，游刃有余。

其一生要事，多与冯道相涉，或仕途进退，或他事浮沉，皆有关联。
后周时期，冯道离世，黄止水闻讯，知故人凋零、世事已变，遂自举葬礼、办丧仪，对外宣称身故，示人“黄止水已随旧事俱逝”。

后隐于青州山水间，自号“放排翁”。棍法悟自江流，取水势之柔韧。因早年操刀过甚，运棍间犹带雕琢之痕，转折顿挫，似有刻镂之意，然借排势起伏，自成殊音。
en:
The Old Raftsman was originally named Huang Zhishui.
He experienced much in his youth and possesses a profound understanding of the world. He is equally adept at wielding a carving knife for exquisite woodwork and handling a pole to navigate river rafts. Balancing hardness and softness, he maneuvers through life with effortless grace.
The major events of his life were closely tied to the legendary official Feng Dao, intimately linked to his rise and fall in politics and the turbulent tides of fate.
During the Later Zhou dynasty, upon hearing of Feng Dao's passing, Huang realized that his old friends were withering away and the world had irreversibly changed. Thus, he hosted his own funeral and mourning rites, declaring to the world that "Huang Zhishui has passed away along with the old days."
He then retreated into the mountains and waters of Qingzhou, styling himself the "Old Raftsman." He enlightened his staff techniques from the river currents, absorbing the resilience of the water. Because he wielded a carving knife so heavily in his early years, his staff movements still carry the distinct marks of a woodcarver's chisel. Every twist and pause feels like an act of precise sculpting, yet by borrowing the rhythmic rise and fall of a river raft, he strikes a unique and formidable chord of his own.

团团曾经是一只胆子很小的小猫，面对没见过的事物，第一反应就是将自己团起来。
在猫妈妈离去后，它一路跌撞奔波才寻觅到了一处看起来颇为静谧的屋舍。只是后来团团才知道，这里看起来静谧，只是因为当时还未至待漏时。于是没过多久，它便被一群五大三粗，穿着袍子的人吓醒了。
好在那些人虽然看起来高大凶猛，却都对团团十分温柔，不急不躁，慢慢靠近并安抚它，让它渐渐放下了防备。
而后，团团在他们的带领下，进行了大量“强兵练习”：逐敌行迹、寻其弱处、伺机而动、一击即中！……
现如今，团团已经是文明殿内走路姿势最嚣张、叫声最响亮的小猫了。
en:
Tuantuan used to be a timid little kitten. Whenever it met something unfamiliar, its first instinct was to curl up into a tight ball.

After its mother was gone, it stumbled and wandered for a long time before finding a building that seemed wonderfully quiet.
Only later did Tuantuan learn the truth. It was quiet because the early court hour hadn't arrived yet.

Not long after, it was jolted awake by a group of big, broad-shouldered people in robes.
They looked fierce. They were not.
They spoke softly, never rushed, and inched closer to soothe it until Tuantuan finally let its guard down.

After that, under their guidance, Tuantuan went through intensive "combat training":
Track the enemy.
Find the weak spot.
Wait for the opening.
Strike in one hit!

These days, Tuantuan is the loudest meower and the most swaggering walker in all of Wenming Hall.

后伶宦当道，长安梦醒。范黎拏舟归青州，茫茫然不知此身何在。忽闻江上舟子放歌，响遏行云，恰如去时。
即岸，舟子斟酒相劝：“请君满饮青州酿。”范黎饮之，甘醇如故，酒酣而泣，醒后归涌泉镇，设坛讲学。
en:
In years past, when Fan Li passed the imperial examinations, the Governor of Qingzhou held a Luming Banquet in his honor. Throughout the feast they drank deeply of Qingzhou Brew, and the Governor raised his cup and said: "With talents such as yours, you ought to be drinking the Imperial Wine."
Years later, when eunuchs and jesters held sway at court, Fan Li awoke from his Chang'an dream. He took a boat back to Qingzhou, adrift and lost, uncertain of his place in the world. Then, from the river, he heard a boatman singing, his voice stopping the clouds, just as it had been when Fan Li first departed.
Upon reaching the shore, the boatman poured him a cup and urged: "Please, drink your fill of Qingzhou Brew." Fan Li drank. The taste was as sweet and mellow as ever. He wept in his wine, and when he sobered, made his way back to Wellspring Town to teach.

zh:
古穷奇效于秦，助平六国，天下一统。献金人图纸，始皇帝遂集天下兵，令铸金人十二。穷奇之义，穷天下之奇，以极智掌极力，镇万世太平。
然秦渐暴而民苦，穷奇自裂为二。其一为墨山道，枷金人身、斫金人首，誓不复效秦。金人之技，至此绝辍。
汉时，儒墨论道，墨山道僻入山中，金人移葬此地。
重观此重器，不改我判言：古穷奇欲以地磁驱之，纵再研百年，可行之数亦廖。守此地者，以今者之才不敢言昔人，自困于此，惑甚。以我所知，据理而行。不惜身，不惜名，此方墨者道。
至于道义……
穷奇之义近于墨，而我门行之愈远矣。
参金人地磁之法更做改益，得司南剑术。
前人未竟事，今人可更胜之。
——刻于开运四年二月
en:
In ancient times, the Qiongqi served Qin, assisting in the subjugation of the Six States and the unification of the world. By offering the blueprints of the Golden Colossi, the First Emperor rallied the world's weaponry and ordered the casting of twelve such giants. The essence of Qiongqi was to exhaust the wonders of the realm, wielding ultimate power through ultimate wisdom to secure eternal peace.
However, as Qin grew tyrannical and the people suffered, Qiongqi fractured into two. One half became Mohist Hill. They chained the bodies of the Golden Colossi and severed their heads, swearing never to serve Qin again. Thus, the craft of the Golden Colossi was lost to time.
During the Han Dynasty, when Confucian and Mohist scholars debated the Dao, Mohist Hill retreated into the secluded mountains, relocating the remains of the Golden Colossi to this very place.
Reexamining these great constructs, my judgment remains unchanged: the ancient Qiongqi intended to power them with geomagnetism. Yet, even if we study this for another century, the chances of success are minuscule. Those guarding this place dare not speak of the ancients with their present meager talents, trapping themselves in deep delusion. I shall act upon the principles I know. To spare neither life nor reputation is the true path of a Mohist.
As for morality...
The ideals of Qiongqi once closely mirrored the Mohist way, yet our order has strayed ever further from it.
By studying the geomagnetic methods of the Golden Colossi and making improvements, I have derived the Lodestar Swordplay.
What the ancients left unfinished, the present generation can surpass.

Carved in the second month of the fourth year of Kaiyun.

zh:
阿然是个好孩子，阿然会陪刘奶奶聊天，轻轻摸摸刘奶奶的腿，刘奶奶告诉她，这是契丹人打进城的时候，摔伤的，于是阿然皱着眉头说契丹人的坏话，再将自己的小被子盖在刘奶奶的腿上。

阿然会和每一个人打招呼，阿然的声音总是亮堂堂的，大家都喜欢听阿然絮絮叨叨地说话，她把从她爹爹那里的故事告诉大伙儿，像个走街串巷的小小说书人。
有了阿然，这样大家都不用去江氏茶坊花钱听故事了，在鱼摊上吃面的大伙儿总这么说。

阿然喜欢荷花酥，但爹爹带给阿然的荷花酥，阿然总会留下一些。
她要留给最喜欢的爹爹，给很难出门的刘奶奶，给总在肉摊和她闲聊的刘叔叔，给让她来尝尝新的招牌菜的孙叔叔，给一起讲故事的玩伴，给总站在她这边的任小平他娘，还有谁呢，还有任小平！她才不给总和她对着干的任小平。
她想要给的人太多了，所以她的荷花酥总是不够分。
于是阿然留给自己的荷花酥总是少一些，留三块不行，留两块，留一块吧。

话本子里的人都是这么做的，阿然听着话本子长大，活的像个话本子里的故事。
世上的人都喜欢话本子，都喜欢话本子里的故事，所有人都应该过喜欢的生活，那就是话本子里的生活。
en:
Ran was a good child. Ran would sit with Grannie Liu and keep her company, gently patting the old woman's leg. Grannie Liu told her the injury came from when the Khitan soldiers stormed the city, and Ran would frown, muttering curses about the Khitans before carefully tucking her own little quilt over Grannie Liu's knees.

Ran greeted everyone she met, her voice always bright and clear. People loved listening to her chatter. She'd spin tales she'd picked up from her father, like a tiny storyteller wandering the streets. "With Ran around, who needs to waste coin at Jiang's Teahouse for stories?" the folks at the noodle stall often said.

Ran adored lotus pastries, but she never finished the ones her father brought her. She always saved some. She set aside pieces for her beloved father, for Grannie Liu who rarely went out, for Uncle Liu at the butcher's stall who chatted with her, for Uncle Sun who let her taste new dishes, for her story-sharing playmates, for Ren Xiaoping's mother who always took her side, and who else? Oh, Ren Xiaoping! But she'd never give him any, not after he always argued with her. There were too many people she wanted to share with, so her pastries were never enough. So Ran always kept the smallest portion for herself: first three pieces, then two, then just one.

She'd grown up on storybooks, and she lived like a character straight out of one.The world loved storybooks and the stories within them. Everyone deserved to live the life they adored, and that life ought to be just like the tales.

我的好大侠：
为鱼而渔，人之常情，但我本意并非如此。
想寻一处静谧，安放纷乱思绪，垂钓当为上选。
说来有趣，只消盯着水面等待鱼儿，事儿就想明白了，心情也舒畅不少！
大概这就是心静鱼来，愿者上钩？
虽意不在鱼，不料鱼获愈丰，分予附近的小童，还剩沉甸甸的一篓。
不如这样……剩下的鱼全归你，你负责烤，我勉强帮你分担吃一半！
这主意不错吧，我的好大侠？
en:
My dear hero,
Fishing for fish is only natural, but that was not quite my purpose.
I only wanted a quiet place to settle a restless mind, and fishing seemed just the thing. Funny, really. All it takes is watching the water and waiting for a bite, and somehow everything starts to fall into place. Even the mood grows lighter.
Perhaps that is what it means for fish to come when the heart is still, and for the willing to take the hook.
I was not fishing for the catch, yet the catch kept coming. I shared some with the children nearby, and still had a heavy basket left.
So how about this. The rest of the fish are yours. You can do the grilling, and I will kindly help by eating half.
Not a bad idea, is it, my dear hero?

少年的竹枪终于变作如今的手杖，脸上有了些风霜的小老头，仍一次次登上那封龙山，只是健步如飞的两条腿变作了三条腿。

A bamboo stick as a spear, old wine at the waist. Practicing chivalry, a carefree crane, wouldn't that be joyful?
Later, fishing in various places, this old bamboo was mostly used for clearing the way. The world is vast, where can't you go?
Only later did he have to admit that everyone grows old. Living a carefree life, but always wandering, he aged faster than most.
Not as good at martial arts as Halcyon, not as strategic as Raven, not as skilled in mechanisms as that senior disciple, and in farming, military, Daoism, law, etc., surpassed by many younger talents... Fortunately, he knew a little of everything.
Later, those better than me called me Master.
The boy's bamboo spear finally became today's walking stick. The little old man with some weather on his face still climbs Dragonbend Mountain repeatedly. Only his two swift legs have become three.
The sound of reading is loud on the mountain. Down the mountain, some young lad's matter, just like a scene from yesterday: a bamboo stick as a spear, off to practice chivalry?

法事未成。

Old Monk's Torn Record II

The living remain temporarily in the temple. For the dead, we bind paper effigies as bodies.
When one dies in a strange land, the soul cannot find its way home. The effigy serves as the body. The name serves as the guide. The incense paves the road.
You must never paint eyes on the effigies. With eyes, they see the mortal realm. Seeing the mortal realm, they refuse to leave.

On the night of the Ghost Festival, I sought to burn the paper and send the souls away. Alas, heavy rain extinguished the incense. The sodden paper would not burn. The ritual failed.
I, too, have caught the sickness. My strength wanes by the day, and I fear I cannot guard this place much longer.

If anyone should arrive later and find this ruined temple, I beg you to light a stick of incense and prepare an altar of offerings.

To bury is not merely to hide, but to align with the current of living qi.

zh: 木风箱是中国传统冶金与炊事工具，属双向送风活塞式鼓风器。该装置主要由箱体、活塞、活门与推拉杆构成，通过人力驱动活塞往复运动，利用气压差原理实现持续鼓风。据《天工开物》记载，该技术至迟到明代已有成熟应用，但榆林窟壁画证明其实际应用可追溯至宋代。相较于欧洲18世纪才出现的同类技术，中国木风箱在冶金效率与机械设计方面具有显著领先性。
en: The wooden bellows was a traditional Chinese device used in both metalworking and cooking, a double-acting piston blower made of a wooden chamber, piston, valves, and a push-pull handle. As the piston moved back and forth by hand, it maintained a continuous draft by means of air-pressure differentials. According to Divinecraft, the technology was already highly developed by the Ming dynasty, while murals at the Yulin Caves show that it was in practical use as early as the Song. Compared with similar devices in Europe, which did not appear until the eighteenth century, the Chinese wooden bellows was remarkably advanced in both mechanical design and smelting efficiency.

The lucky charm is ready for our esteemed guest. I wonder when you plan to return home today? You're a year older now—be more sensible and stop talking about fighting and killing in the Jianghu. What's so great about the Jianghu? You'll only end up getting hurt!

zh:
离除夕还有一个月时，江无浪就开始琢磨，要给家里带个小礼物。
恰好同船的老汉同他念叨，现在的娃娃都喜欢小马。江无浪摸了摸钱袋……最后选了块木头，提起了刻刀。
握惯重剑的手，握着小小刻刀时，却笨拙得不像话。木头废了一地，碎屑堆成小山。终于，临近除夕时，一只歪歪扭扭的小木马躺在了他掌心——笑得憨憨的，有几分像那孩子咧嘴的模样。
江无浪看了会儿，而后收进怀里。
愿这笑脸，永远这般无拘无碍。
en:
A full month before Spring Festival's Eve, Jiang Wulang was already thinking about what to bring home.
An old man on the boat told him that children liked toy horses these days. Jiang Wulang checked his coin bag, thought it over, and bought a block of wood instead.
A man used to handling a heavy sword had no business carving something that small. He ruined piece after piece. Wood shavings piled up around him. Finally, just before Spring Festival's Eve, a crooked little wooden horse lay in his palm. It wore a goofy smile that looked a little like the child it was meant for.
Jiang Wulang looked at it for a while, then tucked it away.
May that smile last forever.

$T(30)心里想着，那被打倒的“恶匪”，会不会其实也没那么坏呢？
也许他只是走错了路，挨了这一顿打，反倒醒了过来？
也许他和大侠二人不打不相识，日后就成了顶好的朋友，一同闯荡江湖去了？

en:
The gongs rang out high and loud. The cymbals came in bright and clear. The erhu carried the tune along. As the music rose and fell, light and shadow moved across the screen, and the shadow play performed a familiar story: a hero saved the girl and defeated the outlaw.
The outlaw fell. The girl was saved. The two of them left together.
In front of the stage, a child sat with their chin propped in their hand, watching without blinking.
But $T(30)'s mind had already gone somewhere else: What if the outlaw was not really that bad?
Maybe he had just gone down the wrong road. Maybe that beating was what finally brought him to his senses.
Maybe he and the hero talked afterward. Maybe one fight was all it took for them to understand each other. Maybe they even became friends and set off together.
By the time the lights on the stage dimmed, the story there was over. But the one in the child's head was only just beginning.

zh:
龟奶奶又一次检查自己的聚宝盆。前些日子，这里头多出来好多钱。她问了人，他们说，这是宋元通宝。
噢……那这是好钱呢。宋元通宝，可以给盈盈买双新鞋子，到处走走跑跑，鞋子都磨破了……可以给老大攒点——不对不对，老大没回来，但是，老幺回来啦。
老幺是个好孩儿，来去都风风火火的，很凶的人闯进来的时候，就拦在她和盈盈面前的。
龟奶奶算着，聚宝盆生出来的钱，宋元通宝，能买好多饼子、馍馍、馒头、面条……再不用给老幺喝稀粥啦。对了，麦子也收了，给盈盈和老幺，都攒点买地钱。
也不能都攒着，老幺要是回来啊，就买点——
#Y买点麦香集的烧鸭面。听小伙吆喝着，烧鸭能有三吃，好香呢，给老幺好好尝尝。#E
en:
Granny Turtle checked her Treasure Basin once again. Lately, a lot more coins have appeared inside it.
She asked around, and people told her they were Song Coins.
Oh... then these are good coins. With Song Coins, she could buy Yingying a new pair of shoes. The girl ran and skipped everywhere, and her shoes were all worn through... She could save a little for the eldest, too. No, no, the eldest hadn't come home yet, but the youngest had.
The youngest was a good child, always coming and going in a whirlwind. When that fierce-looking man barged in, it was the youngest who stood right in front of her and Yingying.
Granny Turtle calculated in her head. The coins from the Treasure Basin, these Song Coins, could buy so many things: flatbreads, steamed buns, rolls, noodles... The youngest would never have to live on thin gruel again. Ah, yes, the wheat had been harvested too. She should save a little toward buying land for both Yingying and the youngest.
But she couldn't just save it all. If the youngest came back, she ought to buy...
#YRoast duck noodles from Wheatwind Bazaar. She heard the young hawker calling out that the roast duck could be eaten in three ways, and it smelled so fragrant. She must let the youngest have a proper taste of it.#E

可我认识你时，你手里却空无一物。
那时的你，只是一个哭泣的、无助的小女孩。你千里迢迢赶来，却被大大的奠字拦在门外。
你再也见不到爷爷了。可你的剑还在等你，在那个小小的木匣之中。
他们把你推出来，摔在地上，你又一遍遍地站起来，走上前去。
“那是我的剑”你哭着，“可是爷爷说，那是我的剑。”
我看着她，像一颗瘦瘦小小的钉子，倔强地扎进了雪地里。
en:
But when I met you, your hands were empty.
You were just a weeping, helpless little girl. You had traveled so far, only to be stopped by the mourning banners at the gate.
You would never see your grandfather again. But your sword was waiting for you, inside that small wooden box.
They shoved you out, threw you to the ground, but you stood back up and walked forward, again and again.
"That's my sword," you cried. "Grandfather said that's my sword!"
I watched a thin, tiny nail being driven stubbornly into the snow.

zh:
阿景与阿达拖着步子挪回营地。阿达瘫在草垛上彻底歇了心思，阿景却咽不下这口气，偏要探出张叔的来历。经历种种，他不再莽撞行事，只缩在柴垛后盯着那抹衣角。
而后，古卷每补全一寸，张叔的疯症便褪去三分。他常蹲在月光下摩挲泛黄纸页，指节蹭着卷边沙沙作响。直到某游侠补完最后一笔残墨，张叔忽然笑了，眼尾皱起两道深深沟壑。
是夜，阿景照旧猫在苇丛里。只见张叔立在河滩仰颈大笑，声浪惊起宿鸟。横刀上原本模糊的字样，竟泛起金光，仔细可辩“归义”二字。
“如此，我们便可回家了。”
话音未落，破甲陡然泛起涟漪，张叔的身体竟开始变得模糊，整个人化作流萤没入夜风，向西而去，消失在夜色中。唯余半卷《河西舆图》躺在卵石间。
阿景揉了揉眼睛，不敢相信自己所见。他急忙扑过去抓起图卷。
缓缓展开舆图，只见河西十一州疆域被详尽勾勒，玉门关、阳关等军事要塞亦被清晰标注。 而舆图之末，一封信件悄然滑落。
信笺之上，张叔之字，平和而亲切：
“后生，你跟着我这些天，怕是要叫你失望了。”
“…我想起来了……想起了家，想起了大唐，也想起了我的兵。他们和你们一样，眼睛亮亮的，看着我，等我带他们回去……”
“我们也拼了命的护送过，跨越过，踩着同袍的身体张望过……只是，我们护送的是舆图。跨的是祁连山垭口的冰隙。而我们脚踩脚肩顶肩眺望着的……是沙漠里的狼烟，和狼烟尽头的长安城。”
“对不住啊.....这几日把你们.....当成我的儿郎们.....”
晨光刺眼，阿景冲回营地，欲将此事告知众人。谁知，众人对张叔记忆竟如云烟消散。
“不对，我还有信！”阿景他急急展开信笺，却发现信中的字迹已经消失得无影无踪。
“你怕不是睡昏头了吧？”众人哄笑着离去，阿景摸着脑袋，心中满是困惑。
难道……真是梦一场？但这几日……明明历历在目……
“你怕不是睡昏头了吧？”众人哄笑着离去，阿景摸着脑袋，心中满是困惑。
难道……真是梦一场？但这几日……明明历历在目……
“阿景，速速，不然抢不着饭了！”门口传来阿达催促声。
阿景回神，摇头苦笑，望了望白纸，又望了望自己饥肠辘辘的肚子。
最终，他决定先放下这些烦恼。快速收拾行装，加入那抢饭行列。
门内，那封信纸，在他转身时碎作星芒，混着晨雾散在炊烟里。随着风，向西而去。
en:
Jing and Da dragged their feet back to camp. Da collapsed on a haystack, completely giving up the idea. But Jing couldn't swallow his frustration; he was determined to uncover Uncle Zhang's origins. After all they'd been through, he no longer acted recklessly. Instead, he hid behind a woodpile, watching for a glimpse of that familiar tattered robe. 
Later, as the ancient scroll was gradually restored, inch by inch, Uncle Zhang's madness seemed to recede. He would often crouch in the moonlight, stroking the yellowed paper, his knuckles rasping against the worn edges. Finally, when a wanderer filled in the last stroke of missing ink, Uncle Zhang suddenly smiled, deep creases forming at the corners of his eyes. 
That night, Jing hid as usual in the reeds. He saw Uncle Zhang standing on the riverbank, throwing back his head and laughing loudly, the sound startling roosting birds. The previously blurred characters on the Heng Blade now glimmered with golden light, clearly discernible as the characters "Guiyi." 
"Thus, we can go home now." 
No sooner had the words left his mouth than his broken armor seemed to ripple. Uncle Zhang's body began to blur, dissolving into fireflies that vanished into the night wind, flying westward, disappearing into the darkness. All that remained was half a scroll of the "Hexi Map" lying among the pebbles. 
Jing rubbed his eyes, unable to believe what he had seen. He rushed over and snatched up the map. 
Unfurling it slowly, he saw the territories of the eleven prefectures of Hexi meticulously outlined, with military fortresses like Jade Gate Pass and Yangguan Pass clearly marked. At the end of the map, a letter slipped out. 
Uncle Zhang's message was kind, his tone calm.
"Young man, following me these past few days must have disappointed you." 
"...I remember it... I remember my home, I remember the Great Tang, and I remember my soldiers. They were just like you. Their eyes bright, looking at me as they waited for me to lead them home..."
"We, too, risked our lives escorting, crossing over, standing on the bodies of comrades to look ahead... Only, what we escorted was a map. What we crossed were the icy crevasses of the Qilian Mountains' passes. And what we stood shoulder-to-shoulder, straining to see... were the beacon fires in the desert, and beyond those fires, Chang'an city." 
"Sorry... these past few days... I mistook you for my boys..."
The morning light was piercing. Jing rushed back to camp, wanting to tell everyone. To his surprise, everyone's memory of Uncle Zhang had dissipated like smoke. 
"No, I still have the letter!" He hurriedly unfolded the letter, only to find the writing had vanished without a trace. 
"You must have been dreaming, right?" The crowd laughed and dispersed. Jing rubbed his head, his heart full of confusion. 
Could it have been... just a dream? But these past few days... they felt so vivid...
"You must have been dreaming, right?" The crowd laughed and dispersed. Jing rubbed his head, his heart full of confusion. 
Could it have been... just a dream? But these past few days... they felt so vivid...
"Jing, hurry up, or we won't get any food!" Da's urging came from the doorway. 
Jing snapped back to reality, shook his head with a bitter smile, glanced at the blank paper, then at his own growling stomach. 
In the end, he decided to put aside these troubles for now. Quickly gathering his things, he joined the rush for food. 
Inside the room, as he turned away, the letter paper scattered into starlight, mingling with the morning mist and dissipating into the cooking smoke. Carried by the wind, it drifted westward.

新朝煌煌，好日当空，而我为昨夜雪也。日出则雪消。太平将至，何处容我？
公无渡河，公唯渡河。堕河而死，当奈公何？

en:
I am Han Shouliang, the last servant of the Zhou, orphan of the House of Han. Hidden in shadows for ten years, spying for the state, I called that loyalty. My father died for his old master, a worthy end to repay imperial grace, and I called that honor.
But the thief who stole the throne turned out to be no thief at all. The people love him, and history will rewrite itself to prove them right. Who can distinguish crime from merit?
The new dynasty shines like the midday sun, while I am the snow of a dying night. When the sun rises, the snow vanishes. Peace is coming, but where is my place?

"Do not cross that river," they said.
He crossed it all the same.
The river took him.
And what is there left to say?

If this peace of yours is real, what does that leave me?

Final Words of Han Shouliang

【众生·四】

【道士】

登南岳事毕谒司马道士
张九龄
将命祈灵岳，回策诣真士。
绝迹寻一径，异香闻数里。
分庭八桂树，肃容两童子。

顾谓同来客，相去九牛毛。

就道士问周易参同契
王昌龄
仙人骑白鹿，发短耳何长。
时余采菖蒲，忽见嵩之阳。
稽首求丹经，乃出怀中方。
披读了不悟，归来问嵇康。
嗟余无道骨，发我入太行。

访戴天山道士不遇
李白
犬吠水声中，桃花带雨浓。
树深时见鹿，溪午不闻钟。
野竹分青霭，飞泉挂碧峰。
无人知所去，愁倚两三松。

【僧人】

寻山僧不遇作
李白
石径入丹壑，松门闭青苔。
闲阶有鸟迹，禅室无人开。
窥窗见白拂，挂壁生尘埃。
使我空叹息，欲去仍裴回。
香云徧山起，花雨从天来。
已有空乐好，况闻青猿哀。
了然绝世事，此地方悠哉。

夜寻僧不遇
于武陵
数歇度烟水，渐非尘俗间。
泉声入秋寺，月色遍寒山。
石路几回雪，竹房犹闭关。
不知双树客，何处与云闲。
en:
【All Beings · IV】

【Taoist】

Visiting Taoist Sima After Completing the Southern Mountain Pilgrimage
Zhang Jiuling
Sent on a mission to the sacred peak, I turned my steps to seek the true master.
Following a lone path, I caught a wondrous fragrance miles away.
Eight cassia trees flank the courtyard; two young acolytes stand in solemn grace.
Entering the chamber, I hope to grasp his sleeve; approaching his seat, I long to speak.
He urges me to abandon clever stratagems, to wander with the Mystic Pearl from the start.
Profound and serene, embracing emptiness; calm and content, showing joyful ease.
He turns to the companion who came with me, saying the distance between us is vast.

Inquiring of the Taoist About the "Zhouyi Cantongqi"
Wang Changling
A sage rides a white deer, with short hair and long ears.
While I was gathering sweetflag, I suddenly saw him on Mount Song's southern slope.
I bowed and begged for the elixir scripture, which he then produced from his bosom.
I perused it but failed to grasp its meaning; returning home, I asked Ji Kang.
Alas, I lack the bone for the Way; he urged me to enter the Taihang Mountains.

Visiting the Taoist on Mount Dai Tian But Not Finding Him
Li Bai
Amid the sound of flowing water, a dog barks; peach blossoms, heavy with rain.
Deep in the woods, deer are sometimes seen; by the noon stream, no bell is heard.
Wild bamboo parts the blue mist; a flying cascade hangs from the emerald peak.
No one knows where he has gone; sorrowful, I lean against two or three pines.

【Monk】

Seeking the Mountain Monk But Not Finding Him
Li Bai
A stone path leads into crimson ravines; pine gates are closed by green moss.
On the idle steps are bird tracks; the meditation room's door is unopened.
Peering through the window, I see a white whisk; on the wall, dust gathers.
It fills me with empty sighs; wishing to leave, yet I linger.
Fragrant clouds rise all over the mountain; a rain of flowers falls from the sky.
Already there is the joy of emptiness, and then I hear the blue apes' mournful cries.
Completely detached from worldly affairs, this place is truly serene.

Seeking the Monk at Night But Not Finding Him
Yu Wuling
Resting several times, I cross the misty waters; gradually, it's no longer the mortal realm.
The sound of springs enters the autumn temple; moonlight spreads over the cold mountains.
The stone path has seen snow how many times? The bamboo chamber remains shut.
I wonder where the guest under the twin trees finds leisure with the clouds.
Midnight Blades Sufferer

取精铁矿，色如玄漆，质坚。
以水碓舂之，复以石碾。

Grinding Notes
Take refined iron ore, black as lacquer, hard in texture.
Pound it with a water pestle, then grind it with a stone mill.
Grind for one day, grains are like rice; grind for two days, like millet; grind for three days, obtain powder as fine as flour.
Further grinding yields no benefit.
Then sieve, keeping the light and fine—re-grind the coarse grains, striving for uniformity.
I have heard, "The finer the ore, the closer the fire." Now I test it.

大侠近来可好？
有一份心意想送与大侠。为免寄送延误，还请先行[<LINK id='link' color='#8c5823' url='https://research-game.163.com/htmls/46rzpk/paper.html?uid={uid}&role_id={pid}&server={hostnum}' is_underline='true'>点此留下信址</LINK>]。待我细细说来：
写这封信，是想给你报个喜。多亏你先前帮忙，我才有了支起摊子的本钱，在开封南郊的麦香集里寻了个落脚处。当初从家里出来时，哪敢想有今日……
爷爷常说，谢人不能只挂在嘴上。想来想去，我把近日攒下的钱寄回富平老家，用大侠的名义承包了五亩柿子地，托爷爷和乡亲们照看。爷爷说，要让你瞧瞧，特意让村里的老画师给画了下来，我都能想象后头红彤彤的模样了！
不过今年老家的天儿有些邪乎……又是旱又是涝的没断过，八成会影响收成……等到了做柿饼的时候，总要送你些尝尝，可能不多，但都是乡亲们的心意。不知大侠住在何处？一定包得仔仔细细的给你送去！
<IMAGE id='im1' image_url='https://h72.fp.ps.netease.com/file/6937da20e62c58e50e751d79u8vpNy7u07' size='1810*2704' color='255;255;255')'></IMAGE>
en:
Dear Wanderer,
How are you? I have a small token of my gratitude for you. To avoid any delay in its arrival, please press [<LINK id='link' color='#8c5823' url='https://research-game.163.com/htmls/46rzpk/paper.html?uid={uid}&role_id={pid}&server={hostnum}' is_underline='true'> to register your mailing address</LINK>] first. Allow me to explain:
I write with glad tidings. Thanks to your help, I've set up my stall at the Wheatwind Bazaar in Kaifeng Suburbs-South. When I left home, I never dreamed such a day…
Grandfather always said gratitude must be more than words. So I've sent my savings back to Fuping, my hometown, to lease five mu of persimmon groves in your name. Grandfather and the villagers tend them. He insisted on having the old painter paint them for you. I can already imagine the fiery red blaze!
But the weather's been cruel this year, drought and flood by turns. The harvest would likely suffer…
When the dried persimmons come, I'll send you some. Not much, perhaps, but grown from honest hearts. Where do you lodge? I'll package them with care and have them delivered.

【万章章句下】

孟子曰：伯夷目不视恶色，耳不听恶声，非其君不事，非其民不使，治则进，乱则退，扩政之所出，扩民之所止，不忍居也。思与乡人处，如以朝衣朝冠坐于涂炭也。当纣之时，居北海之滨，以待天下之清也。故闻伯夷之风者，顽夫廉，懦夫有立志。
伊尹曰：何事非君？何使非民？治亦进，乱亦进，曰：天之生斯民也，使先知觉后知，使先觉觉后觉。予，天民之先觉者，予将以此道觉此民也。思天下之民，匹夫匹妇有不与被尧舜之泽者，如己推而内之沟中，其自任以天下之重也。
柳下惠不羞污君，不辞小官，进不隐贤，必以其道。遗佚而不怨，阨穷而不闵，与乡人处，由由然不忍去也。尔为尔，我为我，虽袒裼裸裎于我侧，尔焉能浼我哉？故闻柳下惠之风者，鄙夫宽，薄夫敦。
孔子之去齐，接淅而行。去鲁，曰：迟迟吾行也，去父母国之道也。可以速而速，可以久而久，可以处而处，可以仕而仕，孔子也。
孟子曰：伯夷，圣之清者也；伊尹，圣之任者也；柳下惠，圣之和者也；孔子，圣之时者也。孔子之谓集大成。集大成也者，金声而玉振之也。金声也者，始条理也；玉振之也者，终条理也。始条理者，智之事也；终条理者，圣之事也。智，譬则巧也；圣，譬则力也。由射于百步之外也，其至，尔力也；其中，非尔力也。
北宫锜问曰：周室班爵禄也，如之何？
孟子曰：其详不可得闻也。诸侯恶其害已也，而皆去其籍。然而轲也尝闻其略也。天子一位，公一位，侯一位，子、男同一位，凡五等也。君一位，卿一位，大夫一位，上士一位，中士一位，下士一位，凡六等。天子之制，地方千里，公、侯皆方百里，伯七十里，子、男五十里，凡四等。不能五十里，不达于天子，附于诸侯，曰附庸。天子之卿受地视侯，大夫受地视伯，元士受地视子、男。大国地方百里，君十卿禄，卿禄四大夫，大夫倍上士，上士倍中士，中士倍下士，下士与庶人在官者同禄，禄足以代其耕也。次国地方七十里，君十卿禄，卿禄三大夫、大夫倍上士，上士倍中士，中士倍下士，下士与庶人在官者同禄，禄足以代其耕也。小国地方五十里，君十卿禄，卿禄二大夫，大夫倍上士，上士倍中士，中士倍下士，下士与庶人在官者同禄，禄足以代其耕也。耕者之所获，一夫百亩，百亩之粪，上农夫食九人，上次食八人，中食七人，中次食六人，下食五人。庶人在官者，其禄以是为差。
万章问曰：敢问友。
孟子曰：不挟长，不挟贵，不挟兄弟而友。友也者，友其德也，不可以有挟也。孟献子，百乘之家也，有友五人焉：乐正裘、牧仲，其三人则予忘之矣。献子之与此五人者，友也，无献子之家者也。此五人者，亦有献子之家，则不与之友矣。非惟百乘之家为然也，虽小国之君亦有之。
费惠公曰：吾于子思则师之矣，吾于颜般则友之矣，王顺、长息则事我者也。非惟小国之君为然也，虽大国之君亦有之。晋平公于亥唐也，入云则入，坐云则坐，食云则食，虽疏食菜羹，未尝不饱。盖不敢不饱也，然终于此而已矣。弗与共天位也，弗与治天职也，弗与食天禄也，士之尊贤者也，非王公尊贤也。舜尚见帝，帝馆甥于贰室，亦飨舜，迭为宾主，是天子而友匹夫也。用下敬上，谓之贵贵；用上敬下，谓之尊贤。贵贵尊贤，其义一也。

en:
【Wan Zhang Chapter II】

Mencius said: Bo Yi would not look with his eyes at a bad sight, nor listen with his ears to a bad sound. He would not serve a prince whom he did not approve, nor command a people whom he did not esteem. In a time of good government he took office; in a time of disorder he retired. He could not bear to dwell in a court from which a corrupt administration emanated, or among a people where oppressive government prevailed. To dwell among boorish villagers seemed to him like sitting in mud or charcoal with court robes and court cap. In the time of Zhou, he dwelt on the shores of the North Sea, waiting for the purification of the world. Therefore, when men now hear the character of Bo Yi, the corrupt become pure, and the weak acquire determination.
Yi Yin said: 'What prince may I not serve? What people may I not command?' In a time of good government he took office, and in a time of disorder he also took office. He said: 'Heaven's production of mankind, making the first know to awaken the later, and the first awaken to awaken the later. I am one of Heaven's people who have awakened first; I will awaken this people by this Way.' He thought that if any man or woman among the people of the world did not share in the benefits of Yao and Shun, it was as if he himself pushed them into a ditch—for he took upon himself the heavy responsibility of the world.
Liu Xia Hui was not ashamed to serve a corrupt prince, and did not decline a low office. When in office, he did not conceal his worth, but always acted according to his principles. When dismissed and neglected, he did not murmur; when straitened and poor, he did not grieve. When dwelling among boorish villagers, he was perfectly at ease and could not bear to leave them. 'You are you, and I am I. Though you stand by my side with breast and arms bare, or with your body naked, how can you defile me?' Therefore, when men now hear the character of Liu Xia Hui, the mean become generous, and the niggardly become liberal.
When Confucius left Qi, he strained off the water in which his rice was soaking and departed. When he left Lu, he said: 'I will take my time about departing—this is the way to leave the state of one's parents.' He could hasten when it was proper to hasten, and delay when it was proper to delay; he could retire when it was proper to retire, and take office when it was proper to take office—this was Confucius.
Mencius said: 'Bo Yi was the sage who was pure; Yi Yin was the sage who undertook responsibility; Liu Xia Hui was the sage who was harmonious; Confucius was the sage who was timely. Confucius may be called the complete concert. In being the complete concert, he is like the sound of the bell-metal beginning, and the jade-stone ending it. The sound of the bell-metal is the beginning of order; the sound of the jade-stone is the end of order. The beginning of order lies in the work of the wise; the end of order lies in the work of the sage. Wisdom may be compared to skill; sageness may be compared to strength. It is like shooting from beyond a hundred paces: its reaching the target is due to your strength, but its hitting the mark is not due to your strength.'
Bei Gong Qi asked: 'How did the house of Zhou regulate rank and emolument?'
Mencius said: 'The particulars of that arrangement cannot be learned. The princes, disliking that they were injurious to themselves, have all destroyed the records of them. Nevertheless, I have heard the outlines of them. The Son of Heaven constituted one degree; the dukes one; the marquises one; the earls, viscounts, and barons one degree—in all, five degrees. The ruler constituted one degree; the chief ministers one; the great officers one; the officers of the first class one; the officers of the middle class one; the officers of the lowest class one—in all, six degrees. The territory of the Son of Heaven was a thousand li square. Dukes and marquises had a hundred li square. Earls had seventy li square. Viscounts and barons had fifty li square—in all, four degrees. A territory not amounting to fifty li could not have access to the Son of Heaven, but was attached to some prince, and was called an appendage. The chief ministers of the Son of Heaven received territory equal to that of a marquis; a great officer received as much as an earl; an officer of the first class as much as a viscount or baron. In a great state of a hundred li square, the ruler had ten times the revenue of a chief minister; a chief minister had four times that of a great officer; a great officer had double that of an officer of the first class; an officer of the first class had double that of one of the middle class; an officer of the middle class had double that of one of the lowest class; an officer of the lowest class had the same revenue as the common people employed in government offices—sufficient to replace their farming. In a state of the next order, of seventy li square, the ruler had ten times the revenue of a chief minister; a chief minister had three times that of a great officer; a great officer had double that of an officer of the first class; an officer of the first class had double that of one of the middle class; an officer of the middle class had double that of one of the lowest class; an officer of the lowest class had the same revenue as the common people employed in government offices—sufficient to replace their farming. In a small state of fifty li square, the ruler had ten times the revenue of a chief minister; a chief minister had double that of a great officer; a great officer had double that of an officer of the first class; an officer of the first class had double that of one of the middle class; an officer of the middle class had double that of one of the lowest class; an officer of the lowest class had the same revenue as the common people employed in government offices—sufficient to replace their farming. As to what the farmers received, each husbandman had a hundred mu. With the manuring of these hundred mu, the best husbandmen could support nine persons, the next best eight, the next seven, the next six, and the lowest five. The salaries of the common people employed in government offices were regulated according to these differences.'
Wan Zhang asked: 'I venture to ask the principles of friendship.'
Mencius replied: 'Friendship should be maintained without any presumption on the ground of one's superior age, or station, or the circumstances of his relatives. Friendship with a man is friendship with his virtue, and does not admit of assumptions of superiority. Meng Xianzi, the head of a family of a hundred chariots, had five friends: Yue Zheng Qiu and Mu Zhong. The other three I have forgotten. Xianzi maintained friendship with these five men because they thought nothing about his family. If they had thought about his family, he would not have maintained friendship with them. Not only the head of a family of a hundred chariots acted thus. The same thing is exemplified in the case of a prince of a small state.
Duke Hui of Fei said: "I regard Zisi as my teacher. I regard Yan Ban as my friend. As to Wang Shun and Chang Xi, they serve me." Not only the prince of a small state acted thus. The same thing is exemplified in the case of a prince of a large state. Duke Ping of Jin, with regard to Hai Tang, when he told him to come in, came; when he told him to sit, sat; when he told him to eat, ate. There might only be coarse rice and soup of vegetables, but he always ate his fill, not daring to do otherwise. Here, however, he stopped, and went no further. He did not share with him his heavenly rank, nor govern with him his heavenly office, nor eat with him his heavenly emolument. This was a scholar's respect for worth, not that shown by a king or a duke to a worthy. Shun went to see the Emperor, who lodged his son-in-law in the second palace. He also feasted Shun, and they were alternately host and guest. Here we have the Son of Heaven maintaining friendship with a common man. Respect shown by inferiors to superiors is called giving honor to the honorable. Respect shown by superiors to inferiors is called giving honor to the worthy. The principle of giving honor to the honorable and giving honor to the worthy is the same.'

On Kaifeng City's southern wall stand three gates. The middle one is called Main South Gate. 
The ancients spoke of the four celestial beasts, each guarding a direction: Azure Dragon in the East, White Tiger in the West, Vermilion Bird in the South, and Black Tortoise in the North. Thus, the southern gate bears the name of the Vermilion Bird. 
Enter the city through Main South Gate and behold:
a long avenue lined with broad markets, ten thousand households. This is South Imperial Street, also called South Gate Avenue, stretching straight to Xuande Gate at the palace's edge. 
Follow its path, and you'll see shops densely packed,
peach and plum trees planted along the road,
crowds weaving endlessly, carts and carriages in a ceaseless flow. Prosperity fills the eye.

如今无心谷中皆是受梦傀之灾所害之人，他们为世人所忌，将自己自封于谷中，只希望能找到破解梦傀之法。
en:
After the Battle of Mount Mang, tales began to circulate of a strange creation known as the Sleeping Puppet—an undying, unyielding being. It was said that a secret sect called Hollow Vale was founded upon its power. Yet for reasons unknown, the sect soon vanished from the Jianghu. As chaos engulfed the Tang dynasty, the poison master Sun Buqi revived the Sleeping Puppet, unleashing a calamity that shook the Jianghu. 
Today, the Hollow Vale is home only to those afflicted by this very scourge. Shunned by all, they have sealed themselves within the valley, clinging to the hope that one day they might be able to break the Sleeping Puppet's curse.

zh:
狼山的第一场雪，还是落下了。
魏芷昔蜷缩在背风的山洞内，耳边充斥风声与隐约的哀嚎，眼前却浮现出与那人第一次见面的夜晚。破庙，风雨，飞尘，蛛网……委实是场很狼狈的开局。但皆是她有意为之。
爹爹说，生逢乱世，他护不了她一世周全。娘亲说，女子存世，当寻一可依仗之人。所以他们才安排了一场违背她心意的会面。她嗤之以鼻。
有一种鸟，永远在飞翔。谁都别想叫那鸟儿坠落。

但在狼山的这场初雪里，她反反复复的想起了那个男人。想他言语间的斟酌与小心翼翼。想他那时隐在篝火后隐隐绰绰的脸。
她那时其实也不算讨厌他，虽然他与她是完全不同的人。他壮志酬筹，他要治国，要平天下。而她心向自由，只想持刀闯天涯。但他身上有一种令她心安的平和。

是的，平和。他平和地倾听她口中的所有江湖，平和地目送她每一次的远去，又平和地在每一个渡口等待她的归来。即便是这最后一次的分离。
“那沧浪剑谱，我势在必得！”
“这次去多久？”
“不知道。若遇上大雪封山……归期自是不定。”
说出那话的时候，她其实有一些后悔。她给二人之间留足了退路，从未许下什么承诺。但他总在等她……她突然觉得，不该再这般肆无忌惮。
“要不，别等了？”
庙外头大雨倾盆，庙内篝火摇曳。他沉默了片刻，最后只是将烤好的红薯递了过来。
“烫，慢些吃。”

那便是他们最后一次的分离了。她摸不清他的答案是什么，但也做好了回去后再不相见的打算。只是，契丹犯境，百姓流离。她这一路走来，有些疲惫。而疲惫过后，生出了一些想念。

风雪还在呼啸。但又好似有一瞬的停滞。
魏芷昔似是感应到了什么，抬头看去。本该在千里之外的人，本该追随他的将领去平定淮南的人，为何会出现在这儿？
“来接你回去。”男人这样说。
魏芷昔沉默了片刻，笑了。
这一次，飞鸟欲归巢。
en:
The first snow of Wolf Mountain still came, in the end.
Wei Zhixi curled up inside a sheltered cave, the wind howling outside, faint cries echoing in the night.
But what she kept seeing, over and over, was the night she first met him, a rundown temple, wind and rain, dust swirling, cobwebs everywhere... a truly miserable beginning.
But that had all been by her own design.
Her father used to say that in troubled times, he couldn't protect her forever.
Her mother said a woman needed someone she could rely on.
That's why they arranged a meeting she never wanted.
She'd always scoffed at that.
Some birds, she thought, are born to fly.
No one can make them fall.

And yet, in this first snowfall on Wolf Mountain, she found herself thinking about that man again.
She remembered how carefully he chose his words, how cautious he was; she remembered the way the firelight flickered over his half-hidden face.
She hadn't really disliked him, even then.
He was nothing like her. He had grand ambitions, to govern, to bring peace to the world. She, on the other hand, only longed for freedom, to live by the sword and roam wherever she pleased.

But there was something steady about him, something that made her feel safe. Yes, steadiness. He'd listened patiently to all her tales of Jianghu, watched her ride off again and again without a word of complaint, always waiting for her return at every ferry. Even now, facing what might be their final parting, he remained the same.
"I have to get that Canglang Sword Manual. I won't be stopped!"
"How long will you be gone this time?"
"I don't know. If the snow blocks the mountain passes... who knows when I'll be back." She regretted those words as soon as she spoke them. She'd always left plenty of room for retreat, never once making a promise. But he'd always waited for her... and suddenly, she felt she shouldn't take that for granted anymore.
"Maybe... don't wait for me this time?"
Outside the temple, the rain poured down. Inside, the fire flickered. He was silent for a moment, then simply handed her a roasted sweet potato. "It's hot. Eat slowly."

That was the last time they parted. She never truly knew how he felt, but she'd made up her mind not to see him again when she returned. But with the Khitan invading and people displaced, she'd grown tired of her journey. And after exhaustion came longing.

The wind and snow still howled outside. But for a moment, everything seemed to pause.
Wei Zhixi felt it and looked up. The man who should have been a thousand miles away, who should have been leading his troops to pacify Huainan, was standing right there.
"I've come to take you home," he said.
Wei Zhixi was quiet for a moment, then smiled.
This time, the wild bird wanted to return to its nest.

zh:
惊蛰又至，忽忆昔年与公洛阳论道，岁月匆匆，竟已十载有余。
今鹤决于封龙山结庐授业。昔日知民之约，鹤且先行，公毋再言。墨轨周辙，各有其途，公当知，汝之言不入吾耳也。此番修书，亦非为道争，实有吉讯相告。
吾曾闻公门下有徒陈白，经术不堪用，德行不彰显，如此不孝堪为公之耻，鹤心甚忧之。你我既为知己，鹤自当为公分忧。鹤某不才，门下三子皆杰，于教之一道颇有心得，公当知也。
封龙山下有栾城一地，民生凋敝，朝廷视若藩外。此正可为吾等学问试行之所——观封龙星火，能照幽谷几何。邑中恰久缺县宰，簿牒刑名诸务，皆可为磨石。陈白虽不足宰栾城，亦聊胜于无，某不细较。盼公速遣其至此，吾自当为公淬锋。
en:
With Insects Awakening upon us once more, I suddenly find myself thinking back to the days when you and I debated the Dao in Luoyang. Time has flown. More than ten years have passed already.
I have now resolved to build my hut on Dragonbend Mountain and take in students there. As for that old vow to understand the people, I shall go ahead and put it into practice first, so you need not say another word. Mohist measures and Zhou roads each have their own course. You, of all people, should know by now that your arguments are wasted on me. I do not write this letter to reopen our old disputes over doctrine. I write because I have good news for you.
I have heard that among your disciples there is one Chen Bai, of little use in the classics and with no great virtue to show for himself. Such an unfilial pupil is enough to shame his master, and I confess it troubles me on your behalf. Since you and I are old friends, it is only fitting that I help lighten your burden. I, Crane, am no great talent, yet the three disciples under my care are all exceptional, and in the matter of teaching I do have some experience. You know that well enough.
At the foot of Dragonbend Mountain lies a place called Luancheng. The people there are destitute, and the court treats it as though it were beyond the borders. That makes it the very place for our learning to be tested. Let us see how far the spark of Mohist Hill can light a dark valley. The district has long been without a magistrate, and all the business of registers, documents, judgments, and punishments may serve as a whetstone. Chen Bai may not be enough to govern Luancheng well, but he is better than no one at all, and I will not be too particular. I hope you will send him here at once. I shall see to tempering him for you myself.

男女未冠笄者，鸡初鸣，咸盥漱，栉、𫄳，拂髦，总角，衿缨，皆佩容臭。昧爽而朝，问何食饮矣。若已食则退，若未食，则佐长者视具
凡内外，鸡初鸣，咸盥漱，衣服，敛枕簟，洒扫室堂及庭，布席，各从其事。
孺子蚤寝晏起，唯所欲，食无时。

en:
【Nei Ze, Chapter 12】

The sovereign and kings commanded the prime minister to teach virtue to all the people.
When a son serves his parents, at the first crow of the rooster, he washes his hands and rinses his mouth, combs his hair, ties it up with a hairpin and a ribbon, brushes his hair, puts on his cap, ties the tassels, wears his formal robes, knee covers, and sash, and tucks his tablet into his belt. On his left side, he carries a kerchief, a knife, a whetstone, a small pouch, and a metal fire-starter; on his right side, he carries a jade ring, an arm guard, a tube for writing, a sheath for a knife, a large pouch, and a wooden fire-starter. He wears shoes with laces tied.
When a wife serves her parents-in-law, it is like serving her own parents. At the first crow of the rooster, she washes her hands and rinses her mouth, combs her hair, ties it up with a hairpin and a ribbon, puts on her clothes and sash. On her left side, she carries a kerchief, a knife, a whetstone, a small pouch, and a metal fire-starter; on her right side, she carries needles, a tube for writing, thread, and silk floss, all placed in a small bag, along with a large pouch, a wooden fire-starter, and a sachet tied to her sash. She wears shoes with laces tied, and goes to the quarters of her parents-in-law. Upon arriving, she speaks in a gentle tone and asks whether they are warm or cold, whether they are ill or in pain, or have any itches, and respectfully tends to them. When they go out or come in, she walks before or behind them, respectfully supporting them. When presenting water for washing, the younger one holds the basin, the elder holds the water pitcher, and they ask to pour water for washing. After washing, they hand over a towel. They ask what is desired and respectfully present it, with a gentle expression to warm their hearts. Congee, millet drink, wine, sweet wine, vegetable soup, meat soup, beans, wheat, hemp seeds, rice, millet, sorghum, and glutinous millet—all are offered as desired. Dates, chestnuts, malt sugar, and honey are used to sweeten; mallow, rush, elm, and elm seeds, dried and fresh, are used to make it smooth; fat and oil are used to enrich it. Only after the parents and parents-in-law have tasted it do they withdraw.
For young men and women who have not yet undergone the capping or hairpin ceremonies, at the first crow of the rooster, they all wash their hands and rinse their mouths, comb their hair, brush it, tie it in two horns, and wear sachets, all carrying fragrant pouches. At dawn, they go to pay respects and ask what has been eaten or drunk. If the elders have already eaten, they withdraw; if not, they assist the elders in inspecting the preparations.
For all members of the household, both inside and outside, at the first crow of the rooster, they all wash their hands and rinse their mouths, put on their clothes, fold away the pillows and mats, sweep the rooms, halls, and courtyard, lay out the mats, and each attends to their own duties.
Young children go to bed early and rise late, doing as they please, eating at no fixed times.

zh:
【滕文公章句上】

滕文公为世子，将之楚，过宋而见孟子。孟子道性善，言必称尧、舜。
世子自楚反，复见孟子。孟子曰：世子疑吾言乎？夫道一而已矣。成𬑗谓齐景公曰：彼丈夫也，我丈夫也，吾何畏彼哉？颜渊曰：舜何人也？予何人也？有为者亦若是。公明仪曰：文王，我师也，周公岂欺我哉？今滕绝长补短，将五十里也，犹可以为善国。书曰：若药不瞑眩，厥疾不瘳。
滕定公薨，世子谓然友曰：昔者孟子尝与我言于宋，于心终不忘。今也不幸至于大故，吾欲使子问于孟子，然后行事。
然友之邹，问于孟子。孟子曰：不亦善乎！亲丧固所自尽也。曾子曰：生，事之以礼；死，葬之以礼，祭之以礼，可谓孝矣。诸侯之礼，吾未之学也；虽然，吾尝闻之矣：三年之丧，𪗋疏之服，𫗞粥之食，自天子达于庶人，三代共之。
然友反命，定为三年之丧。父兄百官皆不欲，曰：吾宗国鲁先君莫之行，吾先君亦莫之行也。至于子之身而反之，不可。且志曰：丧祭从先祖。曰：吾有所受之也。
谓然友曰：吾佗日未尝学问，好驰马试剑。今也父兄百官不我足也，恐其不能尽于大事，子为我问孟子。
然友复之邹，问孟子。
孟子曰：然，不可以佗求者也。孔子曰：君薨，听于冢宰，歠粥，面深墨，即位而哭，百官有司莫敢不哀，先之也。上有好者，下必有甚焉者矣。君子之德，风也，小人之德，草也。草尚之风必偃。是在世子。然友反命。
世子曰：然，是诚在我。
五月居庐，未有命戒。百官族人可谓曰知。及至葬，四方来观之，颜色之戚，哭泣之哀，吊者大悦。
滕文公问为国，孟子曰：民事不可缓也。诗云：昼尔于茅，宵尔索绹。亟其乘屋，其始播百谷。民之为道也，有恒产者有恒心，无恒产者无恒心。苟无恒心，放辟邪侈，无不为已。及陷乎罪，然后从而刑之，是罔民也。焉有仁人在位，罔民而可为也？是故贤君必恭俭礼下，取于民有制。阳虎曰：为富不仁矣，为仁不富矣。
夏后氏五十而贡，殷人七十而助，周人百亩而彻。其实皆什一也。彻者，彻也；助者，藉也。龙子曰：治地莫善于助，莫不善于贡。贡者，校数岁之中以为常。乐岁粒米狼戾，多取之而不为虐，则寡取之。凶年粪其田而不足，则必取盈焉。为民父母，使民盻盻然，将终岁勤动，不得以养其父母，又称贷而益之，使老稚转乎沟壑，恶在其为民父母也？夫世禄，滕固行之矣。诗云：雨我公田，遂及我私。惟助为有公田。由此观之，虽周亦助也。
设为庠序、学校以教之。庠者，养也；校者，教也；序者，射也。夏曰校，殷曰序，周曰庠。学则三代共之，皆所以明人伦也。人伦明于上，小民亲于下。有王者起，必来取法，是为王者师也。
诗云：周虽旧邦，其命惟新，文王之谓也。子力行之，亦以新子之国。使毕战问井地。

en:
【Teng Wen Gong, Chapter One】

When Prince Wen of Teng was heir apparent, on his way to Chu, he passed by Song and visited Mencius. Mencius spoke of the inherent goodness of human nature, always citing Yao and Shun as examples.
When the heir apparent returned from Chu, he visited Mencius again. Mencius said, "Does the heir apparent doubt my words? The Way is one and only one. Cheng Jian said to Duke Jing of Qi, 'He is a man; I am a man. Why should I be afraid of him?' Yan Yuan said, 'What kind of man was Shun? What kind of man am I? He who strives will be like him.' Gongming Yi said, 'King Wen is my teacher. How could the Duke of Zhou deceive me?' Now, if Teng, by cutting off the long and supplementing the short, can make a territory of nearly fifty li, it can still become a good state. The Book of Documents says, 'If the medicine does not cause dizziness, the disease will not be cured.'"
When Duke Ding of Teng passed away, the heir apparent said to Ran You, "Previously, Mencius spoke with me in Song, and I have never forgotten it in my heart. Now, unfortunately, we have encountered this great event. I wish to send you to inquire of Mencius before we proceed with the affairs."
Ran You went to Zou and asked Mencius. Mencius said, "Is this not good indeed! In mourning for parents, one should exert oneself to the utmost. Master Zeng said, 'In life, serve them according to ritual; in death, bury them according to ritual, and sacrifice to them according to ritual. This can be called filial piety.' As for the rituals of the feudal lords, I have not studied them. Nevertheless, I have heard of them: the three-year mourning period, wearing coarse hemp garments, eating congee—this applies from the Son of Heaven down to the common people, and was shared by the three dynasties."
Ran You returned with this reply, and it was decided to observe the three-year mourning. The elder relatives and all the officials were unwilling, saying, "Our ancestral state of Lu, its former rulers did not practice this; our former rulers also did not practice this. For you to reverse this now is not permissible. Moreover, the records say, 'Funerals and sacrifices follow the ancestors.' We say, 'We have received this tradition.'"
The heir apparent said to Ran You, "In the past, I never devoted myself to study, preferring to gallop on horses and test swords. Now, the elder relatives and officials do not consider me sufficient. I fear I cannot fulfill the great affair properly. Please inquire of Mencius for me."
Ran You went again to Zou and asked Mencius.
Mencius said, "Yes, one cannot seek it from others. Confucius said, 'When the ruler passes away, the heir apparent listens to the prime minister, drinks congee, his face deeply darkened, takes his position and weeps. Then none of the officials and officers dare not to grieve, for he has taken the lead.' Where those above have a preference, those below will certainly have it even more. The virtue of a gentleman is like the wind; the virtue of a petty man is like grass. When the wind blows over the grass, it must bend. This lies with the heir apparent." Ran You returned with this reply.
The heir apparent said, "Yes, it truly lies with me."
For five months he dwelt in the mourning hut, issuing no commands or prohibitions. The officials and clansmen could be said to understand. When it came to the burial, people came from all directions to observe. The sorrow in his countenance, the grief in his weeping—those who came to offer condolences were greatly pleased.
Prince Wen of Teng asked about governing a state. Mencius said, "The people's affairs cannot be delayed. The Book of Songs says: 'By day gather thatch; by night twist ropes. Hasten to repair the roof; soon you will sow the various grains.' For the people, the constant principle is this: those who have constant means of livelihood have constant hearts; those who lack constant means of livelihood lack constant hearts. If they lack constant hearts, they will become dissolute, depraved, and unrestrained, stopping at nothing. When they fall into crime, and only then punish them—this is to entrap the people. How can a benevolent man in position entrap the people? Therefore, a worthy ruler must be respectful, frugal, and courteous to his subordinates, taking from the people according to regulation. Yang Hu said, 'To be wealthy is not to be benevolent; to be benevolent is not to be wealthy.'"
"The Xia dynasty allotted fifty mu and levied a tribute; the Yin people allotted seventy mu and practiced the 'zhu' system; the Zhou people allotted one hundred mu and practiced the 'che' system. In essence, all were one-tenth. 'Che' means to penetrate; 'zhu' means to borrow. Master Long said, 'For governing the land, nothing is better than the 'zhu' system; nothing is worse than the tribute system.' The tribute system averages the harvest of several years to set a constant rate. In plentiful years, when grain is abundant, taking more is not oppressive, yet they take less. In lean years, even manuring the fields is insufficient, yet they insist on taking the full amount. As parents of the people, to make them toil anxiously all year, unable to support their own parents, and then to borrow more to make up the difference, causing the old and young to die in ditches—wherein lies their being parents of the people? As for hereditary salaries, Teng has long practiced them. The Book of Songs says: 'May the rain fall on our public fields, and then upon our private fields.' Only the 'zhu' system has public fields. From this perspective, even the Zhou dynasty used the 'zhu' system."
"Establish village schools, local schools, and academies to educate them. 'Xiang' means to nourish; 'xiao' means to teach; 'xu' means to shoot. The Xia called them 'xiao'; the Yin called them 'xu'; the Zhou called them 'xiang'. As for learning, the three dynasties shared it, all to illuminate human relationships. When human relationships are illuminated above, the common people will be affectionate below. Should a true king arise, he would certainly come to adopt these methods, making you a teacher for kings."
"The Book of Songs says: 'Although Zhou is an old state, its mandate is renewed.' This refers to King Wen. Strive to practice this, and it will also renew your state." He sent Bi Zhan to inquire about the well-field system.

zh:
按道理，阿九是不该和昙香这种醉花阴弟子走得太近的。
这人处处招摇，处处留情，又处处不留心，来得快，走得更快，徒留一道暗香朦胧的影子，只教人惆怅。就像是今日，分明是昙香先约的她楼中小酌，却又迟迟不见。
阿九暗地里计较过昙香无数回，可每回又忍不住在心里想——毕竟他们醉花阴弟子都是这样的，这会儿指不定在和什么好心肝碰面，我同那人计较什么？怎么偏偏看她更多生几分气恼？

那日神仙渡的花树下，她见昙香想要招徕一位俊秀游侠入醉花阴，出言相劝，邀那侠士入梨园，不料事过却被这醉花阴弟子缠上了，天天腻味在她身边，左一个品歌舞，右一个排戏文，两人如同双生花一般，日日长在了一块儿。
梨园中人于舞乐一道，重其技艺；而醉花阴之于歌舞，则偏重其中的情思。于昙香口中，阿九总能听到诸多不同于门内教坊的见解。
天下歌舞戏剧，形制殊异，大道却相通。她品评歌舞戏文时，整个人好似卸下了一层懒洋洋的风流外壳，流露出些更敏锐的神色，和平日里的气质恍若两人。每逢这种时刻，阿九总是呆呆地望着昙香，这世界上怎会有如此多面之人，教人忍不住对她多加猜想？
那人凝神望过来：“小心肝，怎么这么看着我，姐姐说的哪里不对？”
阿九怔住，老实说：“你，你说的很对……我只是不知道为什么，见着你这样，就说不出话来。”
昙香哑然，接而大笑，笑得整个人软在了阿九身上，怎么推也推不开。
梨园的兄弟姐妹们都说这是醉花阴弟子的风流手段，专门戏弄像她这样无知无觉的梨园弟子，可每每昙香邀约，阿九想横下心拒绝之时，只消抬眼一见昙香那笑眯眯的猫儿眼，又怎么也说不出口了。
罢了罢了，身入红尘，体味世情，本也是梨园弟子重要的修行。

窗外的花影纷乱，落英绕树，风吹又起。
阿九拧眉盯着眼前的话本，却怎么也看不下去，好像书里的爱啊恨啊都飘到了天上，而她的心里被什么别的东西填满了，乱得很，怎么也理不清。
她的目光从话本密密麻麻的字上，飘到了窗外一片孤零零的花瓣上，轻飘飘，慢悠悠，落在了地上——今日她怎么来得这么晚？莫非她不来了？
呸呸呸，阿九恼得大力晃了晃脑袋，不能再老是想着她的事了！——戏文，最重要的是眼前的戏文！
“叮铃铃——叮铃铃——”
听见那人身上熟悉的铃铛声，阿九又控制不住地马上抬起头望了过去。昙香拂去身上的落花，含笑盈盈地向她走了过来，似觉琼枝玉树，恰如那日相逢。
她携了一支洁白的梨花，带来了一场芬芳的雪。
春日长，燕飞忙。
若是能与眼前之人相伴一辈子，这因果里几分是嗔，几分是怜，几分是慕，几分是爱，似也不重要了。
en:
By all logic, Ajiu shouldn't be growing so close to someone like Tanxiang, a Velvet Shade disciple. 
Tanxiang is a restless spirit—flamboyant and flirtatious, yet somehow careless. She appears suddenly and vanishes even quicker, leaving behind only a faint, lingering fragrance that stirs bittersweet longing. Take today, for instance: it was clearly Tanxiang who invited Ajiu to a quiet drink in her quarters, yet she still hasn't arrived. 
Ajiu has silently wrestled with her frustrations toward Tanxiang countless times. Yet each time, she catches herself thinking—after all, this is how Velvet Shade disciples are. Perhaps she's off meeting some secret beloved. What's the point in resenting her? And yet, inexplicably, it's Tanxiang who stirs the deeper waves of annoyance in her heart. 

One day, beneath the blossom-laden tree at Heaven's Pier, Ajiu witnessed Tanxiang trying to recruit a dashing wanderer into Velvet Shade. She intervened, gently urging the wanderer to join the Masked Troupe instead. But to her surprise, after that day Tanxiang began shadowing her, lingering close—sometimes commenting on songs and dances, other times rehearsing scripts at her side. Like twin blossoms, they grew inseparable, their days entwined. 
Within the Masked Troupe, mastery of dance and music is prized above all. But for Velvet Shade, song and dance carry a weight of emotion and longing. Ajiu usually heard Tanxiang's perspectives that diverged beautifully from the sober teachings of the Masked Troupe. 
Theatrical styles and customs may differ, but their spirit is unified. When Tanxiang critiques a performance or a script, she seems to shed her usual languid charm, revealing a keener, more vibrant intensity—almost as if she were someone else entirely. In those fleeting moments, Ajiu would find herself quietly gazing at her, struck by Tanxiang's complexity, leaving her heart guessing and yearning. 
Noticing her stare, Tanxiang looked up, a knowing smile playing at her lips: "Why do you look at me like that, sweetheart? Did I say something wrong?" 
Ajiu blinked, caught off guard. "No, you're right... It's just that when I see you like this, I find myself speechless." 
Tanxiang laughed then, a soft, genuine sound that seemed to melt into Ajiu's very soul as she leaned in—willingly close—no matter how she tried to gently push her away. 
Everyone in the Masked Troupe said Tanxiang's charm was merely a flirtatious trick—a playful game Velvet Shade disciples liked to play on unsuspecting Masked Troupe novices like Ajiu. Yet every time Tanxiang extended an invitation, all it took was one glance into those softly smiling, cat-like eyes for Ajiu's resolve to melt away. 
Well, perhaps it was for the best. To walk the world and taste its joys and sorrows—that was part of a Masked Troupe disciple's true cultivation. 

Outside the window, flower shadows danced in gentle chaos, petals drifting around the trees, stirred again by the whisper of the breeze. 
Ajiu frowned, eyes fixed on the dense storybook before her, but no matter how hard she tried, she couldn't focus. The love and longing in the words seemed to rise and scatter into the sky, while her heart was filled with something altogether different—something tangled and restless, impossible to unravel. 
Her gaze lifted from the crowded lines to a solitary petal drifting slowly outside, floating down to rest on the ground. Why had she arrived so late today? Was she not coming at all? 
Enough, enough! Ajiu scolded herself, shaking her head firmly. She couldn't let her thoughts wander this way, not again. 
—No. The story before her, the script in her hands—that's what truly mattered. 
"Ding-ling, ding-ling." 
The familiar jingle caught her ear, and she looked up without thinking. Tanxiang brushed stray petals from her robes, her smile gentle and radiant, as graceful as the first time they met—like a living statue carved from porcelain. 
In her hand, a single pure white pear blossom, carrying with it a soft, fragrant snowfall. 
Spring stretches long, and busy swallows soar across the sky. 
If she could spend a lifetime beside the woman in front of her, then how much of their bond was impatience, tenderness, admiration, or love—it no longer made any difference. In the end, it was simply enough.

zh:
塞上某处酒家，伊刀和褚清泉坐在房檐之上。
伊刀不知喝了多少，说话瓮声瓮气，“呵！这人活一世，最、最该看重的是什么？”
伊刀转头看向一边的褚清泉，“问你话！”
“有人重义、有人重利，还有人呀……什么都不管不顾，只重信诺。”褚清泉慢悠悠地回话，说罢也抬起酒坛，喝了一大口。
“这话没错，我死人刀横行一世，不怕死！就怕去见爹娘的时候，被说是无信之徒！”
“放心，我可以见证。你这人，烂。但论守信重诺，没人比得过你！”
“哈哈哈哈哈！来，喝酒——！”
“别再喝了。若你酒后生事，闹出大动静，不好办。”
“娘的，絮絮叨叨，老子喝酒也碍你事！”
“这样吧，今日到此为止。我答应你，将来亲自敬你一坛上品离人泪。”
“一坛？”
“十坛。”
“好——一言为定。老子就信你这一回！”
褚清泉不再回话，斜靠在房瓦上，微醺地复诵着什么，声音不大。
伊刀听不清褚清泉在念什么，只觉磨烦，喝不到酒胸口不快，便摇晃着起身，拔刀醉舞。
 
很久之后，伊刀才会知道，当时褚清泉在吟咏的，是一首长诗。
“三杯吐然诺，五岳倒为轻……” 
“眼花耳热后，意气素霓生……”
 
褚清泉将《侠客行》吟罢，死人刀也将将舞完。
en:
At a tavern somewhere beyond the frontier, Yi Dao and Chu Qingquan sat perched upon the eaves.
Yi Dao had lost count of his cups, his voice thick and resonant with drink. "Hah! In this one life of ours... what is it that a man should prize above all else?"
He turned to Chu Qingquan. "I'm talking to you!"
"Some prize honor, others prize profit... and then there are those who forsake all else, prizing only a promise kept."
"Spot on! I, the Killerblade, fear nothing in this world, not even death! My only dread is facing my kin in the afterlife and being named a man of broken faith!"
"Rest easy. I shall bear witness. You are a scoundrel, to be sure, but when it comes to honoring a promise, no one does it better."
"Hahahaha! Come, drink!"
"Cease your drinking. If you stir up a storm in your cups, it will be a mess to settle."
"Confound it! Stop nagging. What's my drinking to you?"
"Let us end it here today. I promise you: one day, I shall personally toast you with a jar of the finest Parting Tears."
"One jar?"
"Ten."
"Fine, it's a deal. I'll take your word for it this once!"
Chu Qingquan offered no reply. Slumped against the tiles in a haze of wine, he began to chant something in a low murmur.
Yi Dao couldn't catch the words; he found it a nuisance. With the thirst still burning in his chest, he wobbled to his feet, unsheathed his blade, and danced a drunken dance.
Long after, Yi Dao would realize that what Chu Qingquan had been reciting was an ancient ballad.
"Three cups down, a promise is cast; the Five Great Peaks weigh light at last..." 
"With blurred eyes and ears aglow, a spirit like the white rainbow begins to grow..."
As the final lines of A Warrior's Journey faded, the Killerblade's dance reached its end.

【大传第十六】

礼，不王不禘。
王者禘。其祖之所自出，以其祖配之。诸侯及其大祖，大夫、士有大事，省于其君，干祫及其高祖。
牧之野，武王之大事也。既事而退，柴于上帝，祈于社，设奠于牧室，遂率天下诸侯，执豆笾，逡奔走，追王大王亶父、王季历、文王昌，不以卑临尊也。
上治祖祢，尊尊也；下治子孙，亲亲也。旁治昆弟，合族以食，序以昭缪，别之以礼义，人道竭矣。○圣人南面而听天下，所且先者五，民不与焉：一曰治亲，二曰报功，三曰举贤，四曰使能，五曰存爱。五者一得于天下，民无不足，无不赡者。五者一物纰缪，民莫得其死。圣人南面而治天下，必自人道始矣。立权度量，考文章，改正朔，易服色，殊徽号，异器械，别衣服，此其所得与民变革者也。其不可得变革者则有矣，亲亲也，尊尊也，长长也，男女有别，此其不可得与民变革者也。
同姓从宗，合族属，异姓主名，治际会，名著而男女有别。其夫属乎父道者，妻皆母道也。其夫属乎子道者，妻皆妇道也。谓弟之妻妇者，是嫂亦可谓之母乎？名者，人治之大者也，可无慎乎？
四世而缌，服之穷也；五世祖免，杀同姓也。六世，亲属竭矣。其庶姓别于上，而戚单于下，昏姻可以通乎？系之以姓而弗别，缀之以食而弗殊，虽百世而昏姻不通者，周道然也。
……
en:
【The Great Transmission, Chapter Sixteen】

According to the rites, only the king may perform the Di sacrifice; a king performs it to honor the origin of his ancestors, matching them with his own ancestor. Feudal lords may extend to their founding ancestor; great officers and scholars, when there are major events, must seek approval from their ruler before performing the combined Xia sacrifice extending to their great-great-grandfather.
At the field of Mu, King Wu accomplished a great deed. After the event, he withdrew, offered a burnt sacrifice to God on high, prayed at the altar of the soil, set up offerings in the chamber of Mu, and then led the feudal lords of the realm, bearing vessels and baskets, hastening in reverence, to honor King Tai, Danfu; King Ji, Lili; and King Wen, Chang—not allowing the humble to overshadow the noble.
Above, he regulated ancestors and fathers, honoring the honorable; below, he regulated descendants, cherishing the cherished. Sideways, he regulated brothers, uniting the clan through shared meals, ordering them by generation, distinguishing them with rites and righteousness—thus the way of humanity was fully realized. ○The sage, facing south, governs the realm; five matters take precedence, and the people are not among them: first, regulating kinship; second, rewarding merit; third, promoting the worthy; fourth, employing the capable; fifth, preserving goodwill. If these five are all achieved in the realm, the people will lack nothing and have no insufficiency. If any of these five is flawed or erroneous, the people will not meet a proper end. The sage, facing south, governs the realm, necessarily beginning from the way of humanity. Establishing weights and measures, examining writings and regulations, correcting the calendar, changing ceremonial colors, distinguishing insignia, altering implements, and differentiating garments—these are matters that can be changed with the people. But there are things that cannot be changed: cherishing the cherished, honoring the honorable, respecting the elder, and distinguishing between male and female—these cannot be altered with the people.
Those of the same surname follow the clan lineage, uniting the kin; those of different surnames are governed by titles, regulating interactions—when titles are clear, the distinction between male and female is maintained. If a husband belongs to the category of fathers, his wife belongs to the category of mothers; if a husband belongs to the category of sons, his wife belongs to the category of daughters-in-law. To call a younger brother's wife a daughter-in-law—can an elder brother's wife then be called a mother? Titles are the great foundation of human governance; how can one not be cautious?
After four generations, mourning is reduced to the fine hemp, the limit of mourning garments; after five generations, one wears the unhemmed mourning sash, cutting off ties with the same surname. After six generations, kinship ties are exhausted. When collateral branches are distinguished above and affection diminishes below, can marriages be arranged between them? Binding them by surname without distinction, connecting them through shared meals without separation—even after a hundred generations, marriages are not permitted; such is the way of the Zhou.

雩真，你素来聪慧胜我，剑术胜我，心性胜我，却何以甘从执剑之人，沦为他人手中之剑呢？
冬夜雪地，天地虚白，你从公主府摇摇晃晃而来，一身血染。我把很多很多药敷在你身上，也把很多很多话砸向你，痛苦的话，愤怒的话，伤人的话，无济于事的话。
而你只是垂着头，不发一言。
我知道，我治不好你的病了。于是雪停的时候，我走了。
冬日暖阳如火，善照天下有情人、有怨事。只是它照不到我了，雩真。
en:
My master always said that ailments of the heart are the hardest to cure, for they run long and deep. You didn't believe it. You found someone you thought could cure you: Princess Taiping. Her daughter.
The Princess said, "You and Master Wuliang are just like me and the Empress." You caught the faintest glimpse of her mother in her, and threw yourself right in.
Yuzhen, you've always been smarter than me, a better swordswoman, stronger of heart. So why were you content to go from wielder of swords to a sword wielded by another?
That snowy winter night, when the world was a void of white, you staggered out of the Princess's manor, drenched in blood. I put so much medicine on your wounds, threw so many words at you. Words of pain, words of anger. Words meant to hurt. Words of no avail.
But you just hung your head in silence.
I knew then I couldn't cure you. So when the snow stopped, I left.
The winter sun burns like fire, shining on all the lovers and grievances in the world. But, Yuzhen, it no longer shines on me.

This treasured sword, which Lan Ao paid a fortune for and later shattered in defiance, was once wielded by famed masters. 

The warrior wearied by service to a corrupt lord had lost touch with his own formidable palm technique. 
Bestowed the Autumn Water sword along with political favor, he abandoned his palms for steel. 
The sword was what preserved his dignity, the last thing that allowed him to call himself a "hero." 
But in the end, he surrendered even that—offering it up to a disgraced minister. 
Dress it up however one likes, the truth remains: it was servitude, quiet and humbled.

As the respite draws near, Kaifeng Prefecture issues three rules: 
First, merchants and owners should understand workers' needs and not skimp on benefits. 
Second, wanderers should practice righteousness and not attempt to coerce businesses into operating.
Third, celebrations of dancing and singing are encouraged in neighbourhoods as long as laws are not violated. 
This decree is hereby announced. Please be advised.

第二天，她发现自己怀孕了。

en:
She dug the boy out of the sand, casually tossing a freshly made Qianghuang flower pendant onto his face. 
Breathing in its cool fragrance, the boy awoke and from then on never left her side. 
At a tea stall with smoke curling up, the woman quietly made pendants. The man bustled about, stealing glances at her between tasks. 
That night the wind was fierce. She dreamed of her childhood self. 
Sand rising to her chest again, she waved her arms, clutching a cool Qianghuang flower, stubbornly dragging herself toward an unextinguished lamp. 
The next day, she discovered she was pregnant. 
Nightmares again seized her nights. Unable to sleep, she left half a note and set out alone to find peace.

en: Fengqiu Gate was the western gate on the northern wall of Kaifeng city, capital of the Later Liang during the Five Dynasties period. In the first year of the Tongguang era under the Later Tang, Li Siyuan's army marched on Daliang through Fengqiu Gate. Later, in the third year of the Tian Fu era under the Later Jin, it was renamed once again as "Xuanyang Gate," though common folk still referred to it as Fengqiu Gate.

zh:
【先进第十一】

子曰：“先进于礼乐，野人也；后进于礼乐，君子也。如用之，则吾从先进。”
子曰：“从我于陈、蔡者，皆不及门者也。”
子曰：“德行：颜渊、闵子骞、冉伯牛、仲弓。言语：宰我、子贡。政事：冉有、季路。文学：子游、子夏。
子曰：“回也，非助我者也，于吾言无所不说。”
子曰：“孝哉！闵子骞。人不间于其父母兄弟之言。”
南容三复白圭，孔子以其兄之子妻之。
季康子问：“弟子孰为好学？”孔子对曰：“有颜回者好学，不迁怒，不贰过，不幸短命死矣。今也则亡，未闻好学者也。”
颜渊死，颜路请子之车。子曰：“才不才，亦各言其子也。鲤死，有棺而无椁，吾不可徒行以为之椁。以吾从大夫之后，吾以不可徒行也。”
颜渊死，子曰：“噫！天丧予？天丧予！”
颜渊死，子哭之恸。从者曰：“子恸矣！”子曰：“有恸乎？非夫人之为恸，而谁为恸？”
颜渊死，门人欲厚葬之。子曰：“不可。门人厚葬之。”子曰：“回也视予犹父也，予不得视犹子也。非我也，夫二三子也！”
季路问事鬼神。子曰：“未能事人，焉能事鬼？”曰：“敢问事死。”曰：“未知生，焉知死？”
闵子骞侍侧，訚訚如也。子路，行行如也。冉子、子贡，侃侃如也。子乐。若由也，不得其死然。
鲁人为长府。闵子骞曰：“仍旧贯，如之何？何必改作？子曰：“夫人不言，言必有中。”
子曰：“由之鼓瑟，奚为于丘之门？门人不敬子路。子曰：“由也升堂矣，未入于室也。”
子贡问：“师与啇也孰贤乎？”子曰：“师也过，啇也不及。”曰：“然则师愈与？”子曰：“过犹不及也。”
季氏富于周公，而求也为之聚敛而附益之。子曰：“非吾徒也。小子鸣鼓而攻之，可也。”
柴也愚，参也鲁。师，僻也。由，唁也。
子曰：“回也其庶乎！屡空。赐不受命，而货殖焉，忆则屡中。”
子张问善人之道。子曰：“不践迹，亦不入于室。”
子曰：“论笃是与？君子者乎？色庄者乎？”

en:
【Book XI, Xian Jin】

The Master said, "The men of former times, in the matters of ceremonies and music, were rustics, it is said, while the men of these latter times, in ceremonies and music, are accomplished gentlemen. If I have occasion to use those things, I follow the men of former times."
The Master said, "Of those who were with me in Chen and Cai, there are none to be found to enter my door."
The Master said, "Exemplary in virtuous conduct were Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Boniu, and Zhonggong; in speech, Zai Wo and Zigong; in government affairs, Ran You and Ji Lu; in literature and culture, Ziyou and Zixia."
The Master said, "Hui gives me no assistance. There is nothing that I say in which he does not delight."
The Master said, "Filial indeed is Min Ziqian! Other people say nothing of him different from the report of his parents and brothers."
Nan Rong was frequently repeating the lines about a white scepter stone. Confucius gave him the daughter of his elder brother to wife.
Ji Kang asked which of the disciples loved to learn. Confucius replied to him, "There was Yan Hui who loved to learn. He did not transfer his anger; he did not repeat a fault. Unfortunately, his appointed time was short and he died. Now there is no one. I have not yet heard of anyone who loves to learn."
When Yan Yuan died, Yan Lu begged the carriage of the Master to sell and get an outer shell for his son's coffin. The Master said, "Every one calls his son his son, whether talented or not talented. There was Li; when he died, he had a coffin but no outer shell. I would not walk on foot to get a shell for him, because I followed after the high officers, I could not well walk on foot."
When Yan Yuan died, the Master said, "Alas! Heaven is destroying me! Heaven is destroying me!"
When Yan Yuan died, the Master bewailed him exceedingly, and the disciples who were with him said, "Master, your grief is excessive!" "Is it excessive?" said he. "If I am not to mourn bitterly for this man, for whom should I mourn?"
When Yan Yuan died, the disciples wished to give him a great burial, and the Master said, "You may not do so." The disciples did bury him in great style. The Master said, "Hui behaved towards me as his father. I have not been able to treat him as my son. The fault is not mine; it belongs to you, O disciples."
Ji Lu asked about serving the spirits of the dead. The Master said, "While you are not able to serve men, how can you serve their spirits?" Ji Lu added, "I venture to ask about death?" He was answered, "While you do not know life, how can you know about death?"
The disciple Min was standing by his side, looking bland and precise; Zilu, looking bold and soldierly; Ran You and Zigong, with a free and straightforward manner. The Master was pleased. He said, "You, there!—he will not die a natural death."
Some parties in Lu were going to take down and rebuild the Long Treasury. Min Ziqian said, "Suppose it were to be repaired after its old style—why must it be altered and made anew?" The Master said, "This man seldom speaks; when he does, he is sure to hit the point."
The Master said, "What has the lute of You to do in my door?" The other disciples began not to respect Zilu. The Master said, "You has ascended to the hall, though he has not yet passed into the inner apartments."
Zigong asked which of the two, Shi or Shang, was the superior. The Master said, "Shi goes beyond the due mean, and Shang does not come up to it." "Then," said Zigong, "the superiority is with Shi, I suppose." The Master said, "To go beyond is as wrong as to fall short."
The head of the Ji family was richer than the duke of Zhou had been, and yet Qiu collected his imposts for him, and increased his wealth. The Master said, "He is no disciple of mine. My little children, beat the drum and assail him."
Chai is simple. Shen is dull. Shi is specious. You is coarse.
The Master said, "There is Hui! He has nearly attained to perfect virtue. He is often in want. Ci does not acquiesce in the appointments of Heaven, and his goods are increased by him. Yet his judgments are often correct."
Zizhang asked what constituted the excellent man. The Master said, "He does not tread in the footsteps of others, but moreover, he does not enter the chamber of the sage."
The Master said, "If, because a man's discourse appears solid and sincere, we allow him to be a good man, is he really a superior man? or is his gravity only in appearance?"
Zilu asked whether he should immediately carry into practice what he heard. The Master said, "There are your father and elder brothers to be consulted—why should you act on that principle of immediately carrying into practice what you hear?" Ran You asked the same, whether he should immediately carry into practice what he heard, and the Master answered, "Immediately carry into practice what you hear." Gongxi Hua said, "You asked whether he should carry immediately into practice what he heard, and you said, 'There are your father and elder brothers.' Qiu asked whether he should immediately carry into practice what he heard, and you said, 'Carry it immediately into practice.' I, Chi, am perplexed, and venture to ask you for an explanation." The Master said, "Qiu is retiring and slow; therefore, I urged him forward. You has more than his own share of energy; therefore, I kept him back."

The final record was complete as the rumble of Khitan hooves drew closer. Chai Sang felt fear, yet also a sense of release.
He hid his logs near the dry well. Fearing Elder Peng might miss them upon his return, he cut his palm and left a faint trail of blood from the well-mouth all the way into the house.
